context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is a brilliant defense of a core Christian doctrine—divine immutability (that God is unchanging)—within the context of the Trinity.
1. The Work Itself: The Dialogue

St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) was a great synthesizer of patristic theology. This work is a polemical dialogue written to refute Manichaeism. The Manicheans were dualists; they believed in two co-eternal, uncreated first principles: a good God of light and spirit, and an evil god of darkness and matter. For them, the material world was the creation of the evil principle.
2. The Immediate Argument in the Dialogue

The full text you provided shows the Manichean character setting a logical trap for the Orthodox Christian:

    The Manichean's Premise: An eternal, uncreated being must be unchangeable (ἄτρεπτον). If it changes, it means it began to be something it wasn't before, which would mean it isn't truly eternal.

    The Manichean's "Gotcha" Question: "So what about your God? Didn't He change when He begot a Son and brought forth a Spirit? Wasn't there a time He wasn't a Father, and then He became a Father? If so, your God changed and is not truly eternal and unchangeable."

        This is a classic Arian-style argument, repurposed by the Manichean character to attack the Christian God.

3. The Theological Importance of the Orthodox Response (Your Quote)

St. John's response is the classic orthodox refutation of this error, and it is the heart of your quote:

    Denial of Change: The Orthodox speaker starts with an emphatic "By no means!" (Οὐδαμῶς).

    Rejection of a Temporal "Becoming": He clarifies, "I do not say, 'Not being a Father previously, He later became a Father.'" This rejects the idea that God's Fatherhood is an event in time.

    The Eternal Relations: The core of the answer is that the Trinity does not involve change because the relationships are eternal.

        ἀεὶ ἦν πατὴρ ("He was always Father"). God's Fatherhood is not something He acquires. It is part of His eternal nature.

        ἔχων ἐξ αὑτοῦ τὸν αὐτοῦ λόγον ("having from Himself His Word"). The Son (the Word) is not created in time but is eternally generated from the Father.

        διὰ τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ ... τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ ἐκπορευόμενον ("through His Word... His Spirit issuing forth"). The Holy Spirit is not created in time but eternally proceeds from the Father through the Son.

In summary, you have found a masterful passage where St. John of Damascus defends the Trinity by explaining that the generation of the Son and the procession of the Spirit are not temporal events that imply change in God. Rather, they are the eternal, unchanging, and internal relations that constitute the very being of the one, immutable God.

en: Likewise we believe also in one Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life God existing and addressed along with Father and Son: uncreated, full, creative, all-ruling, all-effecting, all-powerful, of infinite power, Lord of all creation and not under any Lord; deifying, not deified; filling, not filled; shared in, not sharing in; sanctifying, not sanctified; the intercessor, receiving the supplications of all; in all things like the Father and Son, proceeding from the Father and communicated through the Son [Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 1:8 (c. A.D. 746)].

context:
Additional Relevant Context

    The Work: St. John of Damascus's Exposition of the Orthodox Faith is not a polemical work written against a specific heresy (like St. Gregory's Against Eunomius). Instead, it is the first great systematic theology or summa of the Greek Fathers. St. John masterfully gathers and synthesizes centuries of Orthodox teaching into a single, coherent whole.

    The Chapter (Book 1, Chapter 8): The massive text you posted is the entire chapter. This chapter is famous for being one of the most comprehensive and concise explanations of the Holy Trinity ever written. It is structured like the Creed:

        It begins by defining the one God.

        It then discusses God the Father as the sole source.

        It moves to a long and detailed explanation of God the Son and His eternal generation.

        Finally, it culminates in the paragraph you were looking for—a rich and powerful summary of the person and work of the Holy Spirit.

    Theological Importance: This passage is a cornerstone of Eastern Orthodox pneumatology (theology of the Holy Spirit). Note the precise language:

        "Proceeding from the Father" (ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον): This is the classic formula based on John 15:26, affirming the Father as the sole eternal source or cause of the Spirit's personhood.

        "Communicated through the Son" (δι' υἱοῦ μεταδιδόμενον): This is the classic Eastern understanding of the Son's role in the Spirit's mission. The Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father alone but is revealed, sent, and given to creation through the Son. This formula preserves the Father's monarchy while affirming the intimate and inseparable relationship of the Son and Spirit.

You have located a foundational text from the last of the great Greek Church Fathers, a passage that summarizes the Trinitarian faith of the ecumenical councils.

en: And the Holy Spirit is the power of the Father revealing the hidden mysteries of his divinity, proceeding from the Father through the Son in a manner known to himself, but different from that of generation [ibid., 12].
greek: Τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐκφαντορικὴ τοῦ κρυφίου τῆς θεότητος δύναμις τοῦ πατρός, ἐκ πατρὸς μὲν δι' υἱοῦ ἐκπορευομένη, ὡς οἶδεν, οὐ γεννητῶς...
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The full text you provided is even more valuable because it shows exactly what St. John is doing in this chapter. He is systematically outlining the distinctive properties (idiomata) of each of the three divine Persons to show how they are distinct from one another, yet united in a single divine essence.

Here is the context based on the full passage you found:

    The Father as Sole Cause: St. John begins by defining the Father as the "super-essential sun," the "fountain of goodness," and the "abyss of essence." Critically, he calls the Father the source who is a "begetter of the Word (the Son)" and, "through the Word, the producer of the revealing Spirit." For St. John, and for Orthodox theology as a whole, the Father is the sole source, principle, and cause (αἰτία) within the Godhead.

    The Son as Begotten: The Son is defined by His relationship to the Father. He is the "begotten" Word, Wisdom, and Power of the Father. He is from the Father.

    The Holy Spirit as Proceeding (Your Quote): Your quote fits in here. The Holy Spirit is defined by His unique relationship to the Father.

        He is the "revealing power" (ἐκφαντορικὴ... δύναμις), manifesting the hidden things of God.

        His mode of origin is "procession" (ἐκπορευομένη), which is explicitly stated to be "not by way of generation" (οὐ γεννητῶς). This preserves the unique status of the Son as the only-begotten.

        His procession is "from the Father through the Son" (ἐκ πατρὸς... δι' υἱοῦ). This is the classic Orthodox formula. It means the Father is the sole ultimate source of the Spirit's being, but the Son is intimately involved in that eternal procession. This is distinct from the Western Filioque clause, which states the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from a single principle. St. John clarifies this later in the paragraph: the Spirit is called the "Spirit of the Son," not because He proceeds from the Son, but because He proceeds through Him from the Father, for "the Father alone is cause" (μόνος γὰρ αἴτιος ὁ πατήρ).

In essence, you have found a perfect, concise summary of the Cappadocian Fathers' Trinitarian theology, brilliantly synthesized and systematized by St. John of Damascus. This passage clearly defines the Father as the sole Cause, the Son as the eternally Begotten, and the Spirit as the eternally Proceeding.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR There will be no other God, Trypho, nor was there from eternity any other. but he who made this universe. Nor do we think that there is one God for us and another for you, but that he alone is God who led your fathers out of Egypt with a strong hand and a high arm. Nor have we trusted in any other, for there IS no other, but him, in whom you also have trusted, the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob [Dialogue with Trypho 11 C. A.D. 155)].
greek: Οὔτε ἔσται ποτὲ ἄλλος θεός, ὦ Τρύφων, οὔτε ἦν ἀπ' αἰῶνος ... πλὴν τοῦ ποιήσαντος καὶ διατάξαντος τόδε τὸ πᾶν. οὐδὲ ἄλλον μὲν ἡμῶν, ἄλλον δὲ ὑμῶν ἡγούμεθα θεόν, ἀλλ' αὐτὸν ἐκεῖνον τὸν ἐξαγαγόντα τοὺς πατέρας ὑμῶν ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου ἐν χειρὶ κραταιᾷ καὶ βραχίονι ὑψηλῷ: οὐδ' εἰς ἄλλον τινὰ ἠλπίκαμεν, οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν, ἀλλ' εἰς τοῦτον εἰς ὃν καὶ ὑμεῖς, τὸν θεὸν τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακώβ.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The rest of the Greek text you provided is absolutely crucial. Immediately after establishing this common ground—that Christians and Jews worship the same one God—St. Justin makes a dramatic pivot to explain the fundamental difference.

The argument unfolds in these steps:

1. The Point of Departure: The Law of Moses is Not the Way

Justin immediately follows the quote by saying:

    "But we have not hoped through Moses or through the Law; for then we would have done the same thing as you."

    (ἠλπίσαμεν δὲ οὐ διὰ Μωυσέως οὐδὲ διὰ τοῦ νόμου: ἦ γὰρ ἂν τὸ αὐτὸ ὑμῖν ἐποιοῦμεν.)

This is the core of his argument. He agrees on who God is but disagrees on how humanity is to be saved and united with Him.

2. The New Law and the New Covenant

Justin then argues that the Law of Moses was temporary and particular, whereas Christ has established a universal and eternal covenant.

    "For I have read, O Trypho, that there would be a final law and a covenant more sovereign than all, which now all men must keep who seek the inheritance of God. For the law given at Horeb is already old and for you alone, but this one is for all, absolutely."

He is declaring that the Mosaic Covenant has been superseded by the New Covenant in Christ.

3. Proof from the Jewish Prophets

To prove his point from Scripture that Trypho would accept, Justin quotes two key passages:

    Isaiah 51:4-5: "...for a law will go forth from me, and my judgment for a light to the nations... the nations will hope in my arm."

    Jeremiah 31:31-32: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant which I made with their fathers..."

By using these prophets, Justin argues that the Jewish scriptures themselves predicted the obsolescence of the Mosaic Law and the coming of a new, universal covenant for all nations.

4. The Climax: The Church is the New Israel

Finally, Justin makes his most radical claim: the Christians, gathered from all nations through the crucified Christ, are the true fulfillment of God's promises.

    "For the true, spiritual Israel, and the descendants of Judah, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham... are we, who have been led to God through this crucified Christ."

He redefines what it means to be "Israel," shifting the identity from ethnic lineage to faith in Christ, just as Abraham himself was justified by faith.

In Summary: The full passage you provided is a perfect example of early Christian apologetics. Justin begins by building a bridge of common ground (monotheism), then walks across it to deliver his main point: that Christ is the fulfillment of the prophecies, the bringer of the New Covenant, and the founder of the true, spiritual Israel.

en: [WJe too would observe the fleshly circumcision, and the Sabbaths, and in short all the feasts, if we did not know for what reason they were enjoined [on] you-namely, on account of your transgressions and the hardness of your heart. . . . [H]ow is it, Trypho, that we would not observe those rites that do not harm us-I speak of fleshly circumcision and Sabbaths and feasts? . . . God enjoined you to keep the Sabbath, and imposed on you other precepts for a sign, as I have already said, on account of your unrighteousness and that of your fathers [Dialogue with Trypho 18, 21 (c. A.D. 155)].

context:
Additional Relevant Context

The block of text you provided (Chapters 18-21) contains the core of St. Justin's argument for why Christians do not observe the ceremonial precepts of the Mosaic Law. The context is a debate with Trypho, a learned Jew, who has challenged the Christians on this very point.

Here is the flow of Justin's argument across these chapters:

1. Chapter 18: The Law as a Remedial Measure for Israel.
Justin lays out his central thesis: The ceremonial laws (circumcision, Sabbath, feasts, dietary rules) were not given as universal and eternal requirements for righteousness. They were given specifically to the Jewish people for a remedial reason: "on account of your transgressions and the hardness of your heart." He makes a powerful rhetorical point: Christians are willing to suffer martyrdom for their faith. Why would they refuse to observe something as simple as the Sabbath if they believed it was God's universal will? The fact that they don't shows that they understand its purpose was temporary and specific to Israel.

2. Chapter 19: The Witness of the Righteous before Moses.
This is a classic argument used by the early Church Fathers. To prove that the Mosaic Law was not the only path to righteousness, Justin lists numerous figures who were considered righteous by God before the Law was given at Sinai. These include:

    Adam, Abel, Enoch, Lot, and Noah: All were uncircumcised and did not keep the Sabbath, yet they were pleasing to God.

    Melchizedek: He was an uncircumcised priest to whom Abraham himself, the father of circumcision, paid tithes.
    This proves that God's favor is not dependent on these physical rites.

3. Chapter 20: The Purpose of the Dietary Laws.
Justin applies the same logic to the dietary restrictions. He argues they were not given because certain animals are inherently "unclean," but to constantly remind the Israelites of God, since they were "prone and quick to depart from the knowledge of Him." He explicitly links this to their apostasy with the golden calf in the desert. The laws were a pedagogical tool for a people prone to idolatry.

4. Chapter 21: The Prophetic Proof from Ezekiel.
Justin concludes his argument by bringing in the testimony of the prophet Ezekiel. He quotes Ezekiel 20, which explicitly states that the Sabbath was given as a "sign" (σημεῖον) between God and Israel. This reinforces his point that it was a specific marker for a particular covenant, not a universal moral law. He then delivers his most powerful scriptural proof by quoting a shocking verse from Ezekiel 20:25:

    "And I gave them precepts that were not good, and ordinances in which they shall not live."

Justin uses this to argue that God, dealing with a rebellious people, gave them a harsh law that, while holy, was a law of discipline rather than the ultimate law of life and grace that would come through Christ.

In essence, Justin's entire argument is that the ceremonial law was a temporary and pedagogical covenant for Israel, made necessary by their sinfulness. With the coming of Christ and the establishment of the New Covenant, the "signs" of the old one have been fulfilled and are no longer necessary for the People of God.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR Hence God speaks by the mouth of Malachi, one of the twelve [prophets ], as I said before, about the sacrifices at that time presented by you: I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord; and I will not accept your sacrifices at your hands: for, from the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same, my name has been glorified among the Gentiles, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the Gentiles, says the Lord: but you profane it" [Mal 1:10-12]. [So] he then speaks of those Gentiles, namely us, who in every place offer sacrifices to him, that iS, the bread of the Eucharist, and also the cup of the Eucharist [Dialogue with Trypho 41 (C. A.D. 155)7.
greek: ...ὅθεν περὶ μὲν τῶν ὑφ' ὑμῶν τότε προσφερομένων θυσιῶν λέγει ὁ θεός, ὡς προέφην, διὰ Μαλαχίου, ἑνὸς τῶν δώδεκα: Οὐκ ἔστι θέλημά μου ἐν ὑμῖν, λέγει κύριος, καὶ τὰς θυσίας ὑμῶν οὐ προσδέξομαι ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν ὑμῶν: διότι ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς ἡλίου ἕως δυσμῶν τὸ ὄνομά μου δεδόξασται ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι, καὶ ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ θυμίαμα προσφέρεται τῷ ὀνόματί μου καὶ θυσία καθαρά, ὅτι μέγα τὸ ὄνομά μου ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι, λέγει κύριος, ὑμεῖς δὲ βεβηλοῦτε αὐτό. περὶ δὲ τῶν ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ὑφ' ἡμῶν τῶν ἐθνῶν προσφερομένων αὐτῷ θυσιῶν, τοῦτ' ἔστι τοῦ ἄρτου τῆς εὐχαριστίας καὶ τοῦ ποτηρίου ὁμοίως τῆς εὐχαριστίας, προλέγει τότε...
context:
Additional Relevant Content and Context

The rest of the Greek text you provided is crucial for understanding St. Justin's full argument. He is using a method called typology, where people, events, and rituals in the Old Testament are seen as prefiguring the realities of the New Covenant.
1. Context from the Beginning of the Passage (Before the Malachi Quote)

    Καὶ ἡ τῆς σεμιδάλεως δὲ προσφορά... τύπος ἦν τοῦ ἄρτου τῆς εὐχαριστίας...

    "And the offering of fine flour... which was prescribed to be offered for those cleansed of leprosy, was a type (τύπος) of the bread of the Eucharist..."

Relevance: St. Justin doesn't just pull the Malachi prophecy out of thin air. He first establishes his method by pointing to an Old Testament ritual—the flour offering for a cleansed leper (Leviticus 14:10)—and explicitly states that it was a type, or prefigurement, of the Eucharistic bread. This sets the stage for his argument that Old Testament prophecies also point to the Eucharist.
2. Context from the End of the Passage (After the Malachi Quote)

    ἡ δὲ ἐντολὴ τῆς περιτομῆς, κελεύουσα τῇ ὀγδόῃ ἡμέρᾳ... τύπος ἦν τῆς ἀληθινῆς περιτομῆς, ἣν περιετμήθημεν... διὰ τοῦ ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἀναστάντος τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων ἡμέρᾳ...

    "And the commandment of circumcision, which commanded that infants be circumcised on the eighth day, was a type (τύπος) of the true circumcision by which we are circumcised from error and wickedness through Jesus Christ our Lord, who rose from the dead on the first day of the week..."

Relevance: After interpreting Malachi, Justin immediately provides another example of typology. He argues that circumcision on the eighth day prefigured Christian baptism and the new life received through Christ's resurrection on Sunday (which he refers to as the "eighth day," following the seven-day week). This reinforces that his interpretation of Malachi is part of a consistent interpretive framework for the entire Old Testament.
3. Theological Significance of the Passage

    The Eucharist as a Sacrifice: This is one of the earliest and most explicit non-biblical texts that identifies the Eucharist as a sacrifice (θυσία). This became a foundational doctrine for the Catholic and Orthodox Churches.

    Fulfillment of Prophecy: Justin's primary goal is to convince Trypho the Jew that Christianity is the true fulfillment of the Jewish scriptures. He uses the prophecy of Malachi to argue that God Himself foretold the rejection of the Temple sacrifices and their replacement by a new, universal, and "pure" sacrifice.

    Universality of the Church: The prophecy's reference to offerings "in every place" and "among the Gentiles" is key for Justin. It proves that the new covenant is not limited to Jerusalem or the Jewish people, but is global, celebrated by Christians everywhere.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR God speaks in the creation of man with the very same design, in the following words: "Let us make man after our image and likeness.' I shall quote again the words narrated by Moses himself, from which we can indisputably learn that [God] conversed with someone distinct from himself and also rational being. But this offspring who was truly brought forth from the Father, was with the Father before all the creatures, and the Father communed with him [Dialogue with Trypho 62 (c. A.D. 155)].

    ...ἀλλὰ τοῦτο τὸ τῷ ὄντι ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς προβληθὲν γέννημα πρὸ πάντων τῶν ποιημάτων συνῆν τῷ πατρί, καὶ τούτῳ ὁ πατὴρ προσομιλεῖ...
context:
Additional Relevant Content and Context

In this chapter, St. Justin Martyr is making a sophisticated argument to his Jewish dialogue partner, Trypho. His primary goal is to prove from the Hebrew Scriptures that the God who created the world is not a solitary monad, but that He had a divine companion with whom He spoke. This companion, Justin argues, is the Son or Logos of God.

Here is a step-by-step breakdown of Justin's argument in the full text you provided:

1. The Primary Proof-Text: Genesis 1:26
Justin begins by quoting the creation of man: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." He emphasizes the plural pronouns ("us," "our") as evidence that God the Father was speaking to another person.

2. Anticipating and Refuting Jewish Interpretations
Justin is a skilled debater. He knows what Trypho will say, so he addresses the common Jewish interpretations of this verse first:

    Objection 1: God was speaking to Himself. Justin dismisses this as illogical.

    Objection 2: God was speaking to the elements (earth, water, etc.). Justin also finds this absurd.

    Objection 3 (The most common one): God was speaking to the angels. This is the main argument he needs to defeat.

3. The Knock-Down Argument: Genesis 3:22
To demolish the "God spoke to angels" theory, Justin introduces a second, even more powerful proof-text. After the Fall, God says, "Behold, Adam has become like one of us."

    Justin's Logic: God would never say this to angels. To say "one of us" implies that the speaker and the one spoken to are of the same kind or class. It would be blasphemous for God to group Himself with created angels in this way.

    His Conclusion: Therefore, the Person God was speaking to must also be divine. This proves He was speaking to "someone who was numerically distinct from himself and also a rational being" of a divine nature.

4. The Theological Climax: Identifying the Divine Companion
Having proven that God spoke to another divine being, Justin then identifies who this being is:

    "But this offspring who was truly brought forth from the Father, was with the Father before all the creatures, and the Father communed with him."

Here, Justin identifies this divine companion as the Logos (Word/Reason) of God, whom he calls an "offspring" (γέννημα) "brought forth" (προβληθὲν) from the Father before all creation. This is a cornerstone of Logos-Christology. He explicitly connects this figure to "Wisdom" from the book of Proverbs.

5. Further Corroboration: Joshua 5
As a final piece of evidence, Justin brings up the account of Joshua meeting the "Commander of the army of the LORD." He points out that this figure accepted worship from Joshua and that the ground He stood on was holy—actions and attributes appropriate only for God. Justin identifies this Commander as another appearance of the pre-incarnate Son.

In summary, this chapter is a masterclass in early Christian apologetics, demonstrating how the first Christian thinkers used the Hebrew Scriptures to argue for the plurality of Persons within the one Godhead, long before the formal language of the Trinity was developed at Nicaea.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR For as Adam was told that on the day he ate of the tree he would die. we know that he did not complete a thousand years. We have perceived, moreover, that the expression "The day of the Lord is as thousand years" is connected with this subject [Dialogue with Trypho 81 (c. A.D. 155)].

context:
2. Additional Relevant Context

The passage you quoted is the interpretive key to the entire chapter. Justin Martyr is making a sophisticated argument for a literal 1000-year reign of Christ on earth (a belief known as premillennialism or chiliasm). Here is the flow of his logic in Chapter 81:

    Prophetic Basis (Isaiah): He begins by quoting a long passage from Isaiah 65, which describes a new heaven and a new earth where people will live long, peaceful lives in a renewed Jerusalem. This is his Old Testament foundation for a future, earthly kingdom.

    The "Tree of Life" and the 1000 Years: Justin focuses on a specific phrase from the Isaiah prophecy: "For as the days of the tree of life, so shall be the days of my people." He sees this as a mystical reference pointing back to Genesis and signifying a 1000-year period.

    The Adam Typology (Your Quote): This is where your quote comes in. Justin uses a typological argument to prove that a "divine day" equals 1000 years.

        The Problem: God told Adam, "in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die" (Gen 2:17). But Adam lived to be 930 years old. How could he die "on that day"?

        Justin's Solution: He connects this with Psalm 90:4 (and 2 Peter 3:8), "a day of the Lord is as a thousand years." Therefore, the "day" on which Adam was sentenced to die was a 1000-year period. Since Adam died at 930, he did indeed die within that first divine day, thus fulfilling the prophecy in a mystical sense.

    New Testament Confirmation (St. John): Having established his interpretive principle, Justin provides New Testament proof. He explicitly refers to the Book of Revelation:

        "And further, a certain man among us, whose name was John, one of the apostles of Christ, in a revelation made to him, prophesied that those who have believed in our Christ would spend a thousand years in Jerusalem."

    Distinction from the Final State: Justin is careful to distinguish this 1000-year earthly kingdom from the final, eternal state. He concludes the chapter by noting that after the millennium, the universal and eternal resurrection will occur, at which point believers will be "like the angels," no longer marrying or giving in marriage (quoting Jesus from Luke 20:35-36).

In summary, your quote is the central pillar of Justin's argument, using Adam's lifespan to prove the "day = 1000 years" principle, which he then applies to prophecies about the Millennial Kingdom.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR For the prophetical gifts remain with us [Christians], even to the present time. And hence you [Jews] ought to understand that [the gifts] formerly among your nation have been transferred to us [Dialogue with Trypho 82 (c. A.D. 155)].
greek: Παρὰ γὰρ ἡμῖν καὶ μέχρι νῦν προφητικὰ χαρίσματά ἐστιν, ἐξ οὗ καὶ αὐτοὶ συνιέναι ὀφείλετε, ὅτι τὰ πάλαι ἐν τῷ γένει ὑμῶν ὄντα εἰς ἡμᾶς μετετέθη.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This single sentence is packed with theological and historical importance. Here's what makes it so significant, based on the rest of the chapter you provided and the broader context of Justin's work.
Immediate Context (What Justin says next)

Immediately after making this bold claim, Justin anticipates Trypho's objection by qualifying his statement. He shows that the transfer of gifts is not perfect or without problems:

    The Parallel of False Prophets: Justin immediately adds, "Just as there were false prophets among the holy prophets who were with you, so now there are also many false teachers among us." This is a crucial admission. He isn't claiming the Christian community is perfect, but that it mirrors the experience of ancient Israel, which had both true and false prophets.

    Christ's Prophecy as Proof: He argues that the existence of these false teachers was actually prophesied by Christ himself. This turns a potential weakness (heresy and division) into a strength, framing it as yet another fulfillment of prophecy and a sign of Christ's divine foreknowledge.

    The Moral Obligation to Speak: Justin explains why he is engaging in this debate. He cites the prophet Ezekiel's duty as a "watchman" for the house of Israel. He feels a divine obligation to speak the truth to Trypho and his fellow Jews, lest he be held accountable by God for their error. This frames the dialogue not as an academic debate, but as a matter of eternal consequence.

Broader Theological and Historical Context

    Argument for Fulfillment (Supersessionism): This is a classic and early example of what is often called "fulfillment theology" or "supersessionism." Justin's core argument throughout the Dialogue is that the Christian Church is the true inheritor of the promises and spiritual life of Israel. The presence of the prophetic spirit, which he claims had ceased in Judaism, is his "living proof" that God's favor has been transferred (μετετέθη) to the Church.

    The Continuing Presence of Charismatic Gifts: This passage is invaluable historical evidence that Christians in the mid-2nd century (c. A.D. 155) still believed in and claimed to witness the active presence of charismatic gifts like prophecy. It powerfully counters the later theological view that such gifts ceased with the death of the last apostle. For Justin, the gifts were a present and verifiable reality.

    Defining Christian Identity: At this time, Christianity was still working to define its own identity in relation to its parent religion, Judaism. Justin's statement is a bold declaration of independence and succession. He is arguing that the Church is not merely a Jewish sect, but is the true and universal People of God, validated by the presence of the Holy Spirit.

In summary, you have found a crucial passage that is central to Justin's argument for the Church as the true people of God, evidenced by the continuing presence of the Holy Spirit's prophetic gifts.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR [Jesus] became man by the Virgin so that the course that was taken by disobedience in the beginning through the agency of the serpent might also be the course by which it would be put down. Eve, a virgin and undefiled, conceived the word of the serpent and bore disobedience and death. But the Virgin Mary received faith and joy when the angel Gabriel announced to her the glad tidings that the Spirit of the Lord would come upon her and the power of the most high would overshadow her, for which reason the holy one being born of her is the Son of God. And she replied, "Be it done unto me according to your word" [Lk 1:38] [Dialogue with Trypho 100 (C. A.D. 155)].
greek: ...καὶ διὰ τῆς παρθένου ἄνθρωπος γεγονέναι, ἵνα καὶ δι' ἧς ὁδοῦ ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως παρακοὴ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἔλαβε, διὰ ταύτης τῆς ὁδοῦ καὶ κατάλυσιν λάβῃ. παρθένος γὰρ οὖσα Εὔα καὶ ἄφθορος, τὸν λόγον τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως συλλαβοῦσα, παρακοὴν καὶ θάνατον ἔτεκε· πίστιν δὲ καὶ χαρὰν λαβοῦσα Μαρία ἡ παρθένος, εὐαγγελιζομένου αὐτῇ Γαβριὴλ ἀγγέλου ὅτι πνεῦμα κυρίου ἐπ' αὐτὴν ἐπελεύσεται καὶ δύναμις ὑψίστου ἐπισκιάσει αὐτήν, διὸ καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἐξ αὐτῆς ἅγιόν ἐστιν υἱὸς θεοῦ, ἀπεκρίνατο: Γένοιτό μοι κατὰ τὸ ῥῆμά σου. καὶ διὰ ταύτης γεγέννηται οὗτος...
context:
Theological Context and Importance

This passage is famous for establishing the Eve/Mary Parallel, a concept later developed more fully by St. Irenaeus of Lyons. Justin's argument is one of perfect theological symmetry, often called "recapitulation":

    Eve:

        A virgin.

        Through disobedience to God's word, she listened to the word of the serpent.

        Her action brought death into the world.

    Mary:

        A virgin.

        Through obedience to God's word, she listened to the word of the angel.

        Her action brought Life (the Son of God) into the world.

Mary's faithful and joyful "Yes" (Γένοιτό μοι... - "Let it be done to me...") is presented as the antidote that "unties the knot" of Eve's disobedience.
The Context of the Rest of Chapter 100

The first part of the Greek text you provided sets the stage for this beautiful conclusion. In it, Justin Martyr argues that:

    Christ is the true "Israel."

    He is the fulfillment of prophecies about Joseph and Judah.

    He is the Son to whom the Father has handed everything.

    He is the "First-born of God," pre-existing all creation.

    He became the "Son of Man" through his birth from the Virgin Mary, who descends from the line of the patriarchs.

It is this final point—Christ becoming man through the Virgin—that leads him directly into the powerful Eve/Mary parallel to explain the profound theological reason for the Incarnation happening in this specific way. You have found a cornerstone text of early Christian theology.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR And more than all other men are we your helpers and allies in promoting peace, seeing that we hold this view, that it is impossible for the wicked, the covetous, the conspirator, and for the virtuous to escape the notice of God, and that each man goes to everlasting punishment or salvation according to the value of his actions. For if all men knew this, no one would choose wickedness even for a little, knowing that he goes to the everlasting punishment of fire; but would by all means restrain himself, and adorn himself with virtue, that he might obtain the good gifts of God, and escape the punishments [First Apology 12 (c. A.D. 151)].
greek: Ἀρωγοὶ δ' ὑμῖν καὶ σύμμαχοι πρὸς εἰρήνην ἐσμὲν πάντων μᾶλλον ἀνθρώπων, οἳ ταῦτα δοξάζομεν, ὡς λαθεῖν θεὸν κακόεργον ἢ πλεονέκτην ἢ ἐπίβουλον ἢ ἐνάρετον ἀδύνατον εἶναι, καὶ ἕκαστον ἐπ' αἰωνίαν κόλασιν ἢ σωτηρίαν κατ' ἀξίαν τῶν πράξεων πορεύεσθαι. εἰ γὰρ οἱ πάντες ἄνθρωποι ταῦτα ἐγίνωσκον, οὐκ ἄν τις τὴν κακίαν πρὸς ὀλίγον ᾑρεῖτο, γινώσκων πορεύεσθαι ἐπ' αἰωνίαν διὰ πυρὸς καταδίκην, ἀλλ' ἐκ παντὸς τρόπου ἑαυτὸν συνεῖχε καὶ ἐκόσμει ἀρετῇ, ὅπως τῶν παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τύχῃ ἀγαθῶν καὶ τῶν κολαστηρίων ἀπηλλαγμένος εἴη.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

To fully appreciate this passage, it's crucial to understand its purpose, audience, and the specific arguments Justin is making.

1. The Audience: An Appeal to the Roman Emperor
Justin is not writing to fellow Christians. He is writing a formal legal and philosophical defense addressed directly to the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius, his adopted sons (including the future emperor Marcus Aurelius), and the Roman Senate. His goal is to stop the unjust persecution of Christians by proving that they are rational, moral, and loyal subjects.

2. The Argument: Christianity as a Source of Social Stability
This is the core of the passage. Justin makes a powerful political and sociological argument. He flips the accusation that Christians are dangerous subversives on its head.

    "Helpers and allies in promoting peace" (Ἀρωγοὶ... καὶ σύμμαχοι πρὸς εἰρήνην): This is a brilliant rhetorical move. He claims that far from being enemies of the state, Christians are the empire's greatest asset in maintaining peace and order.

    A Higher Moral Law: Why are they such good citizens? Because their morality is not based merely on fear of human laws. A criminal can hope to escape the notice of the Roman authorities (λανθάνειν ὑμᾶς δυνατὸν ἐπιστάμενοι). However, Christians believe it is impossible (ἀδύνατον) to escape the notice of an all-seeing God.

3. The Power of Divine Judgment
The key to this superior morality is the Christian doctrine of final judgment.

    Eternal Consequences: Justin states plainly that every person "goes to everlasting punishment or salvation according to the value of his actions" (ἐπ' αἰωνίαν κόλασιν ἢ σωτηρίαν κατ' ἀξίαν τῶν πράξεων).

    A Powerful Deterrent: He argues that if everyone truly believed this, society would be transformed. No one would choose wickedness, "knowing that he goes to the everlasting punishment of fire" (αἰωνίαν διὰ πυρὸς καταδίκην). The fear of eternal damnation is a far more effective deterrent to crime than the fear of temporal execution.

4. The Rest of the Chapter (What Comes After Your Quote)
The remainder of the Greek text you provided builds on this argument with sharp logic and even sarcasm:

    He contrasts the fallible justice of men with the perfect justice of God.

    He mockingly suggests that the Romans seem afraid that if everyone became virtuous, they would run out of people to punish, which he says is the logic of an executioner, not a good ruler.

    He concludes by grounding these teachings in the authority of Jesus Christ, whose prophecies have been fulfilled, proving his divine authority and the truth of his moral commands.

In summary, this passage is a masterstroke of apologetics. Justin is not just defending Christian theology; he is promoting it as a practical solution to the empire's own problems of crime and social disorder, framing Christians as the ultimate model citizens.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR Our teacher of these things is Jesus Christ, who also was born for this purpose, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate, procurator of Judaea, in the times of Tiberius Caesar; and that we reasonably worship him, as he is the Son of the true God himself, and holding him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third, we will prove. For they proclaim our madness to consist in this, that we give to a crucified man a place second to the unchangeable and eternal God, the Creator of all: for they do not discern the mystery herein, to which, as we make it plain to you, we pray you to give heed [First Apology 13 (c. A.D. 151)].
greek: ...τὸν διδάσκαλόν τε τούτων γενόμενον ἡμῖν καὶ εἰς τοῦτο γεννηθέντα Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, τὸν σταυρωθέντα ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου, τοῦ γενομένου ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ ἐπὶ χρόνοις Τιβερίου Καίσαρος ἐπιτρόπου, υἱὸν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ὄντως θεοῦ μαθόντες καὶ ἐν δευτέρᾳ χώρᾳ ἔχοντες, πνεῦμά τε προφητικὸν ἐν τρίτῃ τάξει ὅτι μετὰ λόγου τιμῶμεν ἀποδείξομεν. ἐνταῦθα γὰρ μανίαν ἡμῶν καταφαίνονται, δευτέραν χώραν μετὰ τὸν ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀεὶ ὄντα θεὸν καὶ γεννήτορα τῶν ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπῳ σταυρωθέντι διδόναι ἡμᾶς λέγοντες, ἀγνοοῦντες τὸ ἐν τούτῳ μυστήριον, ᾧ προσέχειν ὑμᾶς ἐξηγουμένων ἡμῶν προτρεπόμεθα.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is a brilliant defense of Christian worship, addressing several key pagan objections simultaneously. Here is the context:

    The Charge of Atheism: The very first words of the Greek chapter you provided are Ἄθεοι μὲν οὖν ὡς οὔκ ἐσμεν... ("That we are not atheists..."). This is the immediate context. Christians were accused of atheism because they refused to worship the Roman gods. Justin's entire argument here is to prove they are not atheists by explaining precisely who they worship. They worship the Creator of all, but they do so in a specific, revealed way.

    The Historical Anchor: Justin is not talking about a mythical figure. He deliberately grounds Jesus in real, verifiable Roman history for his audience (the Emperor and the Senate). He names the Roman procurator Pontius Pilate and the Emperor Tiberius Caesar. This is a key apologetic move: he is saying, "This is not a fairy tale; this happened within your own recorded history."

    A Foundational Proto-Trinitarian Formula: This is one of the most important early, extra-biblical statements about the Trinity. Justin lays out a clear hierarchy of worship:

        First Place: The Creator God, the Father (implied as "the true God himself").

        Second Place: Jesus Christ, the Son.

        Third Place: The Prophetic Spirit.
        This "Father, Son, and Spirit" structure is foundational to Christian Trinitarian theology. While it is not the fully developed doctrine of later councils, it is a clear and powerful witness to the Trinitarian shape of Christian worship in the mid-second century.

    Confronting the "Scandal of the Cross": Justin directly tackles the single greatest objection a Roman pagan would have: the worship of a crucified man. To the Roman mind, crucifixion was the most shameful and degrading death imaginable, reserved for slaves and the worst criminals. To worship someone who suffered this fate seemed like "madness" (μανίαν). Justin acknowledges this perceived absurdity head-on.

    The Appeal to "Mystery": How does Justin resolve this "madness"? He doesn't try to rationalize it away in a simple sentence. Instead, he calls it a "mystery" (μυστήριον). This is an invitation. He is telling his highly educated Roman audience: "You think this is foolish because you do not yet understand the profound divine plan at work. Give us your attention, and we will explain the mystery of the cross to you." This sets the stage for the rest of his apology, where he will use philosophy and prophecy to unfold this very mystery.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR Concerning chastity, [Jesus] uttered such sentiments as these: "Whosoever looks upon a woman to lust after her. has committed adultery with her already in his heart before God." And, "If your right eye offend you, cut out; for it is better for you to enter into the kingdom of heaven with one eye, than, having two eyes, to be cast into everlasting fire." And, "Whosoever shall marry her that is divorced from another husband commits adultery." And, "There are some who have been made eunuchs of men, and some who were born eunuchs, and some who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake; but all cannot receive this saying" [Mt 19:12]. So that all who, by human law, are twice married, and those who look upon a woman to lust after her, are in the eye of our master sinners. For not only he who in act commits adultery is rejected by him, but also he who desires to commit adultery: since not only our works, but also our thoughts, are open before God [First Apology 15 (c. A.D. 151)].

context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is a cornerstone of Justin's defense of Christianity to the Roman authorities. To understand its full impact, we need to consider his audience and purpose.

    Audience and Purpose: St. Justin is writing his First Apology to the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius and the Roman Senate. He is defending Christians against slanderous accusations of atheism, cannibalism, and, most relevant here, sexual immorality (incestuous orgies). His goal is to prove that, far from being immoral, Christians adhere to a moral code that is vastly superior to that of the surrounding Greco-Roman culture.

    Radical Interior Morality: The most powerful element of Justin's argument is the shift from external actions to internal thoughts. Roman law punished the act of adultery (ἔργῳ), but Justin shows that Jesus condemns even the desire (βουλόμενος) and the lustful thought (ἐνθυμήματα). This was a radical concept. He is telling the Emperor that Christian morality is so profound that it purifies the very source of human action: the heart and mind.

    Direct Contrast with Roman Law: Justin makes a pointed comment about "those who, by human law, are twice married" (οἱ νόμῳ ἀνθρωπίνῳ διγαμίας ποιούμενοι). Divorce and remarriage were common and perfectly legal under Roman law. Justin is directly contrasting the permissive "human law" of the Empire with the higher, stricter law of Christ. This is a bold claim to make to the very people who create and enforce that human law.

    A Broader Argument for Christian Virtue: The full text of Chapter 15, which you provided, shows that Justin doesn't stop with chastity. He immediately continues by quoting Jesus's teachings on radical love for enemies, boundless charity to the needy, and detachment from material wealth. By presenting this string of demanding ethical teachings, Justin paints a picture of Christians as the ideal citizens: peaceful, generous, chaste, and honest. This is his ultimate apologetic point: a religion that produces such virtuous people is an asset to the Empire, not a threat, and should be tolerated and respected.

en: But, as we said above, wicked devils perpetrated these things. And we have learned that only those are deified who have lived near God in holiness and virtue; and we believe that those who live wickedly and do not repent are punished in everlasting fire (ibid., 21).

context:
Additional Relevant Context

To understand the power of this quote, you have to see the argument Justin is building throughout the rest of the chapter.

1. The Strategy of Comparison (Synkrisis):
Justin begins by listing pagan myths that resemble Christian teachings. He says to his Roman audience:

    We teach that Jesus, the Word, is the first-begotten of God, was crucified, died, rose, and ascended to heaven. But this is nothing new compared to your so-called "sons of Jupiter."

    You have Hermes, the interpreting "word" (logos).

    You have Asclepius, a healer who was struck by a thunderbolt and then ascended to heaven.

    You have Dionysus, who was torn apart.

    You have Heracles, who gave himself to fire to escape his pains.

    You even deify your dead emperors, producing a witness who swears he saw the Caesar ascending to heaven from the funeral pyre.

His point is: "If you believe all of these stories, why do you single out our story of a divine Son's death and ascension for persecution?"

2. The Moral "Turn":
After showing these surface-level similarities, Justin makes a sharp and devastating turn. He points out the profound immorality of the pagan myths.

    The so-called gods were held up as role models, yet they were depraved.

    Jupiter himself was a patricide, overcome by wicked lusts, and an adulterer with countless women.

    His sons followed his evil example.

    Justin declares that any sane person would be repulsed by such stories about the gods.

3. The Explanation and Climax (Your Quote):
This is where your quote comes in and provides the climax to his argument.

    "But, as we said above, wicked devils perpetrated these things." This is Justin's famous theory of "demonic imitation." He argues that demons, having read the prophecies of the Old Testament, created distorted and immoral counterfeit versions of the Christ story in pagan mythology before Christ came. They did this specifically so that when the true story was told, people would dismiss it as just another myth.

    "And we have learned that only those are deified who have lived near God in holiness and virtue..." This is the ultimate moral contrast. The pagan gods achieved their status through violence, lust, and trickery. In Christianity, Justin argues, immortality and union with God ("deification") is the reward for a life of holiness and virtue.

    "...and we believe that those who live wickedly and do not repent are punished in everlasting fire." This final statement completes the moral framework. Unlike the pagan system where wicked gods are praised, the Christian system promises eternal justice: reward for the righteous and punishment for the unrepentant wicked.

In short, your quote is the powerful conclusion to an argument where Justin both neutralizes Roman prejudice by showing similarities and claims the ultimate moral high ground by highlighting the stark differences in virtue and justice.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR Jesus Christ is the only proper Son who has been begotten by God, his Word and first-begotten, and power; and, becoming man according to his will, he taught us these things for the conversion and restoration of the human race [First Apology 23 (c. A.D. 151)].
greek: καὶ Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς μόνος ἰδίως υἱὸς τῷ θεῷ γεγέννηται, λόγος αὐτοῦ ὑπάρχων καὶ πρωτότοκος καὶ δύναμις, καὶ τῇ βουλῇ αὐτοῦ γενόμενος ἄνθρωπος ταῦτα ἡμᾶς ἐδίδαξεν ἐπ' ἀλλαγῇ καὶ ἐπαναγωγῇ τοῦ ἀνθρωπείου γένους
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This single sentence is one of the most doctrinally rich statements in the entire Apology. To understand its full significance, we can look at three layers of context:
1. Immediate Context (What is Justin arguing in this chapter?)

Right before this sentence, Justin makes a bold claim: Christian teachings, learned from Christ and the prophets, are the "only truths" and are "older than all the writers who have ever lived." He insists that Christians don't ask for their beliefs to be accepted just because they resemble some pagan ideas, but because they are true.

The sentence you quoted is the reason for this unique claim. Christian teaching is uniquely true because its teacher, Jesus Christ, is a unique being: the "only proper Son of God."

Immediately after your quote, Justin anticipates an objection: "But don't your stories sound like our myths about the sons of Zeus?" Justin's answer is that evil demons, knowing the prophecies about Christ, preemptively created counterfeit myths through the pagan poets to discredit the truth when it finally appeared.

So, your quote is the central pillar of the chapter's argument: The uniqueness of the Teacher (Christ) guarantees the uniqueness of the Teaching.
2. Broader Context (The Purpose of the First Apology)

Justin is writing to the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons. His goal is to defend Christianity against charges of atheism and immorality and to present it as the true philosophy. To do this, he must use concepts that his philosophically educated audience would understand. This is why the titles he uses for Christ in this passage are so significant.
3. Theological Significance (The Key Titles for Christ)

This sentence is a miniature Christology. Let's break down the titles Justin uses:

    μόνος ἰδίως υἱὸς (mónos idíōs huiós) — "Only Proper Son": This is Justin's crucial qualifier. The pagan world was full of stories of "sons of gods." Justin uses the adverb ἰδίως (properly, specially, in a unique sense) to draw a sharp line. Jesus is not a son of God like Hercules or Dionysus; His sonship is of a completely different and unique category.

    λόγος (Lógos) — "Word": This is Justin's most famous and influential concept. For his Greek audience, the Logos was the universal divine Reason that ordered the cosmos and was the source of all human rationality. By identifying Jesus as the Logos, Justin makes a brilliant apologetic move:

        He argues that Christianity is the ultimate rational faith.

        He can claim that whatever truth was found in great pagan philosophers like Socrates and Plato was due to the "seed of the Logos" within them. They had a part of the Truth; Christians have the whole Truth, the Logos Himself incarnate.

    πρωτότοκος (prōtótokos) — "First-begotten": A term drawn from Scripture (e.g., Colossians 1:15). It emphasizes Christ's pre-eminence over all creation. He is not a creature but was begotten of the Father before all created things.

    δύναμις (dýnamis) — "Power": This title emphasizes Christ's divine capability and his role as the active agent of God in creation and salvation.

    τῇ βουλῇ αὐτοῦ γενόμενος ἄνθρωπος ("becoming man according to his will"): Justin emphasizes that the Incarnation was a deliberate and free act of the divine will for a specific purpose: the salvation of humanity (ἐπ' ἀλλαγῇ καὶ ἐπαναγωγῇ - for our change and restoration).

In summary, you have identified a foundational passage where St. Justin Martyr defines the uniqueness of Jesus Christ using both biblical and philosophical language to present him as the sole divine teacher of the ultimate truth.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR [W]e have been taught that to expose newborn children is the part of wicked men; and this we have been taught lest we should do anyone an injury, and lest we should sin against God, first, because we see that almost all so exposed (not only the girls, but also the males) are brought up to prostitution. And as the ancients are said to have reared herds of oxen, or goats, or sheep, or grazing horses, so now we see you rear children only for this shameful use; and for this pollution a multitude of females and hermaphrodites, and those who commit unmentionable iniquities, are found in every nation. And you receive the hire of these, and duty and taxes from them, whom you ought to exterminate from your realm. And anyone who uses such persons, in addition to the godless and infamous and impure intercourse, may possibly be having intercourse with his own child, or relative, or brother. And there are some who prostitute even their own children and wives, and some are openly mutilated for the purpose of sodomy; and they refer these mysteries to the mother of the gods [First Apology 27 (c. A.D. 151)1.

context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is not just a moral statement; it is a sophisticated and devastating piece of social and religious critique aimed directly at the Roman Emperor and Senate, to whom the Apology is addressed.

1. The Roman Practice of Infant Exposure: In the Roman world, infant exposure (expositio) was a common and legally permitted practice. The head of the household (pater familias) had the right to decide whether to raise a newborn child. Unwanted infants—often girls, or those with disabilities—were frequently left outside to die of exposure or be taken by slave traders. Justin frames this socially acceptable practice as an act of profound wickedness, a radical departure from Roman norms.

2. Justin's "Turning the Tables" Strategy: Christians were falsely accused of heinous crimes, including cannibalism (misunderstanding the Eucharist) and incestuous orgies (misunderstanding the "holy kiss" and calling each other "brother" and "sister"). Justin's strategy here is brilliant: he points out that the Roman system itself creates the very evils they accuse Christians of.

    You accuse us of killing children? You legally expose your own children to die or, worse, to be trafficked.

    You accuse us of incest? Your system of exposure and prostitution creates a situation where a man could unknowingly commit incest with the very child he abandoned years earlier.

3. The Link Between Exposure and Prostitution: Justin creates an unbreakable logical chain. He argues that infant exposure is not just a passive act of abandonment but the direct source of supply for the Roman sex trade. He chillingly compares the breeding of livestock to the "rearing" of these abandoned children for the sole purpose of sexual exploitation.

4. The Complicity of the State: Justin's most audacious claim is that the Roman state is not a neutral party but an active participant in this depravity. By levying taxes and fees on brothels and prostitutes (μισθοὺς καὶ εἰσφορὰς καὶ τέλη λαμβάνετε - "you receive hire and duties and taxes"), the government profits from the very evil it should be eradicating. This is a direct accusation against the emperors he is addressing.

5. Connecting Social Vice to Pagan Religion: The final stroke of genius is linking this immorality to Roman religion. He mentions those who are "mutilated for the purpose of sodomy" and connect "these mysteries to the mother of the gods." This is a clear reference to the cult of Cybele, a major state-sanctioned goddess whose male priests, the Galli, were famously castrated in ecstatic rituals. By doing this, Justin argues that the sexual brokenness of the Empire is not just a social problem but is rooted in and sanctioned by its own religion.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR We have learned from the prophets, and we believe it is true, that punishments, and chastisements, and good rewards. are rendered according to the merit of each man's actions. context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is one of the earliest and most important Christian defenses of free will. To understand its full impact, we need to look at the immediate problem Justin is solving and the broader philosophical environment he was in.

1. The Immediate Problem: Prophecy vs. Fatalism

In the chapters immediately preceding this one (chapters 30-42), Justin has been making a powerful case for the truth of Christianity by demonstrating how Jesus Christ fulfilled the prophecies of the Old Testament. However, he is a sharp enough thinker to realize how a philosophically trained Roman or Greek would interpret this.

His hypothetical opponent would argue: "If your prophets foreknew and foretold future events, then those events must happen by necessity. Therefore, you Christians are simply believers in fate (heimarmenē), and human actions are not free."

Chapter 43 is Justin's direct answer to this charge. The very first sentence of the chapter, which you provided, sets this up: "Lest some should think from what we have said that we claim things happen by necessity of fate, because they were foreknown and foretold, we will now solve this difficulty."

2. The Philosophical Backdrop: Stoicism and Free Will

The dominant philosophy among educated Romans in the 2nd century was Stoicism. The Stoics had a highly developed concept of fate (heimarmenē) as an unbreakable chain of cause and effect, which they often identified with the divine reason (logos) governing the cosmos. The debate over whether true human freedom could exist within this system was a major philosophical topic.

Justin is deliberately engaging with this well-known debate. He uses the standard philosophical terms:

    εἱμαρμένη (heimarmenē): The Greek philosophical term for fate or destiny.

    τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν (to eph' hēmin): Literally "what is up to us," the classic philosophical term for free will or moral agency.

By refuting fatalism, Justin is showing his educated audience that Christianity is not a crude, deterministic religion but a philosophically robust system that upholds human dignity and moral responsibility.

3. The Core Christian Argument: Moral Responsibility and a Just God

The heart of Justin's argument, captured in your quote, is that morality and justice depend entirely on free will.

    No Free Will, No Morality: If a person is fated to be good or evil, then concepts like "merit," "praise," and "blame" are meaningless. You cannot praise a rock for falling downwards or blame a fire for burning.

    A Just God Requires Free Will: For God to justly reward the virtuous and punish the wicked, human beings must be the true authors of their actions. If God punished someone for an act they were fated to commit, He would be a tyrant, not a just judge.

As he continues in the chapter, Justin makes it clear that God created humanity differently from inanimate objects ("trees and four-footed beasts") precisely by endowing us with the power of free choice (προαίρεσις, prohairesis), which makes us worthy of praise or blame.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR We have been taught that Christ is the firstborn of God, and we have declared that he is the Word of whom every race of men are partakers; and those who live reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them; and among the barbarians, Abraham. and Ananias, and Azarias, and Misael, and Elias, and many others whose actions and names we now decline to recount, because we know it would be tedious. So that even those who lived before Christ, and lived without reason, were wicked and hostile to Christ, and slew those who lived reasonably. But he who, through the power of the Word, according to the will of God the Father and Lord of all, was born of a Virgin as a man, and was named Jesus, and was crucified, and died. and rose again, and ascended into heaven, ar intelligent man will be able to comprehend from what has been said [First Apology 46 (c. A.D. 151)].

context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is not just a standalone thought; it's a brilliant solution to a specific problem Justin faces in his apology to the Roman Emperor.

1. The Problem: The "Chronological Objection"
Justin begins the chapter by anticipating a major criticism: "How can Christianity be the one true faith if your founder, Christ, was born only 150 years ago? What about all the generations of people who lived before him? Are they all condemned without a chance?" (This is what he means by πρὸ ἐτῶν ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα γεγεννῆσθαι τὸν Χριστὸν λέγειν ἡμᾶς - "that we say Christ was born 150 years ago").

2. The Solution: The Doctrine of the Logos Spermatikos
Justin’s answer is profound. He argues that Christ is the eternal Logos (Word/Reason) of God, the very principle of rationality and truth that has been active in the world since creation.

    Logos: Christ is the universal, divine Reason.

    Spermatikos: "Seed-bearing." This Logos has planted "seeds" (sperma) of truth and reason throughout all of humanity, in every culture and every age.

Therefore, anyone in history who lived "with reason" (μετὰ λόγου - meta logou) was, in fact, living in accordance with the "seed" of Christ the Logos within them. This makes them, in a real sense, "Christians before Christ."

3. The Examples: Bridging Greek Philosophy and Hebrew Scripture
Justin’s choice of examples is a masterstroke of apologetics:

    The Greeks (Socrates, Heraclitus): By naming the most revered figures of Greek philosophy, Justin tells his educated Roman audience, "Your greatest thinkers, whom you admire for seeking truth through reason, were on our side! They were following the partial light of the same Christ we now know in His fullness. And like us, they were persecuted for it." Socrates, who was executed for "atheism" and "corrupting the youth," becomes a proto-martyr.

    The Barbarians (Abraham, Elias, etc.): By "barbarians," a Greek term for non-Greeks, Justin means the righteous figures of the Old Testament. This connects his new faith firmly to its ancient Jewish roots, showing that the patriarchs and prophets were also guided by the same pre-incarnate Logos.

4. The Climax: The Incarnation
If the Logos was always active, why did Jesus have to be born? Justin's answer is crucial. The pre-Christian philosophers and prophets had only a "seed" of the Logos. In the incarnation, the entire Logos, the fullness of divine Reason and Truth, became flesh. The birth, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ is not just another seed of truth; it is the complete and final revelation of the Truth itself.

context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is a cornerstone of Justin's apologetic method. To understand its full impact, we need to look at both the immediate and broader context.
Immediate Context (The Argument of Chapter 52)

The entire chapter is built on a powerful logical argument based on fulfilled prophecy:

    The Premise: Justin begins by stating, "Since we prove that all things that have already happened were proclaimed by the prophets before they came to be, it is necessary to have faith also in those things which have been prophesied in the same way, but are yet to happen, that they will most certainly happen."

    The Core Distinction: He then explains that the prophets foretold two comings (Parousias) of Christ.

        The First Coming: Has already happened. It was that of a "dishonored and suffering man."

        The Second Coming: Is yet to happen. It will be glorious and judicial.

    The Quote's Role: Your quote is Justin's summary of what the prophets said about this Second Coming. It lays out the key events: the glorious return, the general resurrection of the body, and the final judgment.

    The Proof: Immediately after your quote, Justin says, "And that these things were foretold to happen, we shall show." He then provides quotations from the Old Testament prophets (specifically citing Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Zechariah) to prove to his Roman audience that these Christian beliefs are not new inventions but were predicted centuries in advance.

Broader Context (The Purpose of the First Apology)

    Audience: Justin is writing to the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius and the Roman Senate. This is a formal, public defense of Christianity.

    Goal: His aim is to persuade the authorities that Christians are not criminals, atheists, or enemies of the state. He argues that Christian belief is the most ancient and rational philosophy.

    The Power of Prophecy: For a Roman audience that highly valued antiquity and tradition (mos maiorum), the argument from prophecy was incredibly powerful. By showing that the life, death, and future return of Christ were predicted in the Jewish Scriptures—which Justin presents as the oldest and most venerable writings in the world—he frames Christianity not as a dangerous novelty, but as the fulfillment of a divine plan that predates Greek philosophy and Roman law.

    Theological Significance: This chapter clearly articulates foundational Christian doctrines: the bodily resurrection (a stark contrast to Greek ideas of a purely spiritual afterlife), the final judgment, and the reality of eternal, conscious punishment (ἐν αἰσθήσει αἰωνίᾳ - "in eternal sensibility/consciousness") for the wicked. This belief in ultimate accountability was used to argue that Christians were, in fact, the most moral and law-abiding of citizens.

en: For the prophets have proclaimed two advents of his: the one which is already past, when he came as a dishonored and suffering man; but the second, when, according to prophecy, he shall come from heaven in glory, accompanied by his angelic host, when he shall raise the bodies of all men who have lived, and shall clothe the worthy with immortality, and shall send those of the wicked, endued with eternal sensibility, into everlasting fire with the wicked devils [ First Apology 52 (c. A.D. 151)].

context:
Additional Relevant Context
1. Immediate Context: The Argument of Chapter 52

St. Justin's entire argument in this chapter is based on prophecy as proof.

    Before the Quote: He begins the chapter by stating his core principle: "Since, therefore, we prove that all things that have already happened were proclaimed by the prophets before they came to pass, we must have faith that the things which were similarly prophesied, but are yet to happen, will certainly come to pass." In other words, because the prophecies about Christ's first coming came true, we can be certain the prophecies about his second coming will also come true.

    The Quote's Function: Your chosen quote serves as the central thesis of the chapter. It lays out exactly what Christians believe about the future based on these prophecies.

    After the Quote: Justin immediately says, "And that these things also were foretold to happen, we will show." He then provides the prophetic proofs for his claims, quoting passages that he interprets as referring to the resurrection of the dead (from Ezekiel), the eternal punishment of the wicked (from Isaiah), and the future repentance of the Jewish people when they see the one they pierced (from Zechariah).

2. Broader Apologetic Context: The Purpose of the First Apology

St. Justin Martyr (c. 100-165 A.D.) wrote his First Apology to the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius. His goal was to defend Christianity against charges of atheism and irrationality and to prove that it was the "true philosophy." The "prophecy as proof" method was his primary tool. By showing that events in Jesus' life and the future of the world were foretold centuries in advance, he argued that Christianity was not a new invention but the divinely planned fulfillment of history.
3. Key Theological Points in the Quote

This passage is remarkably clear and provides a snapshot of core Christian beliefs in the mid-second century:

    Two Advents (Parousias): This is a crucial early Christian doctrine. It resolves the tension in the Hebrew Scriptures between prophecies of a suffering servant Messiah and a glorious, conquering King. Justin explains that both are true, but they refer to two different comings: the first in humility, the second in glory.

    Bodily Resurrection: Justin affirms the resurrection of the physical body for all people, both the righteous and the wicked. This was a radical idea in the Greco-Roman world, where many philosophies saw the body as a prison for the soul.

    Final Judgment and Eternal Punishment: The quote clearly lays out a final judgment with two distinct outcomes. The phrase "eternal sensibility" (ἐν αἰσθήσει αἰωνίᾳ) is particularly significant. It stresses that the punishment of the wicked is not annihilation but a conscious, unending state of torment.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR will also relate the way in which we dedicated ourselves to God when we were made new through Christ. As many as are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say iS true, and undertake to be able to live accordingly, and are instructed to pray and to entreat God with fasting, for the remission of their past sins, we pray and fast with them. Then they are brought by us where there is water, and are regenerated in the same way that we were regenerated. For, in the name of God, the Father and Lord of the universe, and of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they then receive the washing with water. For Christ also said, "Unless you be born again, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven" [First Apology 61 C. A.D. 151)].
greek: Ὃν τρόπον δὲ καὶ ἀνεθήκαμεν ἑαυτοὺς τῷ θεῷ καινοποιηθέντες διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἐξηγησόμεθα... ὅσοι ἂν πεισθῶσι καὶ πιστεύωσιν ἀληθῆ ταῦτα τὰ ὑφ' ἡμῶν διδασκόμενα καὶ λεγόμενα εἶναι, καὶ βιοῦν οὕτως δύνασθαι ὑπισχνῶνται, εὔχεσθαί τε καὶ αἰτεῖν νηστεύοντες παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν προημαρτημένων ἄφεσιν διδάσκονται, ἡμῶν συνευχομένων καὶ συννηστευόντων αὐτοῖς. ἔπειτα ἄγονται ὑφ' ἡμῶν ἔνθα ὕδωρ ἐστί, καὶ τρόπον ἀναγεννήσεως, ὃν καὶ ἡμεῖς αὐτοὶ ἀνεγεννήθημεν, ἀναγεννῶνται: ἐπ' ὀνόματος γὰρ τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων καὶ δεσπότου θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ πνεύματος ἁγίου τὸ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι τότε λουτρὸν ποιοῦνται. καὶ γὰρ ὁ Χριστὸς εἶπεν: Ἂν μὴ ἀναγεννηθῆτε, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν.
context:
The purpose of this chapter is to demystify Christian initiation rituals for a pagan audience, who were often suspicious and believed rumors of strange or sinister practices. Justin presents baptism as a rational, deeply meaningful, and scripturally-grounded ceremony.   2. Additional Relevant Context (from the rest of your text)

The rest of the Greek text you provided is just as important, as it gives Justin's own theological explanation for the rite he has just described. Here is what he adds:

1. Connection to Old Testament Prophecy:
Justin immediately quotes the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 1:16-20): "Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean; remove the evil from your souls..." By doing this, he makes a crucial apologetic point: Christian baptism is not a strange new invention. It is the fulfillment of what God promised through the Hebrew prophets, thus grounding Christianity in ancient, respected scripture.

2. The Theology of "Rebirth":
Justin provides a profound theological contrast between our two births:

    First Birth: A birth of necessity and ignorance. We were born "without our own knowledge or choice," from the physical union of our parents, and raised in "evil habits and wicked training."

    Second Birth (Baptism): A birth of choice and knowledge. It is a free decision made by the convert. The purpose is to obtain "remission of sins previously committed" and to become children of choice, not necessity.

3. The Name and "Illumination":
Justin explains that the name of "God the Father and Lord of the universe" is invoked over the candidate. He notes the philosophical point that God's true name is ineffable and beyond human language. He then gives a second name for the rite of baptism: "Illumination" (φωτισμός, photismos), "since they who learn these things are illuminated in their understanding." This highlights baptism as a moment of receiving divine truth and clarity.

4. The Historical Anchor:
When he repeats the Trinitarian formula, Justin adds a crucial historical detail: "...and in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and in the name of the Holy Spirit..." This is a key anti-mythological statement. By naming the Roman governor, Justin anchors the Christian faith in real, verifiable human history, distinguishing it from the timeless myths of pagan religions.

In summary, this single chapter provides one of the most complete pictures we have of Christian initiation in the mid-2nd century, including the moral requirements for candidates, the communal practice of fasting, the clear Trinitarian formula, and a sophisticated theology of regeneration, free will, and divine revelation.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR As many as are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say is true, and undertake to be able to live accordingly, and are instructed to pray and entreat God with fasting, for the remission of their past sins, we pray and fast with them. Then they are brought by us where there is water, and are regenerated in the same way we were ourselves regenerated. For, in the name of God, the Father and Lord of the universe, and of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they receive the washing with water. For Christ also said, "Unless you be born again, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven" [Jn 3:3] [First Apology 61 (c. A.D. 151)].

context:
Additional Relevant Context from Chapter 61

The rest of the text you provided is Justin's own explanation and theological justification for the practice he has just described. Here is a breakdown of that crucial context:

1. The Apologetic Purpose (Why he's explaining this):
Justin begins the chapter by stating his purpose clearly: "We will explain the manner in which we dedicated ourselves to God... lest, by omitting this, we might seem to be acting wickedly in our explanation." He knows that Christian rituals are seen as secret and suspicious. By openly describing Baptism, he is defending the Church against rumors of dark or immoral ceremonies. He is showing the Roman authorities that it is a rational, moral, and spiritual process.

2. The Contrast Between Two Births (Theology of Regeneration):
Justin provides a profound theological reason for this "regeneration." He contrasts our first birth with this new birth:

    First Birth: We were born "of necessity" and "in ignorance," from the union of our parents, and raised in "wicked habits and evil customs."

    New Birth (Baptism): This is a birth "of choice and of knowledge." It is not something that happens to us against our will, but something we choose. Its purpose is to obtain "remission for our past sins."

3. Scriptural Justification:
Justin grounds the practice in Scripture to show it is not a new invention but fulfills ancient prophecy and Christ's commands:

    Jesus's Command: He directly quotes Jesus's words to Nicodemus from John 3:3, "Unless you be born again, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven," as the direct mandate for this rite.

    The Prophet Isaiah: He links Christian baptism to the Old Testament, quoting Isaiah 1:16-18: "Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the evil from your souls..." This was a crucial apologetic move, arguing that Christianity is the true fulfillment of the revered Hebrew prophets.

4. The Trinitarian Formula and "Illumination":
Justin gives us one of the earliest extra-biblical accounts of the full Trinitarian formula being used in Baptism. He also provides another name for the sacrament:

    The Name: The washing is done explicitly "in the name of God, the Father and Lord of the universe, and of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit."

    Illumination (Phōtismos): He states, "This washing is called Illumination," explaining that the minds of the candidates "are illuminated" by the truths they have learned. This was a very common and beautiful early name for Baptism, emphasizing its connection to receiving knowledge and divine truth.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR We call this food Eucharist, and no one else is permitted to partake of it, except one who believes our teaching to be true and who has been washed in the washing that is for the remission of sins and for regeneration [i.e., has received baptism] and is thereby living as Christ enjoined. For not as common bread nor common drink do we receive these; but since Jesus Christ our Savior was made incarnate by the word of God and had both flesh and blood for our salvation, so too, as we have been taught, the food that has been made into the Eucharist by the eucharistic prayer set down by him, and by the change of which our blood and flesh is nurtured, is both the flesh and the blood of that incarnated Jesus [First Apology 66 (c. A.D. 151)].

context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is a theological and historical goldmine. Its importance comes from who was writing, to whom he was writing, and what he was explaining.
1. The Author and His Audience

    St. Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD): He was a Greek philosopher who converted to Christianity. He is one of the most important of the "Apologists"—early Christian writers who defended the faith against pagan and Jewish accusations. His testimony is incredibly early, written only about 50-60 years after the death of the Apostle John.

    The First Apology: This work is not an internal church document. It is a public, legal defense of Christianity addressed directly to the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius and the Senate. Justin is trying to prove that Christians are not atheists, cannibals, or immoral degenerates, but are virtuous, law-abiding citizens. This context is crucial: he is explaining the most sacred Christian mysteries to a powerful, skeptical, and potentially hostile pagan audience.

2. Theological Significance of the Quote

This short passage establishes several foundational Christian doctrines with stunning clarity:

    The Real Presence: This is arguably the earliest and clearest non-biblical testimony to the doctrine of the Real Presence. Justin's analogy is devastatingly precise: Just as the Incarnation was a real event where the Word became flesh, so too the bread and wine become the real Flesh and Blood of Christ. His statement, "not as common bread and common drink," is an explicit rejection of a purely symbolic understanding.

    Sacramental Discipline (Closed Communion): Justin lays out three strict requirements for receiving the Eucharist:

        Faith: One must believe the Church's teachings are true.

        Baptism: One must have been baptized for the forgiveness of sins and new birth.

        Orthopraxy: One must be living a moral life according to Christ's commandments.
        This shows that from the very beginning, the Eucharist was reserved for initiated members in good standing and was not an open meal for all.

    The Moment of Consecration: He attributes the change to the "eucharistic prayer set down by him" (literally, "the prayer of His word"). This points to the words of institution, spoken by the presider, as the effective means of consecration.

    A Real Change ("Transmutation"): The Greek phrase κατὰ μεταβολὴν (kata metabolēn) means "by way of a change," "transformation," or "transmutation." While not the later technical term "transubstantiation," it clearly indicates a belief in a real, objective change in the elements themselves.

3. Historical Significance from the Rest of the Chapter

The rest of the Greek text you provided adds even more valuable information:

    Apostolic Origin: Justin grounds this entire practice in the teaching of the Apostles, which he calls their "memoirs" or "Gospels" (ἃ καλεῖται εὐαγγέλια). He then paraphrases the words of institution from the Last Supper ("This is my body... This is my blood"), proving that this was not a later invention but was understood as a direct command from Jesus.

    Refutation of Paganism (Mithraism): Justin anticipates a pagan objection. He acknowledges that the pagan mystery religion of Mithraism also has a ritual meal of bread and a cup of water. He counters this not by denying the similarity, but by declaring the Mithraic ritual to be a demonic imitation (μιμησάμενοι οἱ πονηροὶ δαίμονες) of the Christian truth. This was a common apologetic strategy to explain parallels between Christianity and pagan religions.

In summary, this passage is an invaluable window into the liturgical practice and Eucharistic faith of the mid-2nd century Church, showing a belief system that is remarkably consistent with later Catholic and Orthodox doctrine.
