Chapter LXV.—Administration of the sacraments.

But we, after we have thus washed him who has been convinced and has assented to our teaching, bring him to the place where those who are called brethren are assembled, in order that we may offer hearty prayers in common for ourselves and for the baptized [illuminated] person, and for all others in every place, that we may be counted worthy, now that we have learned the truth, by our works also to be found good citizens and keepers of the commandments, so that we may be saved with an everlasting salvation. Having ended the prayers, we salute one another with a kiss.141There is then brought to the president of the brethren142 bread and a cup of wine mixed with water; and he taking them, gives praise and glory to the Father of the universe, through the name of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, and offers thanks at considerable length for our being counted worthy to receive these things at His hands. And when he has concluded the prayers and thanksgivings, all the people present express their assent by saying Amen. This word Amen answers in the Hebrew language to γένοιτο [so be it]. And when the president has given thanks, and all the people have expressed their assent, those who are called by us deacons give to each of those present to partake of the bread and wine mixed with water over which the thanksgiving was pronounced, and to those who are absent they carry away a portion.
greek: [65] Ἡμεῖς δὲ μετὰ τὸ οὕτως λοῦσαι τὸν πεπεισμένον καὶ συγκατατεθειμένον ἐπὶ τοὺς λεγομένους ἀδελφοὺς ἄγομεν, ἔνθα συνηγμένοι εἰσί, κοινὰς εὐχὰς ποιησόμενοι ὑπέρ τε ἑαυτῶν καὶ τοῦ φωτισθέντος καὶ ἄλλων πανταχοῦ πάντων εὐτόνως, ὅπως καταξιωθῶμεν τὰ ἀληθῆ μαθόντες καὶ δι' ἔργων ἀγαθοὶ πολιτευταὶ καὶ φύλακες τῶν ἐντεταλμένων εὑρεθῆναι, ὅπως τὴν αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν σωθῶμεν. ἀλλήλους φιλήματι ἀσπαζόμεθα παυσάμενοι τῶν εὐχῶν. ἔπειτα προσφέρεται τῷ προεστῶτι τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἄρτος καὶ ποτήριον ὕδατος καὶ κράματος, καὶ οὗτος λαβὼν αἶνον καὶ δόξαν τῷ πατρὶ τῶν ὅλων διὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ ἁγίου ἀναπέμπει καὶ εὐχαριστίαν ὑπὲρ τοῦ κατηξιῶσθαι τούτων παρ' αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ πολὺ ποιεῖται: οὗ συντελέσαντος τὰς εὐχὰς καὶ τὴν εὐχαριστίαν πᾶς ὁ παρὼν λαὸς ἐπευφημεῖ λέγων: Ἀμήν. τὸ δὲ Ἀμὴν τῇ Ἑβραΐδι φωνῇ τὸ Γένοιτο σημαίνει. εὐχαριστήσαντος δὲ τοῦ προεστῶτος καὶ ἐπευφημήσαντος παντὸς τοῦ λαοῦ οἱ καλούμενοι παρ' ἡμῖν διάκονοι διδόασιν ἑκάστῳ τῶν παρόντων μεταλαβεῖν ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐχαριστηθέντος ἄρτου καὶ οἴνου καὶ ὕδατος καὶ τοῖς οὐ παροῦσιν ἀποφέρουσι.

Chapter LXVII.—Weekly worship of the Christians.

And we afterwards continually remind each other of these things. And the wealthy among us help the needy; and we always keep together; and for all things wherewith we are supplied, we bless the Maker of all through His Son Jesus Christ, and through the Holy Ghost. And on the day called Sunday,146 all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits; then, when the reader has ceased, the president verbally instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things. Then we all rise together and pray, and, as we before said, when our prayer is ended, bread and wine and water are brought, and the president in like manner offers prayers and thanksgivings, according to his ability,147 and the people assent, saying Amen; and there is a distribution to each, and a participation of that over which thanks have been given,148 and to those who are absent a portion is sent by the deacons. And they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit; and what is collected is deposited with the president, who succours the orphans and widows and those who, through sickness or any other cause, are in want, and those who are in bonds and the strangers sojourning among us, and in a word takes care of all who are in need. But Sunday is the day on which we all hold our common assembly, because it is the first day on which God, having wrought a change in the darkness and matter, made the world; and Jesus Christ our Saviour on the same day rose from the dead. For He was crucified on the day before that of Saturn (Saturday); and on the day after that of Saturn, which is the day of the Sun, having appeared to His apostles and disciples, He taught them these things, which we have submitted to you also for your consideration.
greek: [67] Ἡμεῖς δὲ μετὰ ταῦτα λοιπὸν ἀεὶ τούτων ἀλλήλους ἀναμιμνήσκομεν: καὶ οἱ ἔχοντες τοῖς λειπομένοις πᾶσιν ἐπικουροῦμεν, καὶ σύνεσμεν ἀλλήλοις ἀεί. ἐπὶ πᾶσί τε οἷς προσφερόμεθα εὐλογοῦμεν τὸν ποιητὴν τῶν πάντων διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ διὰ πνεύματος τοῦ ἁγίου. καὶ τῇ τοῦ ἡλίου λεγομένῃ ἡμέρᾳ πάντων κατὰ πόλεις ἢ ἀγροὺς μενόντων ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συνέλευσις γίνεται, καὶ τὰ ἀπομνημονεύματα τῶν ἀποστόλων ἢ τὰ συγγράμματα τῶν προφητῶν ἀναγινώσκεται, μέχρις ἐγχωρεῖ. εἶτα παυσαμένου τοῦ ἀναγινώσκοντος ὁ προεστὼς διὰ λόγου τὴν νουθεσίαν καὶ πρόκλησιν τῆς τῶν καλῶν τούτων μιμήσεως ποιεῖται. ἔπειτα ἀνιστάμεθα κοινῇ πάντες καὶ εὐχὰς πέμπομεν: καί, ὡς προέφημεν, παυσαμένων ἡμῶν τῆς εὐχῆς ἄρτος προσφέρεται καὶ οἶνος καὶ ὕδωρ, καὶ ὁ προεστὼς εὐχὰς ὁμοίως καὶ εὐχαριστίας, ὅση δύναμις αὐτῷ, ἀναπέμπει, καὶ ὁ λαὸς ἐπευφημεῖ λέγων τὸ Ἀμήν, καὶ ἡ διάδοσις καὶ ἡ μετάληψις ἀπὸ τῶν εὐχαριστηθέντων ἑκάστῳ γίνεται, καὶ τοῖς οὐ παροῦσι διὰ τῶν διακόνων πέμπεται. οἱ εὐποροῦντες δὲ καὶ βουλόμενοι κατὰ προαίρεσιν ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ὃ βούλεται δίδωσι, καὶ τὸ συλλεγόμενον παρὰ τῷ προεστῶτι ἀποτίθεται, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπικουρεῖ ὀρφανοῖς τε καὶ χήραις, καὶ τοῖς διὰ νόσον ἢ δι' ἄλλην αἰτίαν λειπομένοις, καὶ τοῖς ἐν δεσμοῖς οὖσι, καὶ τοῖς παρεπιδήμοις οὖσι ξένοις, καὶ ἁπλῶς πᾶσι τοῖς ἐν χρείᾳ οὖσι κηδεμὼν γίνεται. τὴν δὲ τοῦ ἡλίου ἡμέραν κοινῇ πάντες τὴν συνέλευσιν ποιούμεθα, ἐπειδὴ πρώτη ἐστὶν ἡμέρα, ἐν ᾗ ὁ θεὸς τὸ σκότος καὶ τὴν ὕλην τρέψας κόσμον ἐποίησε, καὶ Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ὁ ἡμέτερος σωτὴρ τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀνέστη: τῇ γὰρ πρὸ τῆς κρονικῆς ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτόν, καὶ τῇ μετὰ τὴν κρονικήν, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἡλίου ἡμέρα, φανεὶς τοῖς ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ καὶ μαθηταῖς ἐδίδαξε ταῦτα, ἅπερ εἰς ἐπίσκεψιν καὶ ὑμῖν ἀνεδώκαμεν.

en: But, in truth, he has even called the flesh to the resurrection, and promises to it everlasting life. For where he promises to save man, there he gives the promise to the flesh. For what iS man but the reasonable animal composed of body and soul? Is the soul by itself man? No, but the soul of man. Would the body be called man? No. but it is called the body of man. If, then, neither of these is by itself man, then the two together are called man, and God has called man to life and resurrection, he has called not part, but the whole, which is the soul and the body [ The Resurrection 8 (c. A.D. 153)].

The larger block of Greek you provided gives the full context for this powerful argument. Athenagoras is systematically refuting the arguments of those (likely Gnostics and Platonist philosophers) who denied the physical resurrection.

    The Opposing View: Contempt for the Flesh: The opponents believed the body (σάρξ, "flesh") was an evil, temporary prison for the pure, divine soul. For them, salvation meant the soul's final escape from the body, not its reunion with it. They saw the idea of resurrecting the "filthy" flesh as absurd and undesirable.

    Athenagoras's Preceding Argument (in your text): Before the quote, Athenagoras refutes the claim that the flesh is inherently sinful. He uses a brilliant analogy: a yoke of oxen cannot plow individually. Likewise, neither the soul nor the body can act (or sin) alone. They are a "yoke" (συζυγία). Therefore, if they are judged, they must be judged together.

    The Core Argument of Your Quote: A Holistic Anthropology: This is the philosophical heart of his entire treatise. Athenagoras masterfully argues from the very definition of a human being.

        A "man" is not just a soul.

        A "man" is not just a body.

        A "man" is the composite whole of soul and body.
        This is a profoundly anti-Gnostic and anti-Platonic definition.

    The Inescapable Logical Conclusion: Since God's promise of salvation and resurrection is made to "man," it cannot be a promise made to only a part of man (the soul). To be true to His word, God must save the whole person—the complete soul-body composite. To resurrect only the soul would be to fail to resurrect "man."

    Athenagoras's Following Argument (also in your text): Immediately after your quote, he tackles another objection: that God saves the soul because it is immortal and a "divine spark," but not the flesh, which is mortal. Athenagoras brilliantly turns this around: saving what is already immortal by nature is no great display of God's power or goodness. The true sign of God's power is to raise and make immortal that which is by nature mortal—the flesh. This is the ultimate act of a loving and omnipotent Creator.

en: ST. JUSTIN MARTYR [E]ternal fire was prepared for him who voluntarily departed from God and for all who, without repentance, persevere in apostasy [fragment in St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies 5:26:2 (C. A.D. 153)].

context:
Analysis and Context

The English translation you provided is a very accurate rendering of both the Greek and Latin texts.

    Context: Irenaeus is in the middle of a discussion about the final judgment and the punishment of the devil. He quotes Justin Martyr as an earlier authority to support the traditional Christian teaching that eternal fire is the destination for the devil (the first to "voluntarily depart from God") and for humans who willfully and finally reject God ("persevere in apostasy without repentance").

    Key Themes:

        Voluntary Apostasy (ἑκουσίως / sponte sua): The sin is a willful, free choice to depart from God. This is central to the Church's understanding of mortal sin.

        Perseverance without Repentance (χωρὶς μετανοίας ἐμμένουσι / sine poenitentia perseverant): The ultimate condemnation is not for the act of falling, but for the state of remaining in that fallen state without turning back to God.

The date you provided (c. A.D. 153) is appropriate for the time Justin Martyr was writing. Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies a few decades later, around A.D. 180. The fragment is likely from one of Justin's lost works, perhaps his treatise Against Marcion.    Understanding the Full Context You Found

The larger passage you provided is Irenaeus's brilliant explanation of free will, judgment, and the typical heretical (specifically Gnostic) reaction to these doctrines. It's even more informative than the standalone quote.

Here is a breakdown of the full text you found:

1. The Text Before the Quote: God Gives Free Will

    Si ergo adventus Filii... manifestum, quoniam et Pater ejus omnes quidem similiter fecit, propriam sententiam unumquemque habentem, et sensum liberum...

    Translation & Meaning: "If therefore the coming of the Son... it is manifest that his Father also made all men alike, each one having his own judgment and a free will..."

    Context: Irenaeus establishes that God created everyone with free will. Our choices—whether to believe and do His will or to reject His teaching—are our own.

2. The Core Statement (Attributed to Justin Martyr)

    Post autem adventum Domini ex sermonibus Christi et apostolorum ejus discens manifeste, quoniam ignis æternus ei præparatus est ex sua voluntate abscedenti a Deo, et omnibus qui sine pœnitentia perseverant in apostasia...

    Translation & Meaning: "But after the coming of the Lord, learning manifestly from the words of Christ and His apostles that eternal fire was prepared for him who of his own will departed from God, and for all who without repentance persevere in apostasy..."

    Context: Irenaeus states that this is what the Church has learned from revelation. Since we have free will, there are consequences for our choices. The ultimate consequence for final, unrepentant rejection of God is eternal fire.

3. The Text After the Quote: The Heretical Reaction

    ...per hujusmodi homines blasphemat cum Deum... et peccatum suæ apostasiæ conditori suo imputat, et non suæ voluntati et sententiæ... Sic autem et hi diabolico spiritu pleni, innumeras accusationes inferunt factori nostro... Quapropter et alterum quemdam excogitant Patrem, neque curantem, neque providentem... aut etiam consentientem omnibus peccatis.

    Translation & Meaning: "...through men of this kind, he [the devil] blasphemes God... and he imputes the sin of his apostasy to his Creator, and not to his own will and judgment... Thus also these men, filled with a diabolical spirit, bring countless accusations against our Maker... For which reason they also invent another Father, one who neither cares nor provides for our affairs, or who even consents to all sins."

    Context: This is the brilliant conclusion. Irenaeus explains why the Gnostics reject the God of the Old Testament. Faced with the doctrine of a just God who judges sin, they refuse to take responsibility for their own free will. Instead, they:

        Blaspheme the true God.

        Blame the Creator for their sin.

        Invent a different, "higher" God who is indifferent to their actions and doesn't judge.

You have not only found the quote but also the reason why Irenaeus felt it was so important to preserve it: to combat the Gnostic heresy that sought to eliminate divine justice and human responsibility. Excellent work

en: LACTANTIUS And while Nero reigned, the apostle Peter came to Rome, and, through the power of God committed unto him, wrought certain miracles, and. by turning many to the true religion, built up a faithful and steadfast temple unto the Lord. When Nero heard of those things, and observed that not only in Rome, but in every other place, a great multitude revolted daily from the worship of idols, and, condemning their old ways, went over to the new religion, he, an execrable and pernicious tyrant, sprung forward to raze the heavenly temple and destroy the true faith. He it was who first persecuted the servants of God; he crucified Peter, and slew Paul [Deaths of the Persecutors 2 (c. A.D 318)].

Qua re ad Neronem delata, cum animadverteret non modo Romae, sed ubique quotidie magnam multitudinem deficere a cultu idolorum, et ad religionem novam, damnata vetustate, transire; ut erat execrabilis ac nocens tyrannus, prosilivit ad excidendum coeleste templum, delendamque justitiam, et primus omnium persecutus Dei servos, Petrum cruci affixit, et Paulum interfecit.

The full Latin text you provided gives a rich and complete picture of Lactantius's argument. The context is crucial to understanding the significance of the quote.

1. The Context Before the Quote: Divine Foundation
The chapter does not begin with Nero. It begins with the foundation of the Church itself:

    The crucifixion of Jesus under Tiberius Caesar.

    The Resurrection and the forty days Christ spent with his disciples.

    Christ's commissioning of the apostles to preach the Gospel to the entire world.

    The 25-year period of apostolic mission, from the Ascension "up to the beginning of the Neronian empire," where the apostles "laid the foundations of the Church through all provinces and cities."

Why this is important: Lactantius frames the Church not as a new human movement, but as a divinely ordained mission set in motion by Christ himself. Peter's arrival in Rome is the culmination of this 25-year mission, bringing the foundational apostolic authority to the capital of the empire.

2. The Context After the Quote: Divine Retribution
The chapter does not end with the martyrdoms. It immediately describes Nero's downfall, which is the central theme of the entire book:

    "Nor, however, did he do so with impunity; for God looked upon the affliction of His people."

    Lactantius describes Nero's fall from power and mysterious disappearance, noting that "not even a place of burial on earth was to be found for so evil a beast."

Why this is important: The main purpose of De Mortibus Persecutorum is to show that God brings justice upon those who attack His Church. Nero is presented as the first great example: he was the first to persecute the Church, and he met a fittingly wretched end.

3. The Nero-Antichrist Tradition
Lactantius then includes a fascinating detail of early Christian belief: the idea that Nero did not actually die but was spirited away and would return as a forerunner to the Antichrist. He references a Sibylline prophecy about a "matricide" returning to persecute the Church again at the end of time. This shows how Nero's evil was so profound in the Christian imagination that he became an eschatological figure of ultimate wickedness.

In Summary: Your quote is a historically significant early testimony (c. 318 AD) explicitly linking Peter and Paul's martyrdoms to Nero in Rome. Within Lactantius's work, it serves as the pivotal moment where the divinely founded Church has its first epic clash with the archetypal tyrannical persecutor, a clash that ends in martyrdom but is ultimately vindicated by divine justice.

The passage you've highlighted is the central pillar of Lactantius's argument in this chapter. Here is the broader context to understand its full significance:

1. The Central Question of the Chapter:
As the Latin title states, the chapter's theme is: "Uniusne potestate Dei mundus regatur, an multorum?" ("Is the world governed by the power of one God, or of many?"). Lactantius is writing a systematic refutation of pagan polytheism and making a rational case for monotheism.

2. Lactantius's Logical Arguments Against Polytheism:
Before arriving at your specific quote, Lactantius builds his case with several philosophical arguments and analogies:

    Argument from Perfection: A perfect being cannot be one of many, because to be one of many implies a division of power, which makes each individual being less than perfectly powerful. God, by definition, must possess perfect and complete power, and therefore must be one.

    Analogy of the King: A single king who rules the entire world is more powerful than many kings who rule divided territories.

    Argument from Divine Unity: Anything that can be divided is subject to destruction. Since God is eternal and incorruptible, His power cannot be divided. Therefore, God must be one.

3. The Significance of Your Quote (The Pivot Point):
Your quote is Lactantius's brilliant refutation of the most common pagan counter-argument. The pagan might say: "The world is simply too vast and complex for one being to manage. There must be many gods, each with their own domain (a god of the sea, a god of the sky, etc.)."

Lactantius turns this argument completely on its head. He says:

    You are mistaken to think governance is harder than creation.

    The real miracle is not governing the world, but creating it ex nihilo (from nothing).

    An act of such immense power—bringing the entire universe into being from non-being—could only be accomplished by a single, infinitely powerful will. A committee of gods would have resulted in chaos.

    Therefore, if the harder task (creation from nothing) was done by one God, the comparatively easier task (governing what already exists) can certainly be managed by that same one God.

In essence, your quote marks the moment where Lactantius transforms the universe's vastness from a perceived argument for polytheism into his strongest argument for monotheism.

Eorum inventa sunt astrologia, et aruspicina, et auguratio, et ipsa quae dicuntur oracula, et necromantia, et ars magica, et quiquid praeterea malorum exercent homines, vel palam, vel occulte.

Additional Relevant Context

The context of this passage is crucial to understanding Lactantius's project. He is writing a comprehensive defense of Christianity (an "apology") for an educated Roman audience. His goal is to dismantle pagan philosophy and religion while demonstrating the reasonableness and truth of the Christian faith.

    The Argument in Chapter 16 (The Powerlessness of Demons): Before your quote, the main point of Chapter 16 is that demons are fundamentally powerless against the righteous. Lactantius argues that they can only harm those who fear them and who are not protected by "the powerful and lofty hand of God." He states that the just, by invoking God's name, can command demons and cast them out, causing them to confess their own nature.

    The Use of Hermes Trismegistus: Lactantius's masterstroke here is quoting Hermes Trismegistus, a mythical Egyptian sage highly revered by pagans in the Roman Empire. By citing this respected pagan authority, Lactantius is using an argument his audience cannot easily dismiss. He is essentially saying: "Don't just take my Christian word for it. Even your own wisest philosopher knew that these demons are corrupted heavenly beings and that true piety is the only defense against them." This is a brilliant apologetic strategy.

    The Function of Your Quote: Your quote serves as a powerful bridge. The end of Chapter 16 uses Trismegistus to define what demons are (corrupted, wicked angels). The beginning of Chapter 17 immediately lists what demons do (invent the occult arts to deceive humanity).

    The Argument in Chapter 17 (The Deception of Demons): After your quote, Chapter 17 expands on the idea that all forms of divination and magic are demonic inventions designed to accomplish one goal: to turn humanity away from the worship of the one true God. Lactantius argues that demons use these arts to mix truth with falsehood, perform false miracles, and inhabit idols, all to trick people into worshipping them instead of their Creator. This deception, he concludes, is how they rob humans of the immortality that they themselves have lost.

In summary, your quote is the centerpiece of Lactantius's argument that the entire pagan system of divination, magic, and idol worship is a grand demonic deception, a truth he supports not only with Christian teaching but with the words of a revered pagan sage.

en: LACTANTIUS He became both the Son of God through the Spirit, and the Son of man through the flesh that is, both God and man [Divine Institutes 4:13 (c. A.D. 307)].
latin: Factus est et Dei filius per spiritum, et hominis per carnem; id est, et Deus et homo.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This single sentence is the theological thesis of the entire chapter. Lactantius constructs his argument carefully to lead up to this statement and then spends the rest of the chapter defending it with proofs. Here is the context:

1. The Argument of the "Two Births": Immediately before your quote, Lactantius makes a unique and fascinating argument about Christ having two births, which makes him, like the Father, both "fatherless" (ἀπάτωρ) and "motherless" (ἀμήτωρ).

    First Birth (Spiritual): Christ was generated by God the Father alone, without a mother. In this spiritual birth, He was ἀμήτωρ (motherless).

    Second Birth (Carnal): Christ was conceived in the womb of a virgin, without a human father. In this carnal birth, He was ἀπάτωρ (fatherless).

Lactantius uses this elegant parallel to set up the duality of Christ's nature.

2. The Role as Mediator: This dual nature, born of two births, gives Christ a "middle substance" (mediam inter Deum et hominem substantiam) between God and man. The purpose of this is soteriological (related to salvation). Lactantius explains that by having this dual nature, Christ is able to take our "fragile and weak nature by the hand" (nostram hanc fragilem imbecillemque naturam quasi manu) and lead it to immortality.

3. The Thesis Statement (Your Quote): After establishing the "two births" and the role as Mediator, Lactantius delivers the clear, summary statement you were looking for: "He became both the Son of God through the Spirit, and the Son of man through the flesh; that is, both God and man."

4. The Proof from Prophecy: The rest of the chapter (as indicated by the title, "Concerning Jesus, God and man; and the testimonies of the prophets about him") is dedicated to proving this thesis. Immediately after your quote, Lactantius begins to systematically present evidence that Christ is both God and man, citing:

    Old Testament Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, David, and Moses.

    Pagan Oracles: He even cleverly co-opts a response from the pagan oracle of Apollo of Miletus, interpreting its ambiguous answer to support the Christian claim that Jesus was mortal in the flesh but divine in the Spirit.

In summary, your quote is the central pillar of the chapter's argument. Lactantius first explains the theological necessity for a dual nature (mediation through two births) and then spends the remainder of the chapter providing what he considers to be irrefutable prophetic proof for that dual nature.

[But w]hen we speak of God the Father and God the Son, we do not speak of them as different, nor do we separate them, because the Father cannot exist without the Son, nor can the Son be separated from the Father [ibid., 4:29].

context:
Additional Relevant Context (from the rest of your provided text)

The rest of the chapter that you included is a masterclass in pre-Nicaean Trinitarian theology. Lactantius uses a series of powerful analogies and scriptural proofs to explain how the Father and Son can be distinct Persons yet constitute one God. Here is a breakdown of his arguments:

1. The Central Theological Principle:
Lactantius states that the Father and Son share one mind, one spirit, one substance (una utrique mens, unus spiritus, una substantia est). This is a powerful, early assertion of their unity of being.

2. The Analogy of Source and Stream / Sun and Ray:
This is his most famous analogy.

    The Father is like an overflowing spring (exuberans fons), and the Son is like the stream flowing from it (defluens ex eo rivus).

    The Father is like the sun (sol), and the Son is like the ray extending from the sun (radius a sole porrectus).

    The Point: Just as a stream cannot be separated from its source, and a ray cannot be cut off from the sun, the Son cannot be separated from the Father. The water in the stream is the water of the spring; the light in the ray is the light of the sun.

3. The Analogy of a Roman Household:
Lactantius uses a legal and social analogy from Roman life.

    A father may have a beloved son who lives in his house and shares in his authority. Although the son may be granted the title and power of "lord" (dominus), civil law still considers it one house and one lord (domus una, et unus dominus nominatur).

    The Point: In the same way, the universe is God's one house (una Dei domus), and the Father and Son who dwell in it in perfect unanimity are one God (Deus unus).

4. Scriptural Proof from Isaiah:
Lactantius quotes Isaiah to prove that Scripture refers to the two Persons with a singular name.

    He cites Isaiah 45:14 ("...In you is God, and there is no other God besides you") and Isaiah 44:6 ("...I am the first and I am the last; and besides me there is no God").

    His Argument: Even though the prophet mentions two Persons (God the King, i.e., Christ, and God the Father), he concludes by saying "besides me there is no God," not "besides us." Lactantius argues this was deliberate, because "it was not right for the separation of so great a bond to be made by a plural number."

5. Conclusion: The Necessity of Worshipping the Son:
He concludes that since the Father and Son are one God, it is impossible to worship the Father while ignoring the Son.

    "He who thinks he worships the Father alone, just as he does not worship the Son, so he does not worship the Father either. But he who receives the Son... truly worships the Father together with the Son."

Lactantius's writing is a crucial window into how Christians articulated their faith in the Father and Son before the universal language of the Nicene Creed ("consubstantial," "of one being") was established.

en: LACTANTIUS When we speak of God the Father and God the Son, we do not speak of them as different, nor do we separate them, because the Father cannot exist without the Son, nor can the Son be separated from the Father, since the name of Father cannot be given without the Son, nor can the Son be begotten without the Father. Since, therefore, the Father makes the Son, and the Son the Father, they both have one mind, one spirit, one substance; but the former IS as it were an overflowing fountain, the latter as a stream flowing forth from it: the former as the sun, the latter as it were a ray extended from the sun [Divine Institutes 4:29 (c. A.D. 307)].
latin: Cum dicimus Deum Patrem, et Deum Filium, non diversum dicimus, nec utrumque secernimus; quia nec Pater sine Filio esse potest, nec Filius a Patre secerni, si quidem nec Pater sine Filio nuncupari, nec Filius potest sine Patre generari. Cum igitur et Pater Filium faciat, et Filius Patrem, una utrique mens, unus spiritus, una substantia est: sed ille quasi exuberans fons est, hic tamquam defluens ex eo rivus; ille tamquam sol, hic quasi radius a sole porrectus.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is a brilliant example of early, pre-Nicene Trinitarian theology. Lactantius, known as the "Christian Cicero" for his elegant Latin prose, is writing as an apologist to an educated Roman audience. Here is the context for his argument in this chapter:

1. The Immediate Problem: Defending Monotheism

Lactantius opens the chapter by directly addressing the primary pagan criticism of Christianity: how can Christians claim to worship one God when they "assert that there are two, God the Father and God the Son"?

    Fortasse quaerat aliquis, quomodo, cum Deum nos unum colere dicamus, duos tamen esse asseveremus, Deum Patrem et Deum Filium...
    ("Perhaps someone may ask how, when we say we worship one God, we nevertheless assert that there are two, God the Father and God the Son...")

His entire argument is a defense against the charge of ditheism (believing in two Gods).

2. The Core Argument: Inseparable Unity

The quote you selected is the heart of his answer. Lactantius argues that the Father and Son are not two separate, different beings but are an inseparable unity. His key points are:

    Relational Existence: The Father cannot be a Father without the Son, and the Son cannot be a Son without the Father. Their very identities are mutually dependent and eternal. (nec Pater sine Filio esse potest...)

    Unity of Being: He then makes a profound statement for his time: they share "one mind, one spirit, one substance" (una utrique mens, unus spiritus, una substantia est). His use of the word substantia is extremely significant, as it prefigures the language that would be formally adopted at the Council of Nicaea (325 AD) with the Greek term homoousios (consubstantial, "of one substance").

3. The Use of Analogies: Explaining the Mystery

To help his pagan audience grasp this mystery, Lactantius uses two classic and powerful analogies drawn from nature:

    The Fountain and the Stream (fons / rivus): The Father is the eternal, overflowing source, and the Son is the stream that flows from it. The stream is distinct from the fountain, yet it is made of the very same water and can never be separated from its source.

    The Sun and the Ray (sol / radius): The Father is like the sun, and the Son is like the ray of light extended from it. The ray is not the sun itself, but it is pure sunlight and cannot exist apart from the sun. Both analogies beautifully illustrate distinction of Persons without any separation or difference in nature/substance.

4. Crucial Historical Context: A Pre-Nicene Voice

Lactantius is writing around A.D. 307, nearly two decades before the Council of Nicaea. The Church's theological language was still developing. While his analogies and his use of substantia demonstrate a profoundly orthodox instinct, his language (like that of many early writers) can sometimes sound "subordinationist" to a later, post-Nicene ear (e.g., the Son "flowing forth from" the Father). However, in his own context, he is making a powerful case for the full divinity and eternal unity of the Father and the Son, defending the core of the Christian faith against pagan misunderstanding.

en: LACTANTIUS [It is the Catholic Church alone that retains true worship. This is the fountain of truth, this is the abode of the faith, this is the temple of God: if anyone shall not enter, or if anyone shall leave, he is estranged from the hope of life and eternal salvation. No one should flatter himself with persevering strife. For the contest is about life and salvation, which, unless it iS carefully and diligently kept in view, will be lost and extinguished. But, however, because all the separate assemblies of heretics call themselves Christians in preference to others, and think that theirs is the Catholic Church, it must be known that the true Catholic Church is that in which there is confession and repentance, which treats in a wholesome manner the sins and wounds to which the weakness of the flesh is liable [Divine Institutes 4:30 (c. A.D. 307)].
latin: Sola igitur catholica Ecclesia est, quae verum cultum retinet. Hic est fons veritatis, hoc domicilium fidei, hoc templum Dei: quo si quis non intraverit, vel a quo si quis exiverit, a spe vitae ac salutis aeternae alienus est. Neminem sibi oportet pertinaci concertatione blandiri. Agitur enim de vita et salute: quae nisi caute ac diligenter attenditur, amissa et exstincta erit. Verumtamen, quia singuli quique coetus haereticorum se potissimum Christianos, et suam esse catholicam Ecclesiam putant; sciendum est, illam esse veram, in qua est confessio et poenitentia, quae peccata et vulnera, quibus subjecta est imbecillitas carnis, salubriter curat.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is one of the most significant early Latin statements on ecclesiology (the theology of the Church). To understand its importance, consider the following:

    The Broader Argument: Lactantius wrote The Divine Institutes around A.D. 307, during a period of intense persecution. The work is a comprehensive defense and explanation of Christianity aimed at educated Romans. In Book 4, he is arguing that Christianity is the one true religion and true wisdom, contrasting it with the foolishness of pagan polytheism and the limitations of philosophy.

    The Problem of "Which Church?": By the early 4th century, Christianity was not monolithic. There were numerous heretical and schismatic groups (Gnostics, Marcionites, and rigorist groups like the Novatianists) who all claimed to be the true followers of Christ. A Roman aristocrat considering conversion would rightly ask, "Which group holds the authentic teaching?" Lactantius is answering that question.

    The Exclusivity of the Catholic Church: His opening statement is absolute. It is the "Catholic Church alone" that has true worship. He uses three powerful metaphors to describe it:

        Fountain of Truth (fons veritatis): It is the source from which pure doctrine flows.

        Abode of the Faith (domicilium fidei): It is the house or dwelling-place where the true faith resides.

        Temple of God (templum Dei): It is the sacred space where God is truly present and worshipped.
        The conclusion is stark: to be outside this body is to be estranged from the hope of salvation. This is an early formulation of the doctrine extra Ecclesiam nulla salus (outside the Church, there is no salvation).

    A Pastoral Criterion for Truth: The most brilliant part of this passage is the test Lactantius provides. How do you identify the true Church when so many groups claim the title? He doesn't point to miracles or apostolic succession in this specific passage. Instead, he offers a deeply pastoral and practical criterion: the true Church is the one "in which there is confession and repentance" (in qua est confessio et poenitentia).

    This was a direct refutation of rigorist heresies, particularly Novatianism. The Novatianists argued that the Church was a society of the pure and that those who committed serious sins after baptism (like denying the faith during persecution) could never be forgiven or restored to communion. Lactantius argues the opposite: the true Church is a hospital for sinners. It acknowledges the "weakness of the flesh" (imbecillitas carnis) and provides a "wholesome cure" (salubriter curat) for sins and wounds through confession and penance.

In summary, you have found a landmark passage where Lactantius defines the one, true Catholic Church not only by its exclusive claim to truth but by its merciful, pastoral practice of forgiving sinners.

en: LACTANTIUS For when God forbids us to kill, he not only prohibits us from open violence, which iS not even allowed by the public laws, but he warns us against the commission of those things esteemed lawful among men. Therefore let no one imagine that this is allowed, to strangle newborn children, which is the greatest impiety; for God breathes into their souls for life, and not for death. But men, that there may be no crime with which they may not pollute their hands, deprive souls as yet innocent and simple of the light that they themselves have not given. Can any one, indeed, expect that they would abstain from the blood of others who do not abstain from their own? But these are without any controversy wicked and unjust [Divine Institutes 6:20 (c. A.D. 307)].
latin: Ergo ne illud quidem concedi aliquis existimet, ut recens natos liceat oblidere, quae vel maxima est impietas; ad vitam enim Deus inspirat animas, non ad mortem. Verum homines, ne quod sit facinus, quo manus suas non polluant, rudibus adhuc et simplicibus animis abnegant lucem non a se datam. Expectet vero aliquis ut alieno sanguini parcant, qui non parcunt suo: sed hi sine ulla controversia scelerati et injusti.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The context of this passage is crucial, as it is the climax of a powerful argument Lactantius is building throughout Chapter 20. The chapter's title is: "On the senses and their pleasures... and on the pleasure of the eyes and public spectacles."

Here is the flow of his argument, which places your quote in its proper setting:

    The Dangers of Sense-Pleasure: Lactantius begins the chapter by arguing that Christians must control the pleasures of the five senses, which are traps that lead to vice and spiritual death.

    Focus on the "Pleasure of the Eyes": He quickly narrows his focus to the most dangerous sense-pleasure: the eyes, specifically the pleasure derived from watching Roman public spectacles (spectacula).

    Attack on the Gladiatorial Games: His primary target is the gladiatorial games, which he condemns as "public homicide." He argues that anyone who finds pleasure in watching a man be killed—even a condemned criminal—pollutes their own conscience and becomes a participant in the murder. He writes with disgust: "They call them games, in which human blood is shed... so far has humanity departed from men."

    The Absolute Prohibition on Killing: This attack on the games leads him to a radical principle. He argues that the Christian's desensitization to violence at the arena will spill over into the rest of their life. To counter this, he states that God's commandment, "You shall not kill," is absolute. It applies not only to illegal acts like robbery (latrocinari) but also to actions considered lawful in Roman society. In the paragraph immediately preceding your quote, he makes the stunning claims that a just man cannot serve in the military (neque militare justo licebit) or accuse anyone of a capital crime, because killing with the word is the same as killing with the sword.

    Infanticide as the Ultimate Example: This is where your quote comes in. After establishing the absolute nature of God's prohibition against killing, he uses infanticide as his ultimate example of a "lawful" Roman practice that is a profound impiety. The practice of exposing or strangling unwanted newborns was common and legally permitted in the Roman Empire. Lactantius declares that this, too, is forbidden by God's law. His logic is devastating: if people will kill their own innocent children, how can anyone expect them to spare a stranger?

In short, your quote is not a standalone statement but the powerful conclusion to a broader argument against the moral corruption of Roman society, rooted in its violent entertainment and its disregard for the absolute sanctity of all human life from the moment of birth.

en: But truly parricides complain of the scantiness of their means. and allege that they have not enough for bringing up more children; as though, in truth, their means were in the power of those who possess them, or that God did not daily make the rich poor, and the poor rich. If anyone shall be unable to bring up children on account of poverty, is better to abstain from marriage than with wicked hands to mar the work of God [Divine Institutes 6:20 (C. A.D. 307)].
latin: At enim parricidae facultatum angustias conqueruntur; nec se pluribus liberis educandis sufficere posse praetendunt: quasi vero aut facultates in potestate sint possidentium, aut non quotidie Deus ex divitibus pauperes, et ex pauperibus divites faciat. Quare si quis liberos ob pauperiem non poterit educare, satius est, ut se ab uxoris congressione contineat, quam sceleratis manibus Dei opera corrumpat.

Additional Relevant Context

The quote is the powerful culmination of a much larger argument Lactantius is making in this chapter about the absolute sanctity of human life, which stands in stark contrast to the casual brutality of Roman society. Here is the flow of his reasoning leading up to your passage:

    The Broad Theme is Virtue vs. Vice: The chapter begins by condemning the pagan pursuit of sensual pleasures, particularly the "pleasure of the eyes" found in public spectacles.

    Condemnation of Gladiatorial Games: Lactantius attacks the gladiatorial games as a form of "public homicide." He argues that a Christian, who is bound by justice, cannot participate in or even watch such events because they pollute the conscience.

    God's Command Against Killing is Absolute: This leads him to a crucial theological point. God's command "You shall not kill" is absolute and without exception. It applies not just to illegal acts like robbery, but to acts considered legal and normal in Roman society.

        Latin: Itaque in hoc Dei praecepto nullam prorsus exceptionem fieri oportet, quin occidere hominem sit semper nefas, quem Deus sanctum animal esse voluit.
        English: "Therefore, in this precept of God, no exception at all ought to be made: to kill a human being, whom God willed to be a sacred creature, is always a wicked crime."

    Application to Infanticide: Having established this absolute principle, Lactantius applies it directly to the common Roman practices of dealing with unwanted newborns:

        Direct Killing: He first condemns the outright killing of infants (recens natos liceat oblidere), calling it "the greatest impiety."

        Exposure: He then condemns the more common practice of "exposing" or abandoning infants to die or be picked up by others, arguing it is just as wicked, if not crueler, than strangling them.

    The Refutation of the Excuse (Your Quote): Your passage comes immediately after this condemnation. It serves as Lactantius's direct rebuttal to the primary excuse given by Romans for exposing their children: poverty.

        He labels those who use this excuse "parricides"—a shockingly strong term usually reserved for someone who murders a parent, here applied to those who murder their own offspring.

        He dismisses their economic reasoning with a theological argument: trust in God's providence, who controls wealth and poverty.

        He presents the truly virtuous, Christian alternative: If one genuinely cannot support a child, the moral solution is sexual abstinence, not murder. This contrasts Christian self-control with pagan convenience and violence.

        He concludes by framing infanticide not as a social or economic decision, but as a sacrilegious act: a wicked defilement of God's own creation (Dei opera corrumpat).

In summary, your quote is the ethical climax of a chapter that moves from condemning public violence (gladiators) to private violence (infanticide), all based on the absolute Christian principle of the sanctity of human life as a creation of God.

en: God gave us eyes not to see and desire pleasure, but to see acts performed for the needs of life; so too, the genital [*generating"] part of the body, as the name itself teaches, has been received by us for no other purpose than the generation of offspring [ibid., 6:23:19].
latin: Sicut autem dedit nobis oculos Deus, non ut spectemus, voluptatemque capiamus, sed ut videamus propter eos actus, qui pertinent ad vitae necessitatem, ita genitalem corporis partem, quod nomen ipsum docet, nulla alia causa nisi efficiendae sobolis accepimus.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

The quote is the theological and philosophical anchor for the entire argument of Chapter 23, titled "On the pleasure of touch and lust, and on marriage and continence." Lactantius builds his case in a very structured way:

    God's Original Purpose: Lactantius begins by stating that God created the two sexes and instilled in them a powerful desire for one another. He affirms that this desire is not evil; its God-given purpose is clear: "that by this means, the species might be propagated and multiplied" (ut... propagari et multiplicari genera possent).

    The Adversary's Perversion: He then identifies Satan ("that adversary of ours") as the source of corruption. The devil takes this good, natural desire and perverts it, transferring it "from the right and good to the evil and depraved." This perversion includes lust for what is not one's own (adultery), the creation of brothels (lupanaria), and homosexual acts, which he condemns as "unspeakable unions against nature and against the institution of God" (nefandos coitus contra naturam contraque institutum Dei).

    The Christian Solution: Virtue and Marriage: Faced with this powerful and easily corrupted desire, the Christian's duty is to exercise virtue. For those who cannot control their passions through total continence, God has provided a legitimate outlet: the "prescribed limits of the lawful marriage bed" (intra praescriptum legitimi tori). Within marriage, one can satisfy desire without falling into sin.

    The Teleological Argument (Your Quote): Your quote is the climax of his argument. To prove that the primary and defining purpose of sex is procreation, Lactantius uses an argument from design (a teleological argument).

        The Analogy of the Eyes: He creates a powerful analogy. The eyes give us pleasure, but that is not their purpose. Their purpose is functional: to see, to navigate the world, to perform necessary tasks. Pleasure is a byproduct, not the goal.

        The Argument from Etymology: He applies this same logic to the reproductive organs. He makes a brilliant point that the name itself reveals the purpose: the "genital part" (genitalem partem) is self-evidently for generation (efficiendae sobolis). The root of the word (gignere - to beget) teaches its function.

In summary, your quote is not a standalone statement but the foundational proof in Lactantius's broader argument that sexual desire, while created good by God for the purpose of procreation, must be governed by virtue and confined to marriage to avoid its sinful perversion by the devil.

en: LACTANTIUS Therefore let the philosophers, who enumerate thousands of ages from the beginning of the world, know that the six thousandth year is not yet complete. Therefore, since all the works of God were completed in six days, the world must continue in its present state through six ages, that is, six thousand years. For the great day of God is limited by circle of a thousand years, as the prophet shows who says, 'In your sight, O Lord, a thousand years are as one day" [ Divine Institutes 7:14 (c. A.D. 307)].
latin:
Sciant igitur philosophi, qui ab exordio mundi saeculorum millia enumerant, nondum sextum millesimum annum esse conclusum...

    Ergo quoniam sex diebus cuncta Dei opera perfecta sunt, per saecula sex, id est annorum sex millia, manere hoc statu mundum necesse est. Dies enim magnus Dei mille annorum circulo terminatur, sicut indicat propheta qui dicit: Ante oculos tuos, Domine, mille anni tanquam dies unus.

Additional Relevant Context (from the text you provided)

Your provided text gives the full context for Lactantius's argument. Here is a breakdown of what he is doing:

    Refuting Pagan Philosophies of Time: Lactantius begins the chapter by directly confronting non-Christian views of the world's age. He specifically names Plato, "many other philosophers," and the Chaldeans (Babylonians), who, according to Cicero, claimed to have records going back 470,000 years. Lactantius dismisses this as foolishness (delirant - "they are delirious") because they lack the "divine letters" (Scripture) which provide the true origin and end of the world.

    Establishing a Biblical Timeline: Against the pagan "deep time," Lactantius proposes a timeline based entirely on a typological reading of the Genesis creation account. This is the core of his argument.

    The Six-Day / Six-Thousand-Year Typology: This is the central idea. Lactantius lays out a perfect analogy:

        God's work of creation took six days.

        The history of the world in its current state will last for six "great days."

    The "Day-Age" Principle: To make this typology work, he needs a key to unlock the timing. He finds it in Psalm 90:4 (Psalm 89:4 in the Vulgate): "a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday." This allows him to establish the equation:

        1 Great Day of God = 1,000 Human Years.

        Therefore, 6 Great Days = 6,000 years of world history.

    The Millennial Sabbath: The text you provided continues this logic. Just as God rested on the seventh day and blessed it, so too will there be a seventh "great day" of rest at the end of history.

        ...necesse est, ut in fine sexti millesimi anni malitia omnis aboleatur e terra, et regnet per annos mille justitia; sitque tranquillitas, et requies a laboribus...

        "...it is necessary that at the end of the six thousandth year all wickedness be abolished from the earth, and justice reign for a thousand years; and there will be tranquility and rest from the labors..."

        This thousand-year period is the Millennial Sabbath, a literal era of peace and justice on earth, which Lactantius believed was imminent.

In summary, the passage you've located is Lactantius's masterful attempt to create a complete Christian philosophy of history, refuting paganism and providing believers with a concrete timeline for the end of the age based on a symbolic interpretation of the creation week.

en: LACTANTIUS [A] king shall arise out of Syria, born from an evil spirit, the overthrower and destroyer of the human race, who shall destroy what is left by the former evil, together with himself. But that king will be most disgraceful in himself, and a prophet of lies; and he will call himself God, and will order himself to be worshipped as the Son of God; and power will be given him to do signs and wonders, the sight of which he may entice men to adore him. He will command fire to come down from heaven, and the sun to stand and leave its course, and an image to speak; and these things shall be done at his word. Then he will attempt to destroy the temple of God, and persecute the righteous people [Divine Institutes 7:17 (C. A.D. 307)].
latin: ...alter Rex orietur ex Syria malo spiritu genitus, eversor ac perditor generis humani, qui reliquias illius prioris mali cum ipso simul deleat. ... Rex vero ille teterrimus erit quidem et ipse, sed mendaciorum propheta; et seipsum constituet ac vocabit Deum, et se coli jubebit ut Dei filium: et dabitur ei potestas, ut faciat signa et prodigia, quibus visis, irretiat homines ut adorent eum. Jubebit ignem descendere de coelo, et solem a suis cursibus stare, et imaginem loqui; et fient haec sub verbo ejus... Tunc eruere templum Dei conabitur, et justum populum persequetur...

The passage you've highlighted is Lactantius's vivid description of the Antichrist. However, the full chapter provides a dramatic narrative of the final days, placing this figure within a broader sequence of events.

1. The Coming of the Final Prophet (An Elijah-like Figure):
Before the Antichrist appears, the chapter explains that God will send a "great prophet" with miraculous powers. This prophet will:

    Turn people back to the knowledge of God.

    Perform miracles mirroring those of Elijah and Moses (shutting up the heavens to stop rain, turning water to blood, calling fire from his mouth to consume his enemies).

    Convert many to the worship of the true God.

This figure is Lactantius's interpretation of the "witness" from the Book of Revelation (Chapter 11), who is often identified with the returning prophet Elijah.

2. The Rise of the Antichrist and His Conflict with the Prophet:
Your quote begins by describing the rise of the evil Syrian king in direct opposition to this prophet. The narrative continues:

    The Antichrist will fight against, defeat, and kill God's prophet.

    He will leave the prophet's body unburied for three days.

    After three days, the prophet will miraculously come back to life and be taken up into heaven in the sight of all.

3. The Reign of Terror Begins:
It is only after the removal of this divine witness that the Antichrist's unopposed and horrific reign begins. Your quote describes the start of this period: he demands worship, performs false miracles to deceive humanity, and begins his persecution.

4. The Great Tribulation (What Happens After Your Quote):
The rest of the chapter describes the intensification of this persecution:

    The Antichrist will "mark" his followers like cattle (signabuntur ab eo tanquam pecudes).

    Those who refuse the mark will be hunted, tortured, and killed in exquisite ways.

    He will have a reign of terror lasting "forty-two months" (a direct reference to Revelation 13:5).

    The righteous will flee into the wilderness ("solitudes").

    The Antichrist will pursue them and besiege them on a mountain.

5. The Final Divine Intervention:
Just as the righteous are about to be destroyed, they will cry out to God. God will hear them and send a "great king from heaven" (Christ at his Second Coming) who will destroy the Antichrist and all the wicked with "fire and sword."

In summary, your quote is a crucial part of a larger apocalyptic narrative that Lactantius constructed, drawing heavily on biblical sources like the books of Daniel and Revelation. It is set within the classic end-times drama of a final prophet, a tyrannical Antichrist, a great tribulation, and the ultimate victorious return of Christ.

en: LACTANTIUS But when he shall have judged the righteous, he will also try them with fire. Then they whose sins shall exceed either in weight or in number shall be scorched by the fire and burned. But they whom full justice and maturity of virtue has imbued will not see that fire; for they have something of God in themselves that repels and rejects the violence of the flame. So great is the force of innocence that the flame shrinks from it without doing harm; it has received this power from God, that it burns the wicked, and is under the command of the righteous [Divine Institutes 7:21 (c. A.D. 307)].
latin: Sed et justos cum judicaverit, etiam in igni eos examinabit. Tum quorum peccata vel pondere, vel numero praevaluerint, perstringentur igni atque amburentur: quos autem plena justitia et maturitas virtutis incoxerit, ignem illum non sentient; habent enim aliquid in se Dei, quod vim flammae repellat, ac respuat. Tanta vis est innocentiae, ut ab ea ignis ille refugiat innoxius; qui accepit a Deo hanc potentiam, ut impios urat, justis obtemperet.
