context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Context

The passage is from Book 2, Chapter 27 of Origen's Commentary on John. The immediate context is an allegorical interpretation of the names surrounding the birth of John the Baptist:

    Zacharias: "Memory" (of God).

    Elizabeth: "Oath of my God" or, crucially for this passage, "Seventh of my God."

    John: "Grace of God."

Origen argues that John the Baptist (Grace) is born at the very end of the Old Covenant, which is symbolized by his mother, Elizabeth, as the "Seventh." The Old Testament, he says, is the "culmination of the Sabbath rest" (σαββατισμοῦ κορωνίς).
2. The Theological Argument

This context is the key to understanding the quote. Origen's argument flows like this:

    The "Seventh Day" (the Sabbath, symbolized by Elizabeth) represents the entirety of the Old Covenant law and its rest.

    This Old Covenant system has reached its fulfillment and end. Therefore, it cannot give birth to or generate the new form of rest.

    The new rest is the "rest after the Sabbath"—a clear reference to the Lord's Day (Sunday), the Eighth Day, the day of Resurrection.

    This new reality is not a product of the old law. Instead, "it is our Savior" who actively creates (ἐμποιοῦντος / ingenerante) this new rest within us.

3. Christocentric and Baptismal Focus

The passage is profoundly Christocentric. The new rest is not merely a change in the calendar; it is a participation in Christ's own life. Origen explains that the Savior creates this rest in us by making us "in the likeness of his death, and hence also of his Resurrection." This is a direct reference to the theology of Baptism found in Romans 6:4-5. We enter the true, eternal rest by being sacramentally united to Christ's Paschal Mystery.

In summary, Origen uses the symbolism of the names to draw a sharp theological line between the Sabbath of the Old Covenant and the Lord's Day of the New Covenant. The former is a type that has passed away; the latter is the reality of Resurrection life, actively brought into being by Christ himself in the souls of the baptized.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA And [Jn 1:21] they asked him. "What then? Are you Elijah?" And he said, "I am not." No one can fail to remember in this connection what Jesus says of John [Mt 11:14], "If you will receive it, this is Elijah which is to come." Why, then, does John say to those who ask him, "Are you Elijah?" "I am not." And how can it be also true that John iS Elijah who is to come, according to the words of Malachi [Mal 4:5-6], "And behold send unto you Elijah the Tishbite, before the great and notable day of the Lord come, who shall restore the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbor, lest come, and utterly smite the earth." The words of the angel of the Lord, too, who appeared to Zacharias, as he stood at the right hand of the altar of incense, are similar to the prophecy of Malachi: "And [Lk 1:13] your wife Elizabeth shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John." And a little further on: "And he shall go before his face in the spirit and power of Elijah to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared for him." [Lk 1:17] As for the first point, one might say that John did not know that he was Elijah. This will be the explanation chosen by those who find in our passage support for their doctrine of transcorporation, as if the soul clothed itself in a fresh body and did not remember its former lives. These thinkers will also point out that some of the Jews assented to this doctrine when they spoke about the Savior as if he were one of the old prophets, and had risen not from the tomb but from his birth. His mother Mary was well known. and Joseph the carpenter was supposed to be his father. and t could readily be supposed that he was one of the old prophets risen from the dead. The same person will offer the text in Genesis, "I will destroy the whole resurrection." and will thereby reduce those who find in Scripture solutions of false probabilities a great difficulty in respect of this doctrine. Another, however, a churchman, who repudiates the doctrine of transcorporation as a false one, and does not admit that the soul of John ever was Elijah, may appeal to the words of the angel, and point out that it is not the soul of Elijah that is spoken of at John's birth, but the spirit and power of Elijah [Commentary on John 6:7 (c. A.D. 229)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is a masterful example of Origen's dialectical method of exegesis and a crucial text for early Christian doctrine.
The Central Problem

Origen identifies a clear contradiction in Scripture:

    Jesus says: John the Baptist is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14).

    John the Baptist says: When asked "Are you Elijah?", he replies "I am not" (John 1:21).

Origen does not ignore this difficulty. Instead, he uses it as an opportunity to explore different interpretations and refute a dangerous heresy.
The Two Opposing Arguments

Origen sets up a debate between two hypothetical figures to represent the different schools of thought.

    The Proponent of "Transcorporation" (μετενσωμάτωσις / transcorporatio)

        This is Origen's term for the doctrine of reincarnation or the transmigration of souls, a concept found in some Greek philosophical (e.g., Platonic, Pythagorean) and Gnostic circles.

        Their Argument: John the Baptist literally was Elijah. His soul had been reborn in a new body. The reason he denied it ("I am not") was simply that he did not remember his past life.

        Their "Evidence": They would point to the fact that some Jews thought Jesus was John the Baptist or another prophet "risen" (i.e., reincarnated), suggesting this belief was common.

    "The Churchman" (ὁ ἐκκλησιαστικός / ecclesiasticus)

        This is Origen's term for the orthodox Christian, the one who holds to the rule of faith of the Church. This represents Origen's own position.

        Their Argument: The orthodox Christian "repudiates the doctrine of transcorporation as a false one." John's soul was never Elijah's soul.

        Their Evidence: The key is the precise wording of the angel Gabriel to Zechariah (Luke 1:17). The angel did not say John would have the soul of Elijah, but that he would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah."

Origen's Orthodox Conclusion

By siding with "the Churchman," Origen establishes the definitive Christian interpretation:

    The connection between Elijah and John is one of mission, role, and spiritual power, not of a shared soul or identity.

    John is the "new Elijah" because he fulfills the same prophetic role as a forerunner, preparing the way for the Lord with the same zeal and power.

    The doctrine of reincarnation is explicitly rejected as incompatible with Christian faith.

This passage is therefore historically significant as one of the clearest and most influential refutations of reincarnation by a major Church Father.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA But some say, basing it on tradition in the Gospel according to Peter, as it is called, or "The Book [Protoevangelium] of James," that the brothers of Jesus were sons of Joseph by a former wife, whom he married before Mary. Now those who say so wish to preserve the honor of Mary in virginity to the end, sO that her body, which was appointed to minister to the Word, which said, "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you" [Lk 1:35], might not know intercourse with a man after the Holy Spirit came into her and the power from on high overshadowed her. And think it reasonable that Jesus was the first fruit among men of the purity that consists in chastity, and Mary among women; for it is not pious to ascribe to any other than her the first fruit of virginity [ Commentary on Matthew 10:17 (C. A.D. 249)].

Τοὺς δὲ ἀδελφοὺς Ἰησοῦ, φασί τινες εἶναι, ἐκ παραδόσεως ὁρμώμενοι τοῦ ἐπιγεγραμμένου κατὰ Πέτρον Εὐαγγελίου, ἢ τῆς βίβλου Ἰακώβου, υἱοὺς Ἰωσὴφ ἐκ προτέρας γυναικός, συνῳκηκυίας αὐτῷ πρὸ τῆς Μαρίας.

    Οἱ δὲ ταῦτα λέγοντες τὸ ἀξίωμα τῆς Μαρίας ἐν παρθενίᾳ τηρεῖν μέχρι τέλους βούλονται, ἵνα μὴ τὸ κριθὲν ἐκεῖνο σῶμα διακονήσασθαι τῷ εἰπόντι Λόγῳ· «Πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπελεύσεται ἐπὶ σὲ, καὶ δύναμις Ὑψίστου ἐπισκιάσει σοι,» γνῷ κοίτην ἀνδρὸς μετὰ τὸ ἐπελθεῖν ἐν αὐτῇ Πνεῦμα ἅγιον, καὶ τὴν ἐπεσκιακυῖαν αὐτῇ δύναμιν ἐξ ὕψους. Καὶ οἶμαι λόγον ἔχειν, ἀνδρῶν μὲν καθαρότητος τῆς ἐν ἁγνείᾳ ἀπαρχὴν γεγονέναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν, γυναικῶν δὲ τὴν Μαριάμ· οὐ γὰρ εὔφημον, ἄλλην παρ' ἐκείνην τὴν ἀπαρχὴν τῆς παρθενίας ἐπιγράψασθαι.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Full Citation: The passage is from Origen of Alexandria, Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, Book X, Chapter 17. The standard Migne citation for this text is Patrologia Graeca (PG) 13, columns 876-877.

    Historical Context (The "Brethren of the Lord"): This quote is one of the earliest and most influential patristic texts addressing the question of Jesus's "brothers" (Greek: adelphoi) mentioned in the Gospels. Origen presents a solution that would become dominant in the Eastern Orthodox tradition.

    Source of the Tradition: Origen explicitly states that this explanation does not come from the canonical Gospels but from apocryphal texts:

        "Gospel according to Peter": A now-fragmentary apocryphal gospel.

        "The Book of James": This is the famous Protoevangelium of James, a 2nd-century infancy narrative. This text is the primary source for the tradition that Joseph was an elderly widower who had children from a previous marriage and was chosen as a guardian, not a husband in the typical sense, for Mary.

    Motive: Mary's Perpetual Virginity: Origen is crystal clear about the theological motive behind this tradition: to "preserve the honor of Mary in virginity to the end." He argues that the body consecrated by the Holy Spirit to be the vessel for the Word Incarnate should not subsequently engage in normal marital relations. This is a very early and powerful witness to the developing doctrine of Mary's perpetual virginity.

    "First Fruits of Virginity": The passage concludes with a beautiful and theologically rich parallel. Origen presents Jesus as the "first fruit" (aparchē) of chastity for all men, and Mary as the "first fruit" of virginity for all women. This elevates Mary's virginity from a mere biological fact to a paradigm-shifting spiritual reality, setting a new standard of holiness and consecration for the Church.

en: As for the spirits of the prophets, these are given to them by God and are spoken of as being in a way their property, as "The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" [1 Cor 14:32] and "The spirit of Elijah rested upon Elisha" [2 Kgs 2:15]. Thus, it is said, there iS nothing absurd in supposing that John, "in the spirit and power of Elijah," turned the hearts of the fathers to the children and that it was on account of this spirit that he was called "Elijah who is to come" [ibid.].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. Source and Context:

    Work: Origen of Alexandria, Commentary on the Gospel of John, Book VI, Chapter 7.

    Theological Problem: Origen is tackling a famous scriptural difficulty: Jesus says John the Baptist is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14), but in the Gospel of John, when asked directly "Are you Elijah?", John says, "I am not" (John 1:21).

2. Refutation of Reincarnation:
The primary purpose of this entire section of Origen's commentary is to refute the doctrine of reincarnation or the transmigration of souls (μετενσωμάτωσις, metensomatosis), which some were using to explain the apparent contradiction. Origen, representing the orthodox or "ecclesiastical" view, firmly rejects the idea that Elijah's soul (ψυχή, psyche) was literally reborn in John's body.

3. Origen's Nuanced Solution:
Origen’s solution, articulated in the passage you found, is a brilliant distinction between a person's soul and their spirit.

    The soul (ψυχή) is unique to the individual. Elijah's soul is his own.

    The spirit (πνεῦμα) of a prophet is a gift from God. It is the divine power, the specific charism, and the prophetic office through which they operate.

4. The Power of Biblical Precedent:
To prove this point, Origen uses two key Old Testament passages:

    2 Kings 2:15: When Elisha receives a "double portion" of Elijah's spirit, it is a clear biblical precedent for a prophetic spirit being transferred from one person to another without any hint of reincarnation.

    1 Corinthians 14:32: The fact that the "spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" shows that this divine gift is something a prophet can possess and control; it is "their property" (κτήματα) in a certain sense, distinct from their own soul.

Therefore, John the Baptist can truthfully say "I am not" Elijah (because his soul is not Elijah's), while Jesus can truthfully say he is the coming Elijah (because he operates in the same prophetic spirit and power).

en: If the doctrine [of reincarnation] was widely current, ought not John to have hesitated to pronounce upon it, lest his soul had actually been in Elijah? And here our churchman will appeal to history, and will bid his antagonists [to] ask experts of the secret doctrines of the Hebrews if they really entertain such a belief. For if it should appear that they do not, then the argument based on that supposition is shown to be baseless [ibid.].
latin:
Quomodo autem rationi consentaneum non erat, si multorum tum temporis dogma hoc fuisset, ut dubitaret Joannes de seipso, num quando anima sua in Elia fuerit?

    Quin ad historiam provocabit ecclesiasticus illum priorem auditurum ab his, qui se scire profitentur quæ apud Hebræos arcana sunt, nun dogma aliquod hujusmodi sit apud ipsos; nam si nullo loco appareat, hoc hunc in modum se habere, perspicuum est illius prioris rationem dissipatam esse.

Πῶς δὲ οὐκ ἦν εὔλογον, εἰ πολλῶν τοῦτο δόγμα ἐτύγχανεν, ἐπισχεῖν τὸν Ἰωάννην περὶ αὐτοῦ, μήποτε ἡ ψυχή αὐτοῦ ποτε ἐν Ἠλίᾳ ἦν;

    Καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν δὲ ὁ ἐκκλησιαστικός προκαλέσεται τὸν πρότερον πευσόμενον παρὰ τῶν τὰ ἀπόῤῥητα εγνωκέναι παρ' Ἑβραίοις ἐπαγγελλομένων, εἰ τοιοῦτόν τι δόγμα ἐστὶ παρ' αὐτοῖς· ἐὰν γὰρ μηδαμῶς φαίνηται τοῦθ' οὕτως ἔχον, δῆλον, ὅτι ἐσκέδασται ὁ τοῦ προτέρου λόγος.
context:
Additional Relevant Details and Context

This passage is a masterful example of Origen's dialectical method. He is tackling the apparent contradiction between Jesus saying John "is Elijah" (Matt. 11:14) and John the Baptist saying "I am not" Elijah (John 1:21).

    The Two Debaters: Origen creates a fictional debate to explore the issue.

        The Proponent of Reincarnation: This figure argues that John's soul was indeed Elijah's, but he had simply forgotten his previous life—a common feature in theories of reincarnation (metensomatosis).

        The "Churchman" (ὁ ἐκκλησιαστικός): This is Origen's voice, representing the orthodox position. He systematically dismantles the reincarnationist argument.

    The Churchman's Argument (Your Quote): The quote you selected is the core of the Churchman's refutation, which has two parts:

        A Logical Argument: The Churchman argues that if reincarnation were a widely held and plausible doctrine, John the Baptist—a great prophet filled with the Spirit—would not have given a flat denial. He would have expressed uncertainty or "hesitated" (ἐπισχεῖν) about the matter, acknowledging the possibility. His absolute certainty ("I am not") implies that the doctrine itself is foreign and untrue.

        An Appeal to History: This is the most brilliant part. The Churchman challenges his opponent to go beyond speculation and do historical research. He says, "Go ask the experts in the secret doctrines of the Hebrews" (τὰ ἀπόῤῥητα... παρ' Ἑβραίοις). Origen is confident that an honest inquiry into authentic Jewish tradition will reveal no such doctrine of reincarnation, thereby proving that the opponent's entire premise is "baseless" (ἐσκέδασται - scattered, dissipated).

    Origen's Orthodox Solution: The Churchman's (and Origen's) final solution to the problem is not reincarnation. It is based on the angel's words to Zechariah in Luke 1:17: John would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah," not with the same soul. The connection is one of spiritual succession and typological fulfillment, not a literal transmigration of souls.

You have pinpointed a classic passage where Origen confronts a non-Christian philosophical idea, refutes it using logic and an appeal to historical evidence, and affirms the orthodox scriptural interpretation.

en: Someone might say, however, that Herod and some of those of the people held the false dogma of the transmigration of souls into bodies, so that they thought that the former John had appeared again by a fresh birth, and had come from the dead into life as Jesus. But the time between the birth of John and the birth of Jesus, which was not more than six months, does not permit this false opinion to be believed. And perhaps some idea like this was in the mind of Herod, that the powers that worked in John had passed over to Jesus, in consequence of which he was thought by the people to be John the Baptist. And one might use the following argument: Just as because of the spirit and the power of Elijah, and not because of his soul, it is said about John, "This is Elijah who is to come" [Mt 11:14] . . So Herod thought that the powers in John's case caused in him works of baptism and teaching for John did not do one miracle [In 10:41]- but in Jesus [they caused] miraculous portents [Commentary on Matthew 10:20 (c. A.D. 249)].

Dixerit vero quispiam falsæ illi de corporum permutatione sententiæ Herodem, et e plebe nonnullos adhæsisse, qua adducerentur ut crederent hunc olim Joannem fuisse cum nasceretur, et e mortuis remeasse ad vitam, tanquam Jesum: sed quominus falsa ea opinio probabilis habeatur, impedimento est tempus non sex mensibus longius, quod ortum Joannis et Jesu intercessit.

Λέγοι δ' ἄν τις τὴν τῆς μετενσωματώσεως ψευδοδοξίαν γεγονέναι ἐν τῷ Ἡρώδῃ καί τισι τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ, ἀφ' ἧς ᾤοντο τόν ποτε Ἰωάννην ἐν γενέσει γενέσθαι, καὶ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐληλυθέναι εἰς τὸν βίον, ὡς Ἰησοῦν· ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ ταύτην τὴν ψευδοδοξίαν πιθανὴν ἐᾷ νομισθῆναι ὁ μεταξὺ χρόνος τῆς γενέσεως Ἰωάννου καὶ Ἰησοῦ, οὐ πλεῖον μηνῶν ἓξ τυγχάνων.

    Τάχα δὲ μᾶλλον τοιαύτη τις ὑπόληψις ἦν ἐν τῷ Ἡρώδῃ, ὅτι αἱ ἐνεργήσασαι δυνάμεις ἐν τῷ Ἰωάννῃ μετέστησαν ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ἀφ᾽ ὧν Ἰωάννης Βαπτιστὴς εἶναι πεπίστευτο ἐν τῷ λαῷ· καὶ χρήσαιτό τις ἐπιχειρήματι τοιούτῳ· Ὥσπερ διὰ τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ τὴν δύναμιν Ἠλίου, καὶ οὐ διὰ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ, περὶ Ἰωάννου λέγεται· «Αὐτός ἐστιν Ἠλίας ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι,» ... οὕτως ᾤετο ὁ Ἡρώδης τὰς ἐν Ἰωάννῃ δυνάμεις ἐν μὲν τῷ Ἰωάννῃ ἐνηργηκέναι τὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος καὶ τῆς διδασκαλίας· «Ἰωάννης γὰρ ἐποίησε σημεῖον οὐδὲ ἕν·» ἐν δὲ τῷ Ἰησοῦ τὰς τεραστίους δυνάμεις.
context:
This is a classic example of Origen's brilliant exegetical method, where he explores and refutes incorrect interpretations before proposing a more theologically sound one.

    The Problem: Herod's statement is nonsensical if taken literally. Jesus and John were known contemporaries with different parents. How could Herod think Jesus was John?

    Option 1: Reincarnation (Refuted): Origen first considers the possibility that Herod held a belief in "metensomatosis" (μετενσωμάτωσις), the pagan doctrine of the transmigration of souls into new bodies (reincarnation). He immediately dismisses this with sharp logic: the timeline makes it impossible. John and Jesus were born only six months apart. There was no time for John's soul to die and be reborn in the infant Jesus. This serves as a powerful early Christian refutation of reincarnation.

    Option 2: Transference of "Powers" (Proposed): Origen then offers his preferred explanation. He suggests Herod wasn't thinking of the soul, but of the divine "powers" (δυνάμεις / virtutes) that animated the prophets.

    The Elijah-John Analogy: To support this, he uses the perfect scriptural parallel. The New Testament says John the Baptist came in the "spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17) and Jesus calls him "the Elijah who is to come" (Matt. 11:14). This doesn't mean John's soul was Elijah's. It means the same prophetic spirit and power that worked in Elijah now worked in John.

    Origen's Conclusion: He applies this same logic to Herod's statement. Herod likely thought that the "powers" that were in John (which manifested as baptism and teaching, but notably not miracles) had now transferred to Jesus and were manifesting in a new, more powerful way—as "miraculous portents." This explains both why Herod connected Jesus to John and why Jesus's ministry was different (i.e., full of miracles, whereas John performed none).

en: Now the Canaanite woman, having come, worshipped Jesus as God, saying, 'Lord, help me, but he answered and said, "It is not possible to take the children's bread and cast it to the little dogs." . [O]thers, then, who are strangers to the doctrine of the Church, assume that souls pass from the bodies of men into the bodies of dogs, according to their varying degree of wickedness: but we do not find this at all in the divine Scripture [ibid., 11:17].

    Ἄλλοι μὲν οὖν ὑπολαμβανέτωσαν ξένοι τοῦ ἐκκλησιαστικοῦ λόγου μεταβαίνειν τὰς ψυχὰς ἀπὸ σωμάτων ἀνθρώπων ἐπὶ σώματα κύνεια κατὰ τὴν διάφορον κακίαν· ἡμεῖς δὲ, μηδαμῶς τοῦτο εὑρίσκοντες ἐν τῇ θείᾳ Γραφῇ...
context:
2. Theological Context: Worshipping Jesus "as God"

Origen pays extremely close attention to the titles and actions directed toward Jesus in the Gospels. He notes that some people (like the blind men) call Jesus "Son of David," recognizing him as the messiah. Others, like the demons, call him "Son of God" out of a kind of terrified knowledge. But Origen highlights that the Canaanite woman "worshipped Jesus as God" (προσεκύνει ὡς Θεῷ τῷ Ἰησοῦ). For Origen, this is a profound act demonstrating a higher level of faith. She is not merely appealing to a prophet or a king, but to the divine Lord himself.
3. Theological Context: Refutation of Reincarnation (Metempsychosis)

This is the most significant part of the passage. Origen is famous for his highly speculative theology, particularly concerning the pre-existence of souls. His opponents later accused him of various heresies, sometimes including a belief in reincarnation.

However, this passage is one of the clearest statements where Origen explicitly rejects the doctrine of transmigration of souls into animal bodies (metempsychosis).

    Who He is Arguing Against: When he speaks of "strangers to the doctrine of the Church" (ξένοι τοῦ ἐκκλησιαστικοῦ λόγου), he is referring to Gnostics and followers of certain Greek philosophies (like Platonism and Pythagoreanism) who did teach that human souls could be reincarnated into animals as a form of punishment.

    His Standard of Truth: Origen’s basis for rejecting this doctrine is clear and orthodox: "we do not find this at all in the divine Scripture." This is his ultimate authority for rejecting the teaching.

    Origen's Allegorical Alternative: Instead of literal reincarnation, Origen argues that a "dog" in Scripture is a symbol for a soul that, through sin, shamelessness, and vice, has become irrational like a dog. The change is moral and spiritual, not a physical transmigration of the soul into an animal's body. He writes that a "more rational constitution" can change into a "more irrational one" through vice, and vice-versa through virtue.

This passage is therefore crucial for understanding Origen's actual teaching and defending him against the later accusation that he believed in the transmigration of souls into animals. He firmly rejects it as unscriptural and foreign to the Church.

en: In this place when Jesus said Elijah had come and referred to John the Baptist] it does not appear to me that by Elijah the soul is spoken of, lest fall into the doctrine of transmigration, which is foreign to the Church of God, and not handed down by the apostles, nor anywhere set forth in the Scriptures [ibid., 13:1].

context:
Theological and Historical Context

This passage is profoundly significant for several reasons:

    The Exegetical Problem: Jesus's statement that Elijah had already come (referring to John the Baptist) created a potential theological problem. Some could interpret this to mean that the literal soul of Elijah had been reincarnated in the body of John.

    Origen's Orthodox Stance: Origen confronts this potential misinterpretation head-on. He explicitly states that Jesus is not talking about Elijah's soul. He then gives three powerful reasons for rejecting the doctrine of transmigration of souls (Greek: μετενσωμάτωσις, metensomatosis):

        It is "foreign to the Church of God" (ἀλλότριον τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τοῦ Θεοῦ), meaning it is not part of the authentic Christian faith.

        It was "not handed down by the apostles" (οὔτε παραδιδόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποστόλων), meaning it lacks apostolic authority and is not part of the sacred tradition.

        It is "not anywhere set forth in the Scriptures" (οὔτε ἐμφαινόμενόν που τῶν Γραφῶν), meaning it has no biblical foundation.

    The "Spirit and Power" Interpretation: Origen, consistent with the rest of early Christian interpretation, understood the connection between Elijah and John to be one of "spirit and power" (as described in Luke 1:17), not one of a shared soul. They shared a similar mission, prophetic role, and spiritual intensity as forerunners for the Lord.

    Significance in the "Origenist Controversies": This quote is of immense historical importance because Origen himself was later (posthumously) condemned for heresies, including a complex doctrine of the pre-existence of souls. This very passage is often used by scholars to show that, whatever his speculative theories were about the soul's pre-existence, Origen clearly and firmly rejected the specific doctrine of earthly reincarnation as it was commonly understood (i.e., the transmigration of a single soul into different bodies on earth). He saw it as a non-Christian, un-apostolic, and un-biblical teaching.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA But if the Greeks, who introduce the doctrine of transmigration, laying down things in harmony with it, do not acknowledge that the world is coming to corruption, it is fitting that when they have looked the Scriptures straight in the face, which plainly declare that the world will perish, they should either disbelieve them or invent a series of arguments about the interpretation of things concerning the consummation, which even if they wish they will not be able to do [ibid.].
latin: Quod si qui transitum animarum in varia corpora invehunt ethnici, utpote consentanea doctrinæ huic astruentes, mundi interitum necessario non admittunt, superest ut, postquam Scripturis mundi occasum asserentibus palam refragati fuerint, vel fidem iis non habeant, vel verba reperiant quibus ea quæ ad consummationem pertinent explicare possint, quod facere neutiquam poterunt, etiamsi velint.
greek: Εἰ δὲ ἀναγκαίως οἱ τὴν μετενσωμάτωσιν εἰσάγοντες Ἕλληνες, ὡς ἀκόλουθα αὐτοῖς τιθέντες, οὐδὲ φθείρεσθαι βούλονται τὸν κόσμον, ὥρα καὶ τούτους ἀντιβλέψαντας ταῖς ἐκφαινούσαις Γραφαῖς φθαρήσεσθαι τὸν κόσμον, ἢ ἀπιστῆσαι αὐταῖς, ἢ εὐρεσιλογεῖν περὶ διηγήσεως τῶν κατὰ τὴν συντέλειαν, ὅπερ, κἂν βούλωνται, ποιῆσαι οὐ δυνήσονται.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. The Immediate Context: Elijah and John the Baptist
The entire chapter is a response to the question of whether John the Baptist was a reincarnated Elijah. Origen firmly rejects this. He argues that John came in the "spirit and power" of Elijah (Luke 1:17), not that Elijah's soul had entered John's body. He explicitly states that the doctrine of transmigration (μετενσωμάτωσις) is "foreign to the Church of God" and not taught by the apostles or found in Scripture.

2. Origen's Core Argument Against Reincarnation
Origen's main weapon against the doctrine of reincarnation is Christian eschatology—the teaching about the end of the world. His logic is as follows:

    The doctrine of transmigration requires an endless or extremely long cycle of rebirths for souls to be purified or punished. This implies a world that is essentially eternal.

    The Christian Scriptures, however, are absolutely clear that "the world will perish" (φθαρήσεσθαι τὸν κόσμον). Passages like "Heaven and earth will pass away" (Matt. 24:35) and "the present form of this world is passing away" (1 Cor. 7:31) affirm a definitive end.

    Therefore, the two systems are fundamentally incompatible. You cannot have both an endless cycle of rebirth and a final consummation of the world.

3. The Significance of Your Quote
The passage you selected is Origen's concluding challenge. He pits the pagan philosophers directly against the authority of Scripture. He says if "the Greeks" (the originators of the transmigration doctrine) want to hold their view, they must confront the Bible's clear teaching about the end of the world. This leaves them with only three losing options:

    Disbelieve the Scriptures: Openly reject Christian revelation.

    Invent an interpretation: Try to explain away the plain meaning of the biblical texts about the end times (εὐρεσιλογεῖν - literally "to be clever with words," to quibble or invent specious arguments).

    Fail: Origen concludes that even if they try the second option, they will be unable to succeed, because the biblical teaching is too clear.

This passage is a powerful example of Origen acting as a staunch defender of biblical doctrine against what he saw as a dangerous and incompatible philosophical import.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA f we were to attend carefully to the Gospels, we should also find, in relation to those things that seem to be common to Peter great difference and a preeminence in the things [Jesus] said to Peter, compared with the second class [of apostles]. For it is no small difference that Peter received the keys not of one heaven but of more, and in order that whatever things he binds on earth may be bound not in one heaven but in them all, as compared with the many who bind on earth and loose on earth, so that these things are bound and loosed not in [all] the heavens, as in the case of Peter, but in only one: for they do not reach so high a stage of power as Peter to bind and loose in all the heavens [ Commentary on Matthew 13:31 (c. A.D. 249)].
latin: Quod si nos quoque attendentes diligenter precaremur Evangeliis, inveniremus et in ipsis, juxta ea quae videntur esse communia, magnam differentiam et praestantiam eorum quae dicta sunt ad Petrum prae secundis. Non enim parva differentia est, Petrum claves non unius coeli sed plurium accepisse, et ut quaecumque ligaverit super terram, non in uno coelo, sed in omnibus coelis sint ligata; comparatione multorum qui ligaverunt super terram et solverunt super terram, ut haec non in coelis, sicut Petrus, sed in uno sint ligata et soluta: non enim ad tantum potentiae perveniunt, quantum Petrus, ut in omnibus coelis ligent et solvant.
greek: Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς εὐχόμενοι εὐλαβῶς προσέχοιμεν τοῖς Εὐαγγελίοις, εὕροιμεν ἂν καὶ ἐν αὐτοῖς, κατὰ τὰ δοκοῦντα εἶναι κοινά, πολλὴν διαφορὰν καὶ ὑπεροχὴν τῶν εἰρημένων πρὸς τὸν Πέτρον παρὰ τὰ δεύτερα. Οὐ γὰρ μικρὰ διαφορὰ τὸ τὸν Πέτρον κλεῖδας μὴ ἑνὸς οὐρανοῦ ἀλλὰ πλειόνων εἰληφέναι, καὶ ἵνα ἃ ἂν δήσῃ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, μὴ ἐν ἑνὶ οὐρανῷ ἀλλ' ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς οὐρανοῖς ᾖ δεδεμένα· συγκρίσει τῶν πολλῶν δησάντων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς καὶ λυσάντων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὥστε ταῦτα μὴ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, ὡς τὸν Πέτρον, ἀλλ' ἐν ἑνὶ δεδέσθαι τε καὶ λελύσθαι· οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον ἰσχύος φθάνουσι ὅσον ὁ Πέτρος, ὥστε ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς οὐρανοῖς δεσμεύειν καὶ λύειν.
context:
Additional Context and Details

    Hierarchical View: This passage is a prime example of Origen's view of a certain hierarchy among the apostles. While all apostles receive the power to bind and loose, Peter's authority is presented as greater in scope and degree.

    Spiritual Interpretation: Origen's mention of "more heavens" (πλειόνων οὐρανῶν) reflects his spiritual and cosmological worldview, influenced by Platonic thought. He often speaks of multiple spiritual levels or heavens. For him, Peter's authority operates on the highest spiritual planes, while that of the other apostles is effective on a lower (though still heavenly) plane.

    Significance: This text has been cited for centuries in discussions about the Petrine Primacy. It shows that even in the 3rd century, a major theologian saw a unique preeminence in the authority given to St. Peter, distinguishing it from the authority given to the other apostles collectively.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA And even he who withholds himself from his wife often makes her an adulteress when he does not satisfy her desires, even though he does so under the appearance of greater gravity and self-control. And perhaps this man is more culpable who, sO far as it rests with him, makes her an adulteress when he does not satisfy her desires than he who, for other reason than fornication, has sent her away-for poisoning or murder or any of the most grievous sins. But as a woman is an adulteress, even though she seems to be married to man, while the former husband is still living so also the man who seems to marry her who has been put away, does not so much marry her as commit adultery with her according to the declaration of our Savior [Commentaries on Matthew 14:24 (c. A.D. 249)].

Quemadmodum autem adultera est uxor, etiamsi viro alteri nupta videatur, priore etiamnum vivo; ita et virum repudiatam duxisse visum, non tam ipsius maritum, quam adulterum esse dicendum, a Servatore nostro demonstratum est.

Ὥσπερ δὲ μοιχαλίς ἐστι γυνή, κἂν δοκῇ γαμεῖσθαι ἀνδρὶ, ἔτι ζῶντος τοῦ προτέρου· οὕτως καὶ ἀνὴρ δοκῶν γαμεῖν ἀπολελυμένην οὐ γαμεῖ, κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν ἀπόφασιν, ὅσον μοιχεύει.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Correct Citation: The passage is from Origen's Commentary on Matthew, Book 14, Section 24. The text being commented on is Matthew 19:9, not Matthew 14. This is a very common type of citation where "14" refers to the book number of the commentary, not the chapter of the gospel.

    Source: The parallel Greek and Latin text you provided is from Migne's Patrologia Graeca (PG), Volume 13, columns 1248-1249.

    Theological Context: Origen's argument is remarkably nuanced.

        The Pastoral Problem: He begins by wrestling with a "hard case." Jesus forbids divorce "except for fornication." Origen asks: What if a wife commits a crime that seems worse than fornication, like murdering her own child or trying to poison her husband? He acknowledges that forcing a man to live with a murderer seems unreasonable (ἄλογον), but violating Christ's command is impious (ἀσεβές).

        The Pivot to Internal Culpability: Leaving that difficult question unresolved, Origen pivots to a more subtle point. He argues that a husband can cause his wife to commit adultery not just by the legal act of divorce, but by his personal actions within the marriage.

        The "Pious" Husband: His primary target is the husband who withholds conjugal relations out of a misguided sense of spiritual superiority ("under the appearance of greater gravity and self-control"). Origen, echoing St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 7, states that this action directly creates the occasion for his wife to sin by not satisfying her legitimate desires (μὴ ἐκπληρῶν αὐτῆς τὰς ὀρέξεις).

        A Radical Comparison: He then makes a shocking claim: this "pious" husband is perhaps more culpable (τάχα μᾶλλον ἐπίληπτος) than the man who divorces his murderous wife. Origen's logic is that the latter is reacting to a terrible evil already done, whereas the former, out of his own spiritual pride, is actively creating the conditions for a future sin.

        Conclusion on Remarriage: He finishes by grounding his entire reflection in Jesus's core teaching: just as a woman who remarries while her first husband lives is an adulteress, so too a man who marries a divorced woman "does not so much marry her as commit adultery with her." This reaffirms the indissolubility of marriage as the foundation of his argument.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA Why, when the Lord himself told his disciples that they should baptize all peoples in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, does this apostle [Paul] employ the name of Christ alone in baptism, saying, "We who have been baptized into Christ"; for indeed, legitimate baptism is had only in the name of the Trinity [Commentary on Romans 5:8 (c. A.D. 248)].
latin: Requiras fortassis etiam hoc, quod cum ipse Dominus dixerit ad discipulos ut baptizarent omnes gentes in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus sancti, cur hic Apostolus solius Christi in baptismo nomen assumpserit dicens: "Quicunque baptizati sumus in Christo," cum utique non habeatur legitimum baptisma, nisi sub nomine Trinitatis.

Additional Relevant Details

This passage is significant for several reasons, and the context found in your image is crucial.

1. Origen's Solution to the "Problem":
The quote you selected is Origen posing the question. His brilliant answer comes in the very next sentences of the text you provided:

    Latin Text of the Answer: Sed intuere prudentiam Pauli, quoniam quidem in præsenti loco non tam baptismatis rationem, quam mortis Christi discutere cupiebat... Et non erat utique conveniens, ut ubi de morte dicebat, vel Patrem nominaret, vel Spiritum sanctum.

    English Translation: "But consider the prudence of Paul, since in this present passage he desired to discuss not so much the full rite of baptism as the death of Christ... And it was certainly not suitable, where he was speaking of death, to name either the Father or the Holy Spirit."

In short, Origen's answer is that Paul was not giving the full baptismal formula here. Paul's specific theological point in Romans 6 was about our union with Christ's death, so he appropriately focused only on Christ's name to make his point. He wasn't replacing the Trinitarian formula, but rather highlighting one aspect of its effect.

2. The Original Language is Lost:
Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–254 AD) wrote in Greek. However, his Commentary on Romans survives almost entirely in the Latin translation of Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 345–411 AD). This is a critical piece of information for any scholarly study, as the text we have is filtered through a translator writing over a century later.

3. A Powerful Witness to Early Christian Practice:
This passage is one of the most important early proofs that the Trinitarian formula for baptism was considered standard, essential, and "legitimate" by the mid-3rd century. Origen treats the Trinitarian formula as the undisputed norm and feels the need to explain why Paul's phrasing in Romans 6 is not a contradiction to that norm.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA t is not possible to receive forgiveness of sins without baptism [ Exhortation to Martyrdom 30 (AD. 235)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details & Context

The context of this quote is absolutely crucial, and the surrounding text you provided explains Origen's full, nuanced argument. Taken alone, the quote seems to be only about water baptism, but Origen's main point is actually about the purifying power of martyrdom.

Here is the breakdown of his argument from the full passage:

    The Premise (Your Quote): Origen starts with the established Christian doctrine: there is no forgiveness of sins without baptism.

    The Problem: He is writing to Christians who are already baptized. He immediately notes that, according to the Gospels, one cannot be baptized again with water and Spirit for the forgiveness of sins. This was a major issue in the early Church: what does a Christian do if they commit serious sin after their one-and-only water baptism?

    The Solution: The Baptism of Blood: Origen's powerful answer is that God has given Christians another path to total purification: the baptism of martyrdom. He writes, "...but we have been given the baptism of martyrdom; for so it is called..."

    Scriptural Proof: He proves that martyrdom is called a "baptism" by citing Jesus's own words from the Gospels:

        Mark 10:38: "Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?"

        Luke 12:50: "I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!"

    The Redemptive Power of Martyrdom: Origen then develops a profound theology of martyrdom's sacrificial power. He compares the martyr's death to Christ's own sacrifice:

        Just as Christ's "baptism" on the cross was a "purgation for the world," the baptism of our martyrdom can be a "purgation for many."

        He draws an analogy to the heavenly altar from the Book of Revelation. The souls of the martyrs (qui propter testimonium Jesu securi percussi sunt / αἱ ψυχαὶ τῶν πεπελεκισμένων ἕνεκεν τῆς μαρτυρίας Ἰησοῦ) do not stand at the heavenly altar in vain; they minister forgiveness to those who pray.

        The martyr becomes a priest who, like Christ the High Priest, offers their own self as a sacrifice. This is why they are seen at the heavenly altar, their "proper place."

In summary, the quote you selected is Origen's starting point, not his conclusion. He uses the non-repeatable nature of water baptism to elevate martyrdom into a "second baptism"—a baptism of blood—that offers complete purification and forgiveness for post-baptismal sins, encouraging his audience to face death with courage and hope.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA [T]here are many who think they hold the opinions of Christ, and yet some of these think differently from their predecessors, yet, as the teaching of the Church, transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the churches to the present day, is still preserved, that alone IS to be accepted as truth that differs in no respect from ecclesiastical and apostolic Tradition [Fundamental Doctrines Preface 2 (c. A.D. 225)].
latin: Quoniam ergo multi ex his, qui Christo se credere profitentur, non solum in parvis et minimis discordant, verum etiam in magnis et maximis, id est vel de deo vel de ipso domino Iesu Christo vel de spiritu sancto, nec solum autem de his, sed et de aliis creaturis, id est vel de dominationibus vel de virtutibus sanctis: propter hoc necessarium videtur prius de his singulis certam lineam manifestamque regulam ponere, tum deinde etiam de ceteris quaerere. Sicut enim, multis apud Graecos et barbaros pollicentibus veritatem, desivimus apud omnes eam quaerere, qui eam falsis opinionibus asserebant, posteaquam credidimus filium esse dei Christum et ab ipso nobis hanc discendam esse persuasimus: ita cum multi sint, qui se putant sentire quae Christi sunt, et nonnulli eorum diversa a prioribus sentiant, servatur vero ecclesiastica praedicatio per successionis ordinem ab apostolis tradita et usque ad praesens in ecclesiis permanens, illa sola credenda est veritas, quae in nullo ab ecclesiastica et apostolica traditione discordat.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This statement is not a casual remark; it is the methodological foundation for Origen's entire project in On First Principles, the first systematic theology in Christian history.
1. The Problem: Doctrinal Chaos

Origen was writing in the early 3rd century (c. 225 AD), a time of immense theological diversity and conflict. The New Testament canon was not yet formally finalized, and various Christian groups held wildly different beliefs:

    Gnostics: Claimed to have secret, hidden knowledge (gnosis) passed down from the apostles, teaching that the material world was evil and created by a lesser god.

    Marcionites: Rejected the Old Testament entirely, claiming the God of the Jews was a cruel demiurge, different from the loving Father of Jesus.

    Other Theologians: Even within the mainstream Church, there was vigorous debate on major topics like the nature of the Trinity and the relationship between the Father and the Son.

Origen saw a critical need for a standard, a "rule of faith" (regula fidei), to distinguish authentic Christianity from these competing versions.
2. Origen's Solution: The Two Tiers of Doctrine

In this preface, Origen lays out his solution, which is implicitly a two-tiered system of belief:

    Tier 1: The Apostolic Tradition. This is the non-negotiable core of Christian belief. Origen states that certain essential doctrines have been clearly handed down from the apostles and are preserved publicly in the churches through the bishops ("in orderly succession"). These include the belief in one God, the divinity and humanity of Jesus Christ, the person of the Holy Spirit, the resurrection of the dead, and free will. These are the "first principles."

    Tier 2: Legitimate Theological Inquiry. For subjects not clearly defined in the Apostolic Tradition (e.g., the origin of the soul, the nature of angels, the structure of the cosmos), Origen believed theologians were free—and even obligated—to use reason and Scripture to investigate further.

Your quote is the cornerstone of this entire method. It establishes the absolute authority of Tier 1. Any speculation in Tier 2 is only legitimate if it "differs in no respect from ecclesiastical and apostolic Tradition."
3. The Significance of the Quote

    Anti-Gnostic Polemic: By emphasizing a public, orderly, and continuous tradition found "in the churches," Origen directly refutes the Gnostic claim to a secret, private tradition.

    The Rule of Faith: It provides a clear criterion for orthodoxy. Is a teaching new? Does it contradict what the churches have always taught? If so, it is to be rejected.

    The Foundation for Systematic Theology: It gives Origen the "guardrails" he needs to build his system. He can explore complex philosophical questions as long as he does not violate the foundational truths of the faith.

    Historical Irony: Origen himself would later be condemned by Church councils (long after his death) for some of his speculative theories in Tier 2 (such as the pre-existence of souls and the final restoration of all things, or apokatastasis). It is a profound irony that the very standard he so clearly articulated was eventually used to judge his own more speculative works as having gone too far beyond the Apostolic Tradition.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA The specific points that are clearly handed down through the apostolic preaching are these: First, that there is one God who created and arranged all things, and who. when nothing existed, called all things into existence, and that in the final period this God, just as he had promised through the prophets, sent the Lord Jesus Christ. Secondly, that Jesus Christ himself, who came, was born of the Father before all creatures; and after he had ministered to the Father in the creation of all things. Then, thirdly, the apostles related that the Holy Spirit was associated in honour and dignity with the Father and the Son [Fundamental Doctrines Preface 4 (c. A.D. 225)].
latin:
Species vero eorum, quae per praedicationem apostolicam manifeste traduntur, istae sunt. Primo, quod unus est deus, qui omnia creavit atque composuit, quique, cum nihil esset, esse fecit universa, deus a prima creatura et conditione mundi, omnium iustorum deus, Adam Abel Seth Enos Enoch Noe Sem Abraham Isaac Iacob duodecim patriarcharum Moysi et prophetarum; et quod hic deus in novissimis diebus, sicut per prophetas suos ante promiserat, misit dominum nostrum Iesum Christum...

    Secundo, quia Iesus Christus ipse, qui venit, ante omnem creaturam natus ex patre est. Qui cum in omnium conditione patri ministrasset, per ipsum namque omnia facta sunt, novissimis temporibus se ipsum exinaniens homo factus est, incarnatus est, cum deus esset, et homo factus mansit quod erat, deus...

context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is arguably the single most important section of Origen's preface. It is the foundation for his entire theological project in De Principiis.

1. The "Rule of Faith" (Regula Fidei):
Origen is not creating a new list of beliefs. He is articulating his version of the "Rule of Faith" or "Canon of Truth," a summary of core, non-negotiable Christian doctrines that circulated in the early Church. Fathers like Irenaeus and Tertullian had similar lists. The purpose of this "Rule" was to provide a clear standard to distinguish authentic apostolic Christianity from the teachings of Gnostics, Marcionites, and other groups.

2. The Foundation for Theological Speculation:
The most crucial context is what Origen does with this list. He uses it to make a vital distinction between two types of questions:

    Clearly Preached Doctrines: These are the non-negotiables listed in your quote (one Creator God, the divinity and incarnation of Christ, the divinity of the Holy Spirit, the resurrection, the final judgment, etc.). These are the "guardrails" of the faith.

    Open Questions for Inquiry: Origen explicitly states that while these points are clear, the apostles left many other questions open for investigation by learned Christians using Scripture and reason. These include the nature of the soul, the origin of the devil, the structure of the angelic world, and the deeper meaning of scripture.

3. The Anti-Gnostic Polemic:
Nearly every point in Origen's list is a direct refutation of Gnostic teachings:

    "One God who created all things... when nothing existed": This directly attacks the Gnostic belief in a lesser, ignorant creator god (the Demiurge) who fashioned the world from pre-existing, flawed matter. Origen affirms the good Creator of the Old Testament and creation ex nihilo.

    "Jesus Christ... born of the Father before all creatures": This affirms Christ's unique divine origin and role in creation, refuting Gnostic ideas that "Christ" was a separate, spiritual being who temporarily inhabited the human Jesus.

    "He remained what he was, God": This is a powerful anti-docetic statement, refuting the Gnostic idea that Christ only appeared to be human.

In essence, this passage is Origen's "statement of first principles." He is laying down the unchangeable, apostolic foundation upon which his entire work of theological exploration and speculation in the rest of De Principiis will be built.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA He in the last times, divesting himself [of his glory], became a man, and was incarnate although he was God, and while made a man remained the God that he was [Fundamental Doctrines Preface 4 (c. A.D. 225)].
latin: Hic in novissimis diebus exinaniens seipsum homo factus est, incarnatus est cum deus esset, et homo factus mansit quod erat deus.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This short sentence is incredibly rich and provides a crucial snapshot of orthodox Christology a full century before the Council of Nicaea.

    Part of the Apostolic "Rule of Faith": The most important context is that Origen is not presenting this as his personal speculation. He is listing what he understands to be the core, unchangeable teaching of the Apostles that has been handed down in the Church. This list forms the "first principles" upon which all further theological inquiry must be based. This specific statement is the Church's foundational teaching about the person of Jesus Christ.

    Pre-Nicene Orthodoxy: This passage is a beautiful and concise summary of what would later be defined at the great Ecumenical Councils:

        Full Divinity: "...although he was God" (cum deus esset). Origen affirms Christ's eternal divinity.

        True Incarnation: "...became a man, and was incarnate" (homo factus est, incarnatus est). He affirms the reality of the incarnation and Christ's true humanity.

        The Unchanging Divine Nature: The final clause is the most profound: "...having become a man, remained what he was: God" (homo factus mansit quod erat deus). This is a powerful statement of the immutability of the divine nature. Origen is teaching that the Word of God did not change into a man or cease to be God when he became incarnate. Rather, he took on human nature without any loss or alteration to his divine nature. This is a core principle that would be fiercely defended against later heresies.

    Echoes of Philippians 2 (The Kenosis): The phrase exinaniens seipsum ("emptying himself" or "divesting himself") is a direct reference to the Latin translation of Philippians 2:7. This is the famous kenotic hymn where St. Paul describes Christ, "who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men." For Origen and orthodox theology, this "emptying" does not mean a loss of divinity, but the veiling of his divine glory under the humble reality of human flesh.

In summary, you have located a pillar of early Christian doctrine. It shows that the fundamental tenets of the Incarnation—that Jesus is fully God and fully man, and that his divinity remained unchanged when he became human—were a central part of the apostolic tradition long before they were formally defined in the creeds of Nicaea and Chalcedon.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA The particular points clearly delivered in the teaching of the apostles are as follows: First, that there is one God, who created and arranged all things, and who, when nothing existed, called all things into being -God from the first creation and foundation of the world, the God of all just men, of Adam, Abel, Seth, Enos, Enoch, Noah, Terah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, Moses, and the prophets; and that this God in the last days, as he had announced beforehand through his prophets, sent our Lord Jesus Christ to call to himself in the first place Israel, and in the second place the Gentiles, after the unfaithfulness of the people of Israel. This just and good God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, gave the law and the prophets, and the Gospels, being also the God of the apostles and of the Old and New Testaments [Fundamental Doctrines Preface 4 (c. A.D. 225)].
latin: Species vero eorum, quae per praedicationem apostolicam manifeste traduntur, istae sunt. Primo, quod unus est deus, qui omnia creavit atque composuit, quique, cum nihil esset, esse fecit universa, deus a prima creatura et conditione mundi, omnium iustorum deus, Adam Abel Seth Enos Enoch Noe Sem Abraham Isaac Iacob duodecim patriarchum Moysi et prophetarum; et quod hic deus in novissimis diebus, sicut per prophetas suos ante promiserat, misit dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, primo quidem vocaturum Israel, secundo vero etiam gentes post perfidiam populi Israel. Hic deus iustus et bonus, pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, legem et prophetas et evangelia ipse dedit, qui et apostolorum deus est et veteris et novi testamenti.
context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is not just a simple creed; it is a foundational statement with profound historical and theological significance.

1. The "Rule of Faith" in Practice:
In the previous section you cited (Praefatio 2), Origen established the principle that Apostolic Tradition is the sole standard of truth. Here, in sections 4 through 10, he begins to lay out the content of that tradition. This passage is the very first and most fundamental item on his list of non-negotiable, "clearly delivered" apostolic doctrines. Everything else he discusses in his book will be built upon, or be an exploration of, these foundational truths.

2. A Direct Refutation of Gnosticism and Marcionism:
This entire paragraph is a powerful polemic aimed squarely at the major heresies of the 2nd and early 3rd centuries.

    Gnosticism: Many Gnostic systems taught that there were two gods: a lower, ignorant, or evil creator god (the "Demiurge") who made the material world and gave the Old Testament law, and a higher, remote, and good God who was unknown until revealed by Christ.

    Marcionism: Marcion, a highly influential figure, took this idea to an extreme, completely rejecting the Old Testament and its "wrathful" God as incompatible with the loving Father revealed by Jesus.

3. The Unity of God and Salvation History:
Origen's wording is a deliberate and systematic dismantling of this dualistic heresy:

    "One God, who created... all things": This immediately refutes the idea of a separate creator god. The God of Jesus is the God of Genesis.

    The Long List of Patriarchs: This is not just a boring list. It is a powerful statement of continuity. By explicitly naming everyone from Adam to Moses and the prophets, Origen is emphatically declaring that the God of Creation, the God of Israel, and the God of the Church is one and the same God. He is forging an unbreakable chain of salvation history.

    "This just and good God... gave the law and the prophets, and the Gospels": This is a direct shot at Marcion. Origen insists that the same God is the source of all scripture—Law, Prophets, and Gospels. There is no contradiction.

    "God of the Old and New Testaments": This is the summary statement that seals his argument. The two testaments are not from two different gods; they are the unified revelation of the one true God.

In short, this passage is Origen's foundational declaration that the Christian faith is rooted in history, in the God of Israel, and in the unity of divine revelation across both testaments. It is the bedrock of orthodoxy upon which he will build his entire theological system.

context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is profoundly important for several reasons.

1. The Crucial Backstory (The Problem of Translation):
Origen wrote On First Principles in Greek around A.D. 225. Tragically, the original Greek text is almost entirely lost. What we have is a Latin translation made by Tyrannius Rufinus around A.D. 397. Rufinus, in his preface, openly admitted that he "smoothed over" and altered passages that he felt were controversial or could be misunderstood, in order to protect Origen's reputation. Therefore, the Latin text you are reading is our primary, but slightly filtered, window into Origen's original thought.

2. The Argument: Refuting Materialism and Anthropomorphism:
In this chapter, Origen is making a revolutionary argument against two common beliefs of his time:

    Stoicism: The dominant Stoic philosophy taught that everything, including God, was fundamentally material (a kind of divine fire or breath).

    Simple Christian Belief: Many less-educated Christians imagined God in a physical, human-like form (anthropomorphism), taking Old Testament descriptions literally.

Origen, drawing on the best of Greek philosophy (especially Middle Platonism), argues powerfully that God must be completely incorporeal (non-physical).

3. Key Theological Concepts in the Passage:

    Apophatic Theology: The passage begins with the classic apophatic statement that "our mind is not able to behold God... as he is." We cannot grasp God's essence directly.

    Natural Theology: We can, however, know God indirectly through His creation. Origen echoes St. Paul (Romans 1:20), stating that we understand the Creator "from the beauty of his works."

    Divine Simplicity: The core of the argument is that God is a "simple intellectual nature" (intellectualis natura simplex). "Simple" means un-compounded; God has no parts. If God had parts, something would have had to assemble them, meaning that "something" would be prior to God, which is a contradiction.

    MONAD (μονάς) and HENAD (ἑνάς): These are technical terms from Greek philosophy.

        Monad: The ultimate, indivisible unit; the source of all numbers. For philosophers, it meant the First Principle, the One from which all multiplicity derives.

        Henad: This is a synonym for the "One" (ἕν), emphasizing unity and singularity.
        By using these terms, Origen is identifying the Christian God with the highest principle of Greek metaphysical thought, arguing that God is the absolute, simple, and uncompounded Source of all existence.

Additional Relevant Context

This passage is a cornerstone of Origen's theology of God the Father and is profoundly important for several reasons:

    Divine Incorporeality: Origen is making a radical argument for his time. He is fighting against any form of anthropomorphism (attributing a human body or form to God) and against Stoic ideas of God as a kind of subtle, fiery matter. For Origen, God the Father is absolutely simple, intellectual, and incorporeal (without a body).

    The Nature of Invisibility: The core of his argument is a crucial distinction. God is not invisible in the way a microscopic object is, or the way a blinding light is—i.e., something that could be seen if our senses were better. Origen insists that invisibility is essential to God's very nature. He is not a seeable object that is too powerful for our eyes; He is in a category of being to which sight simply does not apply.

    The Role of the Son: This entire discussion is framed by the quotation from Colossians 1:15, "Who is the image of the invisible God" (imago invisibilis dei), which appears just before your selected passage. For Origen, if the Father is by nature absolutely invisible and unknowable, how do we know Him? Through His perfect Image, the Son (the Logos). The Son is the one who makes the invisible Father known to the created intellect.

    "Seeing" vs. "Knowing": As the text immediately following your quote shows (in the second part of your image), Origen distinguishes sharply between "to see" (videre) and "to know" (cognoscere). Seeing is a function of the body. Knowing is a function of the intellect. We cannot see the Father, but we can know Him through the Son, who is His perfect intellectual image. This is why Origen points out that Jesus says, "No one knows the Father except the Son" (Matt. 11:27), not "No one sees the Father except the Son."

You have selected a passage that is central to the development of classical Christian theology about the absolute transcendence and incorporeality of God.

context:
Additional Relevant Context

This passage is the cornerstone of Origen's entire method of biblical interpretation, which is arguably his most significant and lasting contribution to Christian thought.

    The Problem Origen is Solving: Origen was writing for a sophisticated Greco-Roman audience. Many pagan critics (like Celsus) and Gnostic thinkers mocked the Jewish scriptures (the Old Testament) for what they saw as crude, anthropomorphic, and nonsensical stories about God. Simple, literal readings were becoming a barrier to faith for educated people.

    Origen's Solution: The Threefold Sense of Scripture: Origen proposed that Scripture, like a human being, has three layers of meaning, corresponding to the body, soul, and spirit.

        The Literal (Bodily) Sense: The plain, historical meaning. Origen believed this was sufficient for simple believers and contained the basic story.

        The Moral (Soulish) Sense: The ethical meaning that teaches the individual soul how to live a virtuous life.

        The Spiritual (Mystical/Allegorical) Sense: The highest and truest meaning. This sense reveals profound truths about the spiritual world, about Christ (even in the Old Testament), and about the inner life of the soul in relation to God.

    The "Stumbling Block" as a Divine Clue: The genius of the passage you quoted is that Origen argues that God deliberately placed "stumbling blocks" or absurdities into the literal text. When a thinking person reads that there were three "days" with "evening and morning" before the sun was created, it's a divine signal. God is essentially saying, "Stop! Don't get stuck on the literal meaning here. I have placed this logical impossibility in the text to force you to look deeper for the spiritual meaning." The absurdity of the literal is a doorway to the spiritual.

    Significance and Controversy:

        Foundation of Western Interpretation: Origen's method became the foundation for most Christian biblical interpretation for the next thousand years. St. Ambrose of Milan used it to convert St. Augustine, and it dominated the medieval period.

        The Danger of "Losing" History: The main criticism against Origen, both in his own time and later, was that his focus on the spiritual sense could lead one to dismiss or deny the historical reality of the events described. While Origen did not deny history outright, his emphasis was so heavily on the spiritual that his method was viewed with suspicion by more literal-minded theologians, especially in the school of Antioch.

In summary, this passage is Origen's masterstroke: a defense of Scripture that transforms its apparent weaknesses (literal absurdities) into its greatest strength—a divinely-authored puzzle that invites the reader into a deeper, spiritual relationship with God.   Comparison to the Latin Translation

This is where it gets fascinating. By comparing the original Greek to Rufinus's Latin translation, we can see how Origen's thought was transmitted to the West.

    Origen's Greek: τροπικῶς (tropikōs)

    Rufinus's Latin: figuratae

        Meaning: Both mean "figuratively." Origen's term, "tropologically," is the technical term for this kind of allegorical interpretation (a "trope"). Rufinus uses a more common Latin equivalent.

    Origen's Greek: διὰ δοξούσης ἱστορίας (dia doxousēs historias)

    Rufinus's Latin: per haec quae quadam historiae specie scripta sunt

        Meaning: Origen's Greek is incredibly concise: "through a seeming or apparent history." Rufinus expands this for clarity in Latin: "through these things which are written in a certain form/appearance of history." Both convey the same idea perfectly: the text looks like a literal story, but it isn't meant to be taken that way.

    Origen's Greek: οὐ σωματικῶς γεγενημένης (ou sōmatikōs gegenēmenēs)

    Rufinus's Latin: non tamen secundum historiam corporaliter facta

        Meaning: Origen's Greek is again very direct: "not having happened somatically." The word sōmatikōs refers to the "bodily" or literal sense of Scripture. Rufinus's Latin is slightly more explanatory: "not however having happened corporally according to the history."

In summary: The surviving Greek fragment shows us Origen's precise, technical, and concise language. Rufinus's Latin translation is faithful but slightly more wordy and explanatory, which is common for a translator trying to make a complex idea clear to a new audience. Having this Greek fragment is invaluable for confirming that Rufinus accurately represented the core of Origen's famous interpretive method.

A.D. 225)].

context:
Additional Relevant Context

    The Work - De Principiis: This is the first-ever systematic theology of the Christian faith. Origen is attempting to articulate the "rule of faith" on complex topics like the nature of God, the Son, the Spirit, creation, and free will.

    The Textual Problem: Origen's original Greek text was controversial. Much of it was lost or destroyed. We rely heavily on a Latin translation made by Rufinus around 397 AD. Rufinus admitted to "softening" or clarifying some of Origen's more speculative ideas to protect him from accusations of heresy in the later, more dogmatically precise 4th century. However, the core of the argument here is widely accepted as authentically Origen's.

    Refuting Three Heresies at Once: This single sentence is a theological powerhouse because it refutes three distinct errors:

        "part of the substance of God was converted into the Son": This rejects a materialist or Gnostic view of God. God is not a physical substance that can be divided up like a cake. He is simple, spiritual, and incorporeal.

        "the Son was procreated... out of things non-existent": This is a direct rejection of what would become Arianism. Origen insists the Son comes from the Father, not from nothing. He is truly the Son, not a creature.

        "so that there once was a time when he did not exist": This is the most famous part. The phrase fuerit aliquando quando non fuerit is the Latin equivalent of the Arian slogan, "There was a time when he was not" (ἦν ποτε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν). Origen's condemnation of this idea a century before Arius is profound. He firmly taught the eternal generation of the Son.

    Origen's Positive Analogy: After rejecting the heresies, Origen provides his own analogy: the Son is begotten from the Father "as the will proceeds from the mind." This is a brilliant, purely spiritual analogy. The will is distinct from the mind, yet it comes from the mind, is co-eternal with the mind (you can't have a mind without a will), and is of the same "stuff" as the mind. This was Origen's way of explaining how the Son could be distinct from the Father yet co-eternal and of the same substance, without dividing the Godhead.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA Look at [Peter], the great foundation of the Church, that most solid of rocks, upon whom Christ built the Church [Mt 16:18]. And what does our Lord say to him? "O you of little faith," he says, "why do you doubt?" [Mt 14:31] [Homilies on Exodus 5:4 (c. A.D. 249)].
latin: Vide magno illi Ecclesiæ fundamento, et petræ solidissimæ, super quam Christus fundavit Ecclesiam, quid dicatur a Domino: ‹ Modicæ, inquit, fidei, quare dubitasti? ›
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    The Context is Pastoral Encouragement: The primary point of this passage is not simply to praise Peter, but to comfort the struggling believer. Origen's message is powerful: if even Peter, the "most solid rock," could have a moment of "little faith" and doubt, then we should not lose hope when we find ourselves struggling during our own trials. The entire homily is about the "exodus" from the Egypt of sin, a journey filled with temptations.

    Origen's Broader View of the "Rock": This passage is a very strong affirmation of Peter's foundational role. However, to understand Origen's full theology, it's important to know that in other works (like his Commentary on Matthew), he also interprets the "rock" in a broader sense. He states that the rock is the faith that Peter confessed ("You are the Christ"), and that every believer who makes this same confession becomes a "Peter" or a "rock" upon which the Church is built. For Origen, Peter is the first and primary example of a rock-like faith that all Christians are called to share.

    The Role of Rufinus the Translator: Rufinus's translations were instrumental in preserving many of Origen's works for the Latin-speaking West. However, he was sometimes criticized for "softening" or editing some of Origen's more speculative or controversial ideas to make them more palatable to the orthodoxy of his own time (c. A.D. 400). In this case, however, the affirmation of Peter's role is straightforward and consistent with Origen's known thought.

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source Confirmation

    Author: Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253 A.D.)

    Work: Homilies on Genesis (In Genesim Homilia)

    Location: Homily 1, Section 1

    Translator: Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 345–411 A.D.)

2. Theological and Philosophical Context

This passage is a classic example of Origen's spiritual or allegorical method of interpretation. He explicitly signals this shift in your provided text:

    Secundum litteram... ("According to the letter...")

    Secundum spiritualem vero intelligentiam... ("But according to spiritual understanding...")

The core of his argument is a profound philosophical and theological point about the nature of time:

    Time is a Creature: Origen argues that time itself is part of the created order. It is not an eternal, pre-existing reality in which God works. Time begins with the sequential ordering of creation.

    "One Day" vs. "First Day": The distinction is critical. "First" (prima) implies a sequence and is therefore a temporal concept (first, second, third...). "One" (una) suggests a unified, singular, and perhaps atemporal or pre-temporal event. This "one day" is the foundational moment of creation, outside the flow of sequential time that begins on the "second day."

    Spiritual Meaning: For Origen, this "one day" can be understood as the unity of all spiritual creation in the Word of God, before the fall and fragmentation that introduced the succession of time as we experience it.

3. Influence on Later Fathers

This interpretation was enormously influential, particularly on St. Augustine of Hippo. In his own works on Genesis (especially The Literal Meaning of Genesis) and in his famous meditation on time in the Confessions (Book XI), Augustine develops this idea with even greater philosophical depth. The concept that time itself was created along with the universe became a cornerstone of Christian theology.
4. Analysis of Your Provided Text

The text you supplied is a rich excerpt that shows more of Origen's thinking:

    Christocentric "Beginning": At the start, Origen interprets "In the beginning" (Gen 1:1) not as a temporal start, but as a reference to Christ, the Word, who is the "beginning" in whom all things were made, citing John 1:1.

    The Abyss: He interprets the "abyss" over which there was darkness as the future place of the devil and his angels, citing the demons' plea to Jesus in the Gospel of Luke not to be sent into the "abyss."

This shows how Origen reads the entire Old Testament text through a spiritual and Christological lens, seeking deeper meanings beyond the literal surface. You have found a perfect example of his exegetical method.

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Immediate Context: The Typology of Rahab's House

This entire passage is a profound exercise in biblical typology. Origen is not speaking in the abstract; he is interpreting the story of Rahab the harlot from the Book of Joshua (Joshua chapter 2).

    The Story: When the Israelites were about to conquer Jericho, they sent spies into the city. A prostitute named Rahab hid them and helped them escape. In return, the spies promised that she and her entire family would be spared if she hung a scarlet cord from her window and gathered her family inside her house. When Jericho was destroyed, everyone inside Rahab's house was saved, while everyone outside perished.

    Origen's Interpretation: Origen sees this as a perfect symbol (a "type") of the Church.

        Rahab's House = The Church.

        The Scarlet Cord (signum coccineum) = The Blood of Christ, which is the sign of redemption.

        The Destruction of Jericho = The Final Judgment.

        Safety Inside the House = Salvation within the Church.

        Death Outside the House = Damnation outside the Church.

His statement is therefore a direct allegorical conclusion from the biblical narrative: just as physical salvation from Jericho's destruction was only possible inside Rahab's specific house, so spiritual salvation is only possible inside the one house of the Church, marked by the blood of Christ.
2. Theological Significance: Extra Ecclesiam Nulla Salus

This passage from Origen is one of the earliest and clearest formulations of the Christian doctrine known as Extra Ecclesiam nulla salus ("Outside the Church, there is no salvation").

He makes the identification explicit: "outside this house, that is, outside the Church" (extra hanc domum, id est extra Ecclesiam). This phrase became a cornerstone of Catholic ecclesiology. Origen's contemporary, St. Cyprian of Carthage, would later popularize the doctrine with even more famous phrasing, but Origen's formulation here is foundational.

A.D. 249)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Full Context: The Seven Remissions of Sins

Your quote is the climax of a list where Origen outlines seven ways sins can be forgiven in the New Covenant, contrasting them with the old sacrifices. The full list, which is present in the text you provided, is:

    Baptism: "The first is that by which we are baptized for the remission of sins."

    Martyrdom: "The second remission is in the suffering of martyrdom."

    Almsgiving: "The third is that which is given for alms."

    Forgiving Others: "The fourth remission of sins is made for us through this: that we also forgive the sins of our brothers."

    Converting a Sinner: "The fifth remission of sins is when one converts a sinner from the error of his way."

    Abundant Charity: "A sixth remission is also made through an abundance of charity."

    Penance and Confession: The seventh and final way, which is your quoted passage.

2. Historical and Theological Significance

This passage is of immense importance for the history of the Sacrament of Penance (or Reconciliation).

    Early Witness to Confession: It is one of the earliest and clearest patristic texts describing the practice of confessing one's sins to a priest ("sacerdoti Domini").

    Sin as an Illness: Origen's analogy of seeking "medicine" (quærere medicinam) from the priest became a foundational concept in the theology of confession. The priest is seen not just as a judge but as a spiritual physician who helps heal the soul.

    Penance as "Laborious": His description of penance as "hard and laborious" (dura et laboriosa) reflects the severity of the ancient penitential discipline for grave sins committed after baptism. It was often a long and public process.
