context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Immediate Context of the Passage

You have found a classic example of Origen's allegorical and theological style of interpretation. The entire homily is a commentary on Leviticus 12, which discusses the ritual impurity of a mother after childbirth. Origen finds the literal law puzzling and asks a deeper question: "Why is birth itself, a natural process, associated with sin and the need for purification?"

His answer, which you have located, is that the physical act of birth is a sign of a deeper spiritual reality: every human soul entering the world through flesh is born into a state of sin. He uses a chain of scriptural proofs to support this:

    Psalm 51:5 (50:7): "In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother bore me."

    Job 14:4: "No one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day."

    The Church's own practice: The universal tradition of baptizing infants.

2. Historical and Theological Significance

This passage is one of the most important patristic texts in history for several reasons:

    Early Testimony to Infant Baptism: This is one of the earliest, clearest, and most explicit written statements confirming that infant baptism was a standard, established practice in the Church by the mid-3rd century. Origen does not present it as a new or controversial idea, but as a settled "usage of the Church" (observantiam Ecclesiæ). He even claims this tradition came from the Apostles.

    Link Between Baptism and Original Sin: Origen makes a powerful theological argument: the practice of infant baptism is undeniable proof of the doctrine of original sin. He argues from the principle of lex orandi, lex credendi ("the law of prayer is the law of belief"). The fact that the Church performs this ritual for infants implies a universal belief that infants are born with sin that needs to be washed away.

    Refutation of Pelagianism (Before Pelagius): Nearly 150 years before the Pelagian controversy, Origen provides the exact argument that St. Augustine would later use against Pelagius, who denied that infants were born with original sin. This text became a cornerstone of the orthodox position.

3. Note on the Language

It is important to remember that Origen wrote in Greek. His Homilies on Leviticus survive today only in the Latin translation of Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 345-411 AD). While Rufinus was known to sometimes adapt Origen's more speculative ideas for a Latin audience, on a core practical doctrine like infant baptism, his translation is considered a highly reliable witness to the original thought of Origen and the universal practice of the 3rd-century Church.

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA Not fornication only, but even marriages make us unfit for ecclesiastical honors; for neither a bishop, nor a presbyter, nor a deacon, nor a widow is able to be twice married [ Homilies on Luke 17 (C. A.D. 235)].
latin: Sicut enim ab ecclesiasticis dignitatibus non solum fornicatio, sed et nuptiæ repellunt, neque enim episcopus, nec presbyter, nec diaconus, nec vidua possunt esse digami...
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Source and Context

    Author: Origen of Alexandria (c. A.D. 185–254), one of the most influential theologians of the early Church.

    Work: Homily 17 on the Gospel of Luke. Origen preached this homily in Greek in Caesarea around A.D. 235-240.

    Immediate Context: Origen is commenting on the figure of Anna the prophetess (Luke 2:36-38). He praises her long, chaste widowhood after her first marriage as a model for Christian women. This leads him into a broader discussion of the spiritual value of chastity, virginity, and monogamy within the Church.

2. Theological and Disciplinary Significance

This passage is extremely important for several reasons:

    Apostolic Tradition: Origen is reflecting a discipline that goes back to the pastoral epistles of St. Paul, which state that a bishop and deacons must be "the husband of one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2, 3:12) and that widows enrolled for official church support must have been "the wife of one husband" (1 Timothy 5:9).

    Prohibition of Digamy: The term Origen uses, digami, is the key. It refers to a person who has been married twice (a "digamist"). The passage clearly states that digamy was an absolute impediment to ordination (for men) or to being enrolled in the official order of widows (for women).

    Origen's Rigorous Interpretation: Origen goes even further than simply stating the rule. In the sentences that immediately follow your quote, he argues that a digamist, even if they are a virtuous person, is not part of the "first rank" or the true "Church of God, which has no spot or wrinkle." He says such a person can be saved, but they will not be "crowned" by Christ. This reflects Origen's characteristically rigorous and ascetic view of Christian perfection.

3. Scholarly Citation

For reference in academic works, this passage is typically cited from the Migne collection:

en: ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA Formerly there was baptism in an obscure way. . . Now, however, in full view, there is regeneration in water and in the Holy Spirit. Formerly, in an obscure way, there was manna for food; now, however, in full view, there is the true food, the flesh of the Word of God, as he himself says: "My flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink" [Jn 6:561[ Homilies on Numbers 7:2 (C. A.D. 249)].
latin: Antea in ænigmate fuit baptismus in nube et in mari, nunc autem in specie regeneratio est in aqua et in Spiritu sancto. Tunc in ænigmate erat manna cibus, nunc autem in specie caro Verbi Dei est verus cibus, sicut et ipse dicit, quia ‘Caro mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus.’
context:
Additional Relevant Details & Context

    The Author and Work: Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–254 A.D.) was one of the most influential theologians and biblical scholars of the early Church. His Homilies on Numbers are a series of sermons where he interprets the book of Numbers for a Christian congregation, not just as historical narrative, but as a text rich with spiritual meaning for the life of the Church.

    The Core Theological Method: Typology: This passage is a perfect example of typological exegesis. Origen sees the events and figures of the Old Testament as "types" or "shadows" (aenigmata - literally "riddles" or "obscure figures") that prefigure the fuller, clearer realities of the New Testament, which he calls the species ("form" or "full view").

    The Immediate Context (The Ethiopian Wife): As seen in the larger Latin text you provided, Origen frames this entire discussion around the story of Moses marrying an Ethiopian woman (Numbers 12). He interprets this allegorically:

        Moses represents the Law of the Old Testament.

        The Ethiopian Wife represents the Gentile Church.

        The Union: When the Law (Moses) is joined to the Church (the Ethiopian), its true, spiritual meaning is finally revealed. Before this union, the Law was understood "in an obscure way" (in aenigmate). After, it is understood "in full view" (in specie). This is the framework for the specific contrasts he makes in your quote.

    The Sacramental Contrasts: The quote focuses on two key sacramental "types" and their fulfillment:

        Baptism: The Israelites passing through the Red Sea and being guided by the cloud was a "type" of Christian Baptism (as St. Paul also says in 1 Corinthians 10). Origen contrasts this "shadow" baptism with the true "regeneration in water and in the Holy Spirit."

        The Eucharist: The Manna that fed the Israelites in the desert was a "type" of the Eucharist. Origen contrasts this temporary, physical food with the "true food," which is the very "flesh of the Word of God," quoting Jesus from John 6.

This passage is a beautiful and concise summary of the early Church's understanding of the relationship between the Old and New Covenants, seeing a profound unity and progression in God's plan of salvation, revealed through the sacraments of the Church.

en: ST. PAPIAS OF HIERAPOLIS And Papias, of whom we are now speaking, confesses that he received the words of the apostles from those who followed them, but says that he was himself a hearer of Aristion and the presbyter John. At least he mentions them frequently by name, and gives their traditions in his writings. [There are] other passages from his works in which he relates some other wonderful events that he claims to have received from Tradition [fragment in Eusebius's Church History 3:39:7 (c. A.D. 130)].
latin: Alias quoque supradicti Aristionis enarrationes sermonum Domini, et Joannis presbyteri traditiones refert in suis libris. . . .     Idem præterea scriptor alia nonnulla nudæ vocis traditione ad se pervenisse testatur.
greek: Καὶ ἄλλας δὲ τῇ ἰδίᾳ γραφῇ παραδίδωσιν Ἀριστίωνος τοῦ πρόσθεν δεδηλωμένου τῶν τοῦ Κυρίου λόγων διηγήσεις, καὶ τοῦ πρεσβυτέρου Ἰωάννου παραδόσεις...     Καὶ ἄλλα δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς συγγραφεὺς ὡς ἐκ παραδόσεως ἀγράφου εἰς αὐτὸν ἥκοντα παρατέθειται...
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    A Quote Within a Quote: This is the most critical detail. The original work of St. Papias, the Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord (Λογίων Κυριακῶν Ἐξήγησις), is lost. We only know it through fragments quoted by later Church Fathers. This passage is our most important source, where Eusebius (writing in the early 4th century) quotes and discusses Papias (who wrote in the early 2nd century).

    Eusebius's Low Opinion of Papias: It is crucial to note from the text you provided that Eusebius was not a fan of Papias. He explicitly calls him a man "of very limited intelligence" (Σφόδρα γάρ τοι σμικρὸς ὢν τὸν νοῦν). Eusebius's main issue was Papias's belief in a literal, physical thousand-year reign of Christ on earth (chiliasm or millenarianism), which Eusebius considered a misinterpretation of apostolic teaching.

    The "Two Johns": This passage is the primary source for the historical theory of the "two Johns." Papias, as quoted by Eusebius just before this section, distinguishes between what "the Apostles said" and what "Aristion and the presbyter John, the Lord’s disciples, are saying." Eusebius interprets this to mean there were two prominent figures named John active in Asia Minor: John the Apostle and a different man, John the Presbyter. This has been a subject of immense scholarly debate for centuries.

    Oral vs. Written Tradition: The fragment is invaluable for showing the immense importance of oral tradition in the early 2nd-century Church. Papias explicitly states his preference for the "living and abiding voice" over written books. This passage confirms that he included material from this "unwritten tradition" (παραδόσεως ἀγράφου) in his work.

en: ST. PETER OF ALEXANDRIA Thus Peter, the first of the apostles, having been often apprehended, and thrown into prison, and treated with ignominy, was last of all crucified at Rome [Penance, canon (A.D. 306)1.
latin: Ita Petrus apostolorum primus, sape comprehensus, et custodia traditus, ignominiaque affectus, postremo Romæ crucifixus est.
greek: Οὕτως ὁ πρόκριτος τῶν ἀποστόλων Πέτρος, πολλάκις συλληφθεὶς καὶ φυλακισθεὶς καὶ ἀτιμασθείς, ὕστερον ἐν Ῥώμῃ ἐσταυρώθη.
context:
Additional Relevant Details & Context

This quote is highly significant, but its meaning is fully revealed by the context of the canon in which it appears.

1. The Main Argument of Canon 9:
The primary purpose of this canon is to correct a form of fanatical zeal among some Christians. St. Peter is arguing against those who rashly and voluntarily throw themselves into the hands of the authorities to seek martyrdom. He criticizes those who "as if from a sleep... rush into the contest" without being sought, thereby provoking the persecutors.

2. The Correct Model: Christ and the Apostles:
To counter this misguided zeal, St. Peter presents the proper model for Christian conduct during persecution:

    Jesus Christ: He points out that Jesus often withdrew from those who sought to harm him and did not hand Himself over, but waited for his persecutors to come to him.

    Apostolic Examples: He then cites the great martyrs of the Church as examples of this patient endurance, not reckless self-destruction. They did not seek death, but accepted it when it came as a result of their faithful witness.

3. The Purpose of Your Quote:
The sentence about the Apostle Peter is the climax of a list of proper examples:

    First, Stephen: He was seized (συναρπασθεὶς) by his enemies in Jerusalem.

    Second, James: He was arrested (συλληφθεὶς) by Herod and then beheaded.

    Third, Peter the Apostle: As your quote states, he was repeatedly apprehended and imprisoned before his final martyrdom.

    Fourth, Paul: He was likewise handed over many times and endured countless dangers before being beheaded in Rome.

The key theme is that these heroes of the faith did not turn themselves in. They were arrested, seized, and apprehended. They endured suffering patiently, following the model of Christ. Therefore, your quote serves as a crucial piece of evidence in a larger pastoral argument about the true nature of martyrdom.

4. Historical Significance:
This passage from c. A.D. 306 is an extremely important and early patristic witness from the Christian East (Alexandria, Egypt) affirming the ancient tradition that the Apostle Peter was martyred by crucifixion in Rome.

en: ST. PETER OF ALEXANDRIA [T]hey came to the church of the most blessed Mother of God, and Ever-Virgin Mary, which, as we began to say, he had constructed in the western quarter, in a suburb, for a cemetery of the martyrs [The Genuine Acts of Peter of Alexandria (A.D. 305)].
latin: ...venerunt in ecclesiam beatissimæ Dei Genitricis semperque virginis Mariæ, quam, ut dicere cœperamus, ipse ob martyrum cœmeteria ad occidentalem partem in quodam prosatio (e) construxerat.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Original Language

    Source: The text you are looking at is the Latin translation of the Acta S. Petri Alexandrini Episcopi (The Acts of St. Peter, Bishop of Alexandria). This version is found in Migne's Patrologia Graeca (PG), Volume 18, column 463.

    Original Language: St. Peter was the Patriarch of Alexandria, and the original account of his martyrdom was written in Greek. The Latin text you have is a translation of that original. The footnote (e) Græcismus, pro suburbio confirms this, explaining that the unusual Latin word prosatio is a loanword from the Greek proasteion (προάστειον), meaning "suburb."

2. Immediate Historical Context

The passage describes the events immediately following the martyrdom of St. Peter of Alexandria (c. 311 A.D.).

    A Dispute: After his execution, a "not small contention" (non parva contentio) broke out among the faithful. One group wanted to bury his body in the sanctuary of St. Mark the Evangelist, where he was martyred. Another group wanted to take him to the church that he himself had built—the one mentioned in your quote.

    Intervention: To prevent the dispute from turning into a riot (pugnæ litigium), a group of officials (called senatorum animosa phalanx) intervened.

    The Journey: They seized the holy relics, placed them in a boat (scapham), and sailed around the Pharos lighthouse to a place called Leucado, finally arriving at the church St. Peter had built.

3. Theological and Historical Significance

This quote is highly valued by historians and theologians for several reasons:

    Early Marian Devotion: It is one of the earliest explicit historical references to a church being formally dedicated to "the most blessed Mother of God, and Ever-Virgin Mary" (beatissimæ Dei Genitricis semperque virginis Mariæ). This provides powerful evidence for a well-developed Marian devotion and the use of the title Theotokos (God-bearer, or Dei Genitrix) more than a century before it was dogmatically defined at the Council of Ephesus in 431 A.D.

    Cult of the Martyrs: The church's purpose as a "cemetery of the martyrs" (martyrum cœmeteria) highlights the profound connection in the early Church between the veneration of the martyrs and the honor given to the Virgin Mary. She was seen as the Queen of Martyrs, the ultimate witness to Christ.

    Historical Realism: The specific geographical details—the "western quarter," the "suburb," the journey by boat around the Pharos—lend a strong sense of authenticity and historical grounding to the account.

en: ST. POLYCARP OF SMYRNA Whoever perverts the sayings of the Lord for his own desires, and says that there is neither resurrection nor judgment, is the firstborn of Satan. Let us leave the foolishness and the false teaching of the crowd and turn back to the word that was delivered to us in the beginning [Letter to the Philippians 7 (c. A.D. 135)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is one of the most famous in early Christian literature outside of the New Testament. Its importance comes from its author, its historical context, and the powerful language it uses.
1. The Author: St. Polycarp of Smyrna

Polycarp (c. 69 – c. 155 AD) was a towering figure of the post-apostolic age. He was a Bishop of Smyrna (modern-day Izmir, Turkey) and, most importantly, a direct disciple of St. John the Apostle. This personal connection to the apostles gave his words immense authority in the early Church. He is a crucial link in the chain of Apostolic Tradition.
2. The "Firstborn of Satan" Anecdote

This fiery phrase was not just a general insult; it appears to have been a specific title St. Polycarp used for the arch-heretic Marcion. According to St. Irenaeus (who was a disciple of Polycarp), a famous encounter took place in Rome:

    "And Polycarp himself replied to Marcion, who met him on one occasion and said, 'Dost thou know me?' 'I do know thee, the firstborn of Satan.'"
    — St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, 3.3.4

This anecdote shows that the phrase in the letter was a deeply serious condemnation, likely aimed directly at Marcion and his followers, who were active during this period.
3. The Theological Targets: Docetism and Gnosticism

The full text you provided makes it clear what heresies Polycarp is fighting:

    Denial of the Incarnation: The chapter begins, "For whoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is an antichrist." This is a direct attack on Docetism (from the Greek dokein, "to seem"), a Gnostic-leaning heresy that claimed Jesus was a pure spirit who only appeared to be human.

    Denial of the Resurrection and Judgment: The Gnostics and Marcionites generally held a deep contempt for the physical, material world, which they saw as evil or flawed. Consequently, they denied a future bodily resurrection and a final judgment involving the body.

Polycarp links these theological errors directly to a moral failing: "perverting the sayings of the Lord for his own desires." He saw this false teaching not as an honest mistake, but as a satanic corruption of the Gospel.
4. The Appeal to Apostolic Tradition

The second part of your quote is the classic orthodox response to heresy:

    "...Let us leave the foolishness and the false teaching of the crowd and turn back to the word that was delivered to us in the beginning."

This is one of the earliest and clearest articulations of the principle of Apostolic Tradition. For Polycarp and the early Church, the test of true doctrine was not novelty or philosophical sophistication, but its faithful continuity with what the apostles themselves had taught "from the beginning."

en: ST. POLYCARP OF SMYRNA For whoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is Antichrist [1 Jn 4:3], and whoever does not confess the testimony of the cross is of the devil; and whosoever perverts the oracles of the Lord to his own lusts, and says that there is neither a resurrection nor a judgment, he is the firstborn of Satan [Letter to the Philippians (C. A.D. 135)].
greek: Πᾶς γάρ, ὃς ἂν μὴ ὁμολογῇ, Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθέναι, ἀντίχριστός ἐστιν· καὶ ὃς ἂν μὴ ὁμολογῇ τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ σταυροῦ, ἐκ τοῦ διαβόλου ἐστίν· καὶ ὃς ἂν μεθοδεύῃ τὰ λόγια τοῦ κυρίου πρὸς τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας καὶ λέγῃ μήτε ἀνάστασιν μήτε κρίσιν, οὗτος πρωτότοκός ἐστι τοῦ σατανᾶ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This short passage is incredibly rich with historical and theological significance.

1. Historical Context:

    Author: St. Polycarp was the Bishop of Smyrna (modern-day Izmir, Turkey) and, according to his own student St. Irenaeus, he was a direct disciple of the Apostle John. This places him in the generation immediately following the apostles.

    Date: The letter is dated to around A.D. 135, making it one of the earliest Christian documents outside of the New Testament.

    Purpose: He is writing to the church in Philippi to warn them against false teachers who were spreading dangerous doctrines.

2. The Heresies Being Condemned:
St. Polycarp identifies a threefold error that constitutes being the "firstborn of Satan":

    Denying the Incarnation ("Jesus Christ has come in the flesh"): This is a direct attack on Docetism, an early Gnostic heresy. Docetists believed that matter was evil and therefore Christ, being divine, could not have had a real, physical body. They taught he only seemed (Greek: dokeō) to be human. By quoting/alluding to 1 John 4:2-3, Polycarp uses the Apostle John's own teaching to condemn this.

    Denying the Cross ("the testimony of the cross"): This is a logical consequence of Docetism. If Jesus wasn't truly human, his suffering and death on the cross were not real, but an illusion. For Polycarp, denying the reality of the cross is to deny the very act of salvation.

    Denying Resurrection and Judgment: This was another common feature of Gnostic belief systems, which rejected the physical resurrection of the body in favor of a purely spiritual "escape" from the material world. By denying a final judgment, these teachings also promoted moral laxity ("perverts the oracles of the Lord to his own lusts").

3. The "Firstborn of Satan" Anecdote:
This is not just a random insult. It was St. Polycarp's famous, personal description for a specific heretic. His student, St. Irenaeus, records a story of a personal encounter between Polycarp and the notorious heretic Marcion (who also promoted a form of Docetism).

    "And Polycarp himself replied to Marcion, who met him on one occasion, and said, 'Dost thou know me?' 'I do know thee, the first-born of Satan.'"

    —St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, Chapter 3, Section 4.

This historical anecdote shows that the strong language in his letter was not just rhetorical; it reflected his personal conviction in face-to-face confrontations with heretics.

4. The Pastoral Response (The Verse You Included):
The verse that immediately follows (7.2) is just as important, as it shows Polycarp's solution:

    Greek (7.2): διὸ ἀπολιπόντες τὴν ματαιότητα τῶν πολλῶν καὶ τὰς ψευδοδιδασκαλίας ἐπὶ τὸν ἐξ ἀρxῆς ἡμῖν παραδοθέντα λόγον ἐπιστρέψωμεν...

    Translation: "Wherefore, leaving the vanity of many and their false teachings, let us return to the word which was delivered to us from the beginning..."

His response to heresy is not just condemnation, but a call to return to the Apostolic Tradition—the faith "delivered to us from the beginning"—and to reinforce it with prayer, fasting, and vigilance.

en: ST. POLYCARP OF SMYRNA Stand fast, therefore, in these things, and follow the example of the Lord, being firm and unchangeable in the faith, loving the brotherhood [1 Pt 2:17]. . . When you can do good, do not defer it, because "alms delivers from death" [Tb 4:10; 12:9]. Be all of you subject to one another 1 Pt 5:5], having your conduct blameless among the Gentiles [1 Pt 2:12], and the Lord may not be blasphemed through you. But woe to him who blasphemes the name of the Lord [ls 52:5]! [ Letter to the Philippians 10 (c. A.D. 135)].

Omnes vobis invicem subjecti estote, conversationem vestram irreprehensibilem habentes in gentibus, ut ex bonis operibus vestris et vos laudem accipiatis, et Dominus in vobis non blasphemetur. Væ autem illi, per quem nomen Domini blasphematur.
context:
Original Greek Text

The original Greek text for Chapter 10 is lost.

As the note in your source correctly states (Desiderantur Græco... - "The Greek is missing..."), the complete letter of St. Polycarp does not survive in its original Greek. Only Chapters 13 and a portion of Chapter 9 are extant in Greek because they were quoted by the historian Eusebius of Caesarea in his Ecclesiastical History (Book 3, Chapter 36).

The rest of the letter, including the entirety of Chapter 10 that you are looking for, is known to us only through this single, ancient Latin translation. Therefore, it is impossible to provide the original Greek for this specific passage.
English Translation

(Based on the Latin text)

    "Stand fast, therefore, in these things, and follow the example of the Lord, being firm and unchangeable in the faith, loving the brotherhood... When you can do good, do not defer it, because 'alms delivers from death.' Be all of you subject to one another, having your conduct blameless among the Gentiles, so that from your good works you yourselves may receive praise and the Lord may not be blasphemed through you. But woe to him through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed!"

Additional Relevant Details
1. The Author and His Authority

St. Polycarp (c. A.D. 69–155) was the Bishop of Smyrna (modern-day Izmir, Turkey). He is a towering figure of the post-apostolic age because he was a direct disciple of St. John the Apostle. His letter is a precious link to the teaching of the apostles themselves. It was written around A.D. 135.
2. The Context of the Passage

This passage is the core of St. Polycarp's pastoral exhortation to the Christians in Philippi. Having warned them against the love of money and the heresy of docetism (which denied Christ's true humanity), he moves to a practical summary of the Christian life. The entire chapter is a tapestry woven from New Testament phrases and ethical commands.
3. A Mosaic of Scripture

This short passage is a powerful example of how deeply the first Christians were immersed in the scriptures. Polycarp is not just quoting verses; he is thinking and writing in biblical language. The specific allusions are:

    "loving the brotherhood": A direct echo of 1 Peter 2:17.

    "alms delivers from death": A quotation from the book of Tobit (4:10 and 12:9). This shows the early Church's use and reverence for the Deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament.

    "Be all of you subject to one another": A quotation from 1 Peter 5:5.

    "having your conduct blameless among the Gentiles": A direct quotation from 1 Peter 2:12. The concern for the Church's public witness was paramount.

    "woe to him through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed": This is a common theme, echoing Isaiah 52:5 as it was used by St. Paul in Romans 2:24.

The heavy reliance on 1 Peter suggests that this epistle was particularly beloved and influential in the churches of Asia Minor.

en: ST. POLYCARP OF SMYRNA praise you for all things, I bless you, glorify you, along with the everlasting and heavenly Jesus Christ, your beloved Son, with whom, to you, and the Holy Spirit, be glory both now and to all coming ages. Amen [quoted in Martyrdom of Polycarp 14 (c. A.D. 156) emphasis added].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

This short doxology is one of the most important in all of early Christian literature for several reasons:

    Extreme Antiquity: Dating to the mid-second century (c. A.D. 156), this is one of the earliest and clearest extra-biblical examples of a fully formed Trinitarian doxology used in Christian prayer and worship. It demonstrates that the practice of glorifying the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together was already established in the generation immediately following the Apostles.

    Liturgical Form: The structure is highly liturgical and reflects a pattern that would become foundational for Christian prayer. Praise is offered to the Father, through the Son (as High Priest), with the Holy Spirit. This formulation is theologically rich, preserving both the distinction of the divine Persons and their unity in the act of worship.

    High Christology: Jesus is called the "eternal and heavenly High Priest" (ἀρχιερέως). This title, drawn from the Epistle to the Hebrews, affirms Christ's divinity and his unique role as the mediator through whom all true worship reaches the Father.

    Witness to the Holy Spirit's Divinity: The Holy Spirit is included alongside the Father and the Son as the co-recipient of glory. This is a powerful, implicit affirmation of the Holy Spirit's divine status at a very early date, long before the formal definitions of the Council of Constantinople in 381.

    Context of Martyrdom: These are not words from a calm theological treatise; they are the final, climactic words of a man sealing his life's testimony with his death. His prayer is his ultimate act of witness (martyria) to the Triune God for whom he is dying.

en: PROTOEVANGELIUM OF JAMES And, behold, an angel of the Lord stood by, saying: "Anna, Anna, the Lord has heard your prayer, and you shall conceive, and shall bring forth; and your seed shall be spoken of in all the world." And Anna said: "As the Lord my God lives, if I beget either male or female, I will bring it as a gift to the Lord my God; and it shall minister to him in holy things all the days of its life. And [from the time she was three] Mary was in the temple of the Lord as she were a dove that dwelt there [Protoevangelium of Jamnes 4, 8 (C. A.D. 150)].

    (2) Καὶ εἶπεν Ἄννα· Ζῇ Κύριος ὁ θεός μου, ἐὰν γεννήσω εἴτε ἄρρεν εἴτε θῆλυ, προσάξω αὐτὸ δῶρον Κυρίῳ τῷ θεῷ μου, καὶ ἔσται λειτουργοῦν αὐτῷ πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς αὐτοῦ. . . . (1) Ἦν δὲ Μαριὰμ ἐν τῷ ναῷ Κυρίου ὡσεὶ περιστερὰ νεμομένη, καὶ ἐλάμβανεν τροφὴν ἐκ χειρὸς ἀγγέλου.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
About the Source Text

    Title: Protoevangelium of James (Protoevangelium Jacobi), sometimes called the Infancy Gospel of James.

    Date & Author: Written anonymously around A.D. 150. It is a work of early Christian piety, not a historical account by the Apostle James.

    Status: It is an apocryphal gospel, meaning it is outside the canon of the New Testament. While not considered divinely inspired Scripture, it was immensely popular and influential in the early Church.

    Purpose: The text was written to satisfy the curiosity of early Christians about the life of the Virgin Mary, which is not detailed in the canonical Gospels. It emphasizes her purity, unique origins, and lifelong consecration to God.

Theological and Liturgical Significance

These specific passages are the foundational source for several major Christian traditions and feasts:

    The Parents of Mary: This text is the only ancient source that gives the names of Mary's parents as Joachim and Anna. The feasts of St. Joachim and St. Anna in both the Catholic and Orthodox Churches derive entirely from this tradition.

    The Presentation of Mary: Anna's vow in Chapter 4—to dedicate her child to serve God in the Temple—is the narrative basis for the Feast of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary (celebrated on November 21). Chapter 7 of the text describes her being brought to the Temple at age three to fulfill this vow.

    Mary's Purity and Consecration: The description of Mary being "nurtured like a dove" and fed by an angel in the Temple (Chapter 8) powerfully reinforces the belief in her unique holiness and separation from the world from her earliest childhood. This tradition was a cornerstone for the later development of doctrines like the Immaculate Conception.

Analysis of Key Phrases

    λειτουργοῦν αὐτῷ (leitourgoun autō) - "ministering to him": The Greek word for "ministering" is the root of our word "liturgy." Anna's vow is that her child will be dedicated to the official, sacred worship of God in the Temple.

    ὡσεὶ περιστερὰ νεμομένη (hōsei peristera nemomenē) - "nurtured like a dove": This is a very rich image. The dove is a symbol of purity, gentleness, and the Holy Spirit. The Greek word nemomenē means "fed," "nurtured," or "pastured." The phrase suggests not just that Mary lived there, but that she was cared for in a state of perfect innocence and divine protection, which is confirmed by the next clause stating she was fed by an angel.

About Your Edition

The images you provided are from a scholarly critical edition, most likely the famous 19th-century work by Constantin von Tischendorf, Evangelia Apocrypha. The layout, with the reconstructed Greek text at the top and the detailed list of manuscript variations (apparatus criticus) at the bottom, is characteristic of such an edition and represents a very high standard of textual scholarship.

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source Identification

    Name: The Protoevangelium of James (meaning "First Gospel of James"). It is also commonly known as the Infancy Gospel of James.

    Author: The text claims to be written by James (implying the "brother of the Lord"), but this is universally rejected by scholars. The author is anonymous.

    Date: It is dated to the mid-2nd century (c. 145-170 AD), making it one of the earliest non-canonical gospels.

    Status: This work is apocryphal. It is not, and has never been, part of the canonical New Testament accepted by any major Christian tradition.

2. Historical and Theological Significance

Despite being non-canonical, the Protoevangelium of James has had an immense and profound influence on Christian piety, art, and liturgy, particularly in shaping traditions surrounding the Virgin Mary.

    Mary's Parents: This is the first text to name Mary's parents as Joachim and Anne. Their story of barrenness and miraculous conception of Mary forms the first part of the book.

    The Presentation of Mary: It contains the famous story of Mary, at age three, being presented by her parents to live in the Temple, an event commemorated in the liturgical Feast of the Presentation (November 21).

    Joseph as an Elderly Widower: This is perhaps the most influential detail from the passage you cited. The depiction of Joseph as an old man and a widower with children from a previous marriage became the dominant tradition in both Eastern and Western Christianity. This conveniently explained the "brothers of Jesus" mentioned in the canonical Gospels (Mark 6:3, Matthew 13:55) as being Joseph's children from his first wife, thereby safeguarding the doctrine of the Perpetual Virginity of Mary.

    Influence on Art: Scenes from this book are staples of Christian art. Giotto's famous fresco cycle in the Scrovegni Chapel, for instance, depicts many events from the Protoevangelium, including the "Test of the Rods" and the betrothal of Mary and Joseph.

    The Nativity Scene: It adds details not found in the canonical Gospels, such as the birth of Jesus taking place in a cave, a tradition still very strong in the East.

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Immediate Context of the Scene

This confrontation is the climax of a crisis.

    Joseph's Discovery: In Chapter 13, Joseph returns from his work as a builder to find the six-month-pregnant Mary. He is devastated, assuming she has been unfaithful.

    Angelic Reassurance: In Chapter 14, Joseph, like his counterpart in the Gospel of Matthew, has a dream in which an angel reassures him that the child is from the Holy Spirit.

    Public Accusation: However, in Chapter 15, before Joseph can act, a scribe named Annas visits and sees Mary's condition. He reports it to the high priest, leading to both Joseph and Mary being summoned for a formal inquiry. The quote you've selected is the priest's direct accusation of Mary.

2. The Significance of Mary's Response

Mary's defense is a solemn, legal, and theological statement.

    A Solemn Oath: She begins with "As the Lord my God lives..." (Ζῇ κύριος ὁ θεός μου). This is not a casual phrase; it is the most serious form of oath one could take in a Jewish context, invoking God himself as a witness to the truth of the statement.

    Echoes of the Annunciation: Her words, "I know not a man" (ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω), are a direct echo of her question to the angel Gabriel in the canonical Gospel of Luke 1:34 ("How will this be, since I do not know a man?"). The author of the Protoevangelium places this same declaration in a new, public, and judicial setting, turning it from a question of confusion into a powerful defense of her purity.

3. The "Trial by Ordeal"

This scene of accusation is not the end of the story. It directly leads to the book's most dramatic and miraculous vindication of Mary's virginity in Chapter 16.

    The Water of the Ordeal: The high priest, unconvinced by their verbal testimony, subjects both Mary and Joseph to the "water of the ordeal of the Lord." This is a practice loosely based on the test for an unfaithful wife described in the Book of Numbers 5:11-31.

    Miraculous Vindication: Both Mary and Joseph drink the water, and when neither suffers any harm, the priest publicly declares them innocent. This miraculous trial serves as God's public testimony to the truth of the Virgin Birth.

4. The Purpose of the Narrative

This entire storyline—the public accusation, Mary's tearful defense, and the miraculous trial—is absent from the canonical Gospels. The author of the Protoevangelium created it to:

    Dramatize the Narrative: It fills in the "gaps" left by Matthew and Luke with a story full of human emotion, conflict, and suspense.

    Defend the Virgin Birth: Most importantly, it serves as a powerful piece of apologetics. By inventing a public trial that ends in a divine miracle, the author provides a definitive, "in-story" refutation of any accusation or slander against Mary's purity and the divine origin of Jesus.        Additional Context and Analysis of the Images

The images you provided contain more than just that one quote. They show the full scene of the accusation, including the priest's subsequent interrogation of Joseph.
1. The Accusation of Joseph (Chapter 16)

The first, smaller image you sent shows the very end of Chapter 16, where the priest turns his accusation towards Joseph. The full accusation begins in the text of the second image and concludes in the first.

Original Greek Text (from Chapter 16):

    καὶ εἶπεν ὁ ἱερεύς· ...μὴ ψευδομαρτύρει ἀλλὰ λέγε τὸ ἀληθές· ἔκλεψας τοὺς γάμους αὐτῆς καὶ οὐκ ἐφανέρωσας τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ, καὶ οὐκ ἔκλινας τὴν κεφαλήν σου ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα ὅπως εὐλογηθῇ τὸ σπέρμα σου. καὶ Ἰωσὴφ ἐσίγησεν.

English Translation:

    And the priest said: "...Do not bear false witness, but speak the truth. You have stolen her marriage and not made it known to the sons of Israel, and you did not bow your head under the mighty hand [of God] so that your seed might be blessed." And Joseph was silent.

Context: The priest's accusation against Joseph is that he must have consummated the marriage secretly, without the proper public rites ("you stole her marriage"), thus violating the sacred trust. Joseph's silence in the face of this charge sets the stage for the divine vindication that is to come.
2. The Nature of the Document You're Viewing

The images are from a critical edition of the Greek text. This is a scholarly version of the text, and it's important to understand its features:

    The Main Text: The larger text at the top of the columns is the editor's reconstructed version of what the original Greek most likely said.

    The Critical Apparatus: The dense block of text at the bottom is the "critical apparatus." This is a highly abbreviated set of notes showing where different ancient manuscripts (often referred to by letters like A, B, D, E, P, etc.) have different words or spellings. For example, it shows which manuscripts might omit a word (om.), add a word (add.), or have a different spelling. This tool is essential for scholars studying the history of the text's transmission.

3. Narrative Flow

By providing these images, you have captured the entire judicial accusation scene:

    Chapter 15: The priest accuses Mary.

    Chapter 15: Mary makes her solemn oath of innocence.

    Chapter 16: The priest accuses Joseph.

    Chapter 16: Joseph remains silent.

This complete scene of public accusation is what necessitates the "Trial by the Ordeal Water" that immediately follows, where God himself must intervene to prove their innocence to the community.

context:
Historical and Theological Significance

This small piece of papyrus is monumental for several reasons:

    Earliest Marian Prayer: It is the oldest surviving prayer addressed directly to Mary.

    Early Use of Theotokos: This is the earliest known use of the title Θεοτόκε (Theotoke, the vocative form of Theotokos). Its presence here, in a popular prayer from the 3rd century, demonstrates that the belief in Mary as the "God-bearer" or "Mother of God" was part of Christian piety long before it was formally defined at the Council of Ephesus in A.D. 431. It refutes the idea that the title was a 5th-century theological invention.

    A Prayer for Help: The prayer is a plea for protection and rescue, showing that early Christians looked to Mary as a powerful intercessor in times of danger and persecution (which were rampant in the 3rd century).

The Famous Latin Version

The prayer became immensely popular and has a famous Latin version, known as the Sub Tuum Praesidium, which is still widely used in the Catholic Church today:

    Sub tuum praesidium confugimus, Sancta Dei Genetrix. Nostras deprecationes ne despicias in necessitatibus, sed a periculis cunctis libera nos semper, Virgo gloriosa et benedicta.

greek: θεὸς ὁ καθ' ἡμᾶς οὐκ ἔχει σύστασιν ἐν χρόνῳ, μόνος ἄναρχος ὢν καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπάρχων τῶν ὅλων ἀρχή. πνεῦμα ὁ θεός, οὐ διήκων διὰ τῆς ὕλης, πνευμάτων δὲ ὑλικῶν καὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ σχημάτων κατασκευαστής, ἀόρατός τε καὶ ἀναφής, αἰσθητῶν καὶ ὁρατῶν αὐτὸς γεγονὼς πατήρ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
About the Author and Work

    Tatian the Syrian (c. 120–180 AD): Tatian was a 2nd-century Christian apologist and a student of the great St. Justin Martyr in Rome. His Address to the Greeks is a fierce and sometimes abrasive defense of Christianity, which he presents as a superior "barbarian philosophy." Later in his life, he broke from the orthodox community and founded an ascetic sect known as the Encratites, who were condemned as heretical. However, this work was written during his orthodox period and is a valuable witness to early Christian thought.

Theological Significance of the Quote

This short passage is packed with profound theological statements that contrast Christian doctrine with Greco-Roman paganism and philosophy.

    God's Timelessness and Aseity:

        οὐκ ἔχει σύστασιν ἐν χρόνῳ ("does not have a beginning/constitution in time").

        μόνος ἄναρχος ὢν ("He alone IS without beginning").

        This is a direct attack on pagan mythology, where gods like Zeus and the Olympians had complex birth stories and genealogies. Tatian asserts the Judeo-Christian doctrine of a God who is eternal, uncaused, and stands outside of time. He is the ἀρχή (beginning/principle) of all things, but is Himself ἄναρχος (without beginning).

    God is Spirit (A Critique of Materialism and Stoicism):

        πνεῦμα ὁ θεός ("God is Spirit") is a direct quotation from John 4:24.

        The next phrase, οὐ διήκων διὰ τῆς ὕλης ("not pervading matter"), is crucial. This is a direct polemic against the Stoic philosophical concept of God. The Stoics viewed God (the Logos or pneuma) as a fine, fiery, rational substance that permeated and animated the entire material universe, like a soul in a body.

        Tatian rejects this pantheistic view entirely. For him, God is a transcendent spirit, completely distinct from the matter He creates. He is the maker (κατασκευαστής) of matter and spirits, not a part of them.

    God's Incorporeality and Transcendence:

        ἀόρατός τε καὶ ἀναφής ("invisible and impalpable/untouchable").

        This reinforces the distinction between the Creator and creation. Unlike pagan idols which could be seen and touched, or philosophical principles that were tied to matter, the true God is utterly transcendent and beyond the grasp of the physical senses.

    God as Universal Father/Creator:

        αἰσθητῶν καὶ ὁρατῶν αὐτὸς γεγονὼς πατήρ ("being himself the Father of perceptible/sensible and visible things").

        This phrase is an early echo of the language that would later be formalized in the Nicene Creed ("maker of all things, visible and invisible"). It establishes God's absolute sovereignty as the creator of the entire cosmos, both the material world we can see and the spiritual world we cannot.

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Context: Arguing Against Stoic Philosophy

Immediately after this declaration, Tatian contrasts the Christian doctrine of resurrection with the well-known Stoic doctrine of cyclical recurrence.

    Stoic Belief: The Stoics believed that the universe went through endless cycles (palingenesis). The world would be destroyed by fire (ekpyrosis) and then perfectly recreated, with every person and event repeating exactly as before. For Tatian, this was a pointless, deterministic cycle with no ultimate purpose.

    Christian Contrast: Tatian emphasizes that the Christian resurrection is a one-time, final event (ἅπαξ δὲ τῶν καθ' ἡμᾶς αἰώνων πεπερασμένων - "once our age has been completed"). It is not part of an endless cycle. Its purpose is definitive: for the sake of Judgment (χάριν κρίσεως). The judge is not a mythological figure like Minos or Rhadamanthus, but God the Creator Himself.

2. Philosophical Defense of the Resurrection

Tatian anticipates the pagan listener's skepticism and provides a philosophical defense of the resurrection, making two key points:

    The Analogy from Creation: He argues: "Just as I did not exist before I was born... and yet came into being, in the same way, I who was born and then ceased to be through death... will exist again." His logic is that if God can create a person from non-existence once, He can certainly re-create them a second time.

    The Power of God Over Matter: He addresses the common objection about the destruction and scattering of the body. He says that whether his body is destroyed by fire, dissolved in a river, or torn apart by wild beasts, the constituent matter is not lost. It remains preserved in the "storehouses of a rich master" (ταμείοις ἐναπόκειμαι πλουσίου δεσπότου). God, the King, knows where every particle is and can, when He wills, restore the visible substance to its original form.

en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN The bad man may be justly punished, having become depraved through his own fault, but the just man may be deservedly praised for his virtuous deeds. since in the exercise of his free choice he refrained from transgressing the will of God [Address to the Greeks' (c. A.D. 170)].
greek: ...ὅπως ὁ μὲν φαῦλος δικαίως κολάζηται δι' αὑτὸν γεγονὼς μοχθηρός, ὁ δὲ δίκαιος χάριν τῶν ἀνδραγαθημάτων ἀξίως ἐπαινῆται κατὰ τὸ αὐτεξούσιον τοῦ θεοῦ μὴ παραβὰς τὸ βούλημα.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Immediate Context: Creation and Free Will

The quote is the climax of Tatian's explanation of God's creation of angels and humans. In the sentences immediately preceding your quote, he states:

    "The Logos, before the creation of men, becomes the Creator of angels. And each of the two orders of created beings was made with free will (αὐτεξούσιον), not having the nature of good in itself... but with this nature being perfected in them by their freedom of choice."

Your quote, therefore, serves as the logical conclusion: because humans and angels were created with free will, they are justly held responsible for how they use that freedom.
2. Theological Significance: A Classic Free-Will Theodicy

This passage is a powerful and early example of a Christian theodicy—an explanation for why a good God permits the existence of evil.

    Against Fatalism: Tatian is writing to a Greek audience steeped in concepts of fate (εἱμαρμένη). He directly contrasts the Christian view of self-determination (αὐτεξούσιον) with Greek fatalism. For Tatian, human actions are not predetermined; they are the result of free choice.

    The Origin of Evil: The quote firmly places the origin of evil not in God, but in the creature's misuse of its freedom. The "bad man" becomes depraved "through his own fault" (δι' αὑτὸν γεγονὼς μοχθηρός). This absolves God of being the author of evil and is a cornerstone of orthodox Christian thought.

    Basis for Just Judgment: Because humans are free, God's judgment is just. It is not arbitrary. Punishment is deserved because the choice to do evil was freely made. Likewise, praise (and reward) for virtue is deserved because the just man chose not to transgress God's will.

en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN But men form the material of their apostasy. For, having shown them a plan of the position of the stars, like dice players, they introduced fate, a flagrant injustice. For the judge and the judged are made so by fate [Address to the Greeks 8 (c. A.D. 170)].

context:
Additional Context and Analysis

The text you provided is a brilliant example of early Christian apologetics. Tatian's goal is to dismantle the philosophical and religious worldview of the Greeks. The quote you selected is the opening salvo in his attack on astrological fatalism.

1. Who are "They"? The Architects of Apostasy:
In the preceding chapters, Tatian has been discussing the fallen angels, or demons (daimones). He argues that these beings, after their own fall, sought to lead humanity astray. So when he says "they introduced fate," he is referring specifically to these demons. For Tatian, astrology and the concept of inescapable fate (heimarmenē) are not neutral philosophical ideas; they are a demonic invention designed to enslave humanity.

2. The Argument Against Fate: The Destruction of Morality:
Tatian’s core objection is that fate is a "flagrant injustice" because it eradicates moral responsibility.

    If a person's actions are predetermined by the stars, then there can be no true justice.

    The "judge" is not acting from reason, and the "judged" is not responsible for their crime. Both are merely puppets of destiny.

    This removes any basis for praise, blame, sin, or virtue, which is precisely the demons' goal.

3. The Analogy of the Dice Players:
This is a powerful and dismissive image. Tatian compares the demons to crooked gamblers.

    They lay out the stars like a game board or a "diagram" (διάγραμμα).

    They introduce "fate" as the arbitrary rules of the game.

    Humans are treated like dice (κύβοι), tossed about with no will of their own, all for the cruel amusement of these demonic spectators. This idea is reinforced later in the chapter when he says the demons watch human tragedy as if it were entertainment in a theater (ὥσπερ ἐν θεάτρῳ τερπωλὴν παρέσχε τούτοις).

4. The Broader Attack in Chapter 8:
After refuting the philosophical concept of fate, Tatian spends the rest of the chapter (as seen in your full text) launching a scathing, sarcastic attack on the pagan gods themselves. He points out their internal contradictions and immoral behavior to show that they are not worthy of worship:

    Contradictory Laws: Rhea demands castration, while Aphrodite delights in marriage.

    Immoral Actions: Athena and Asclepius divide the blood of Medusa, one using it to kill and the other to heal. Hephaestus attempts to rape Athena. Zeus commits incest with his daughter, Persephone.

    Weakness and Subjection: He even argues that the gods themselves, including Zeus, are subject to the same passions and fate as humans, proving they are not divine.

In summary, your chosen quote is the philosophical foundation for Tatian's entire argument in this chapter. He first dismantles the intellectual framework of pagan determinism and then proceeds to mock the absurd and immoral stories of the gods who supposedly operate within that framework.

en: Such are the demons; these are they who laid down the doctrine of fate. Their fundamental principle was the placing of animals in the heavens. For the creeping things on the earth, and those that swim in the waters, and the quadrupeds on the mountains, with which they lived when expelled from heaven-these they dignified with celestial honor, so that they might themselves be thought to remain in heaven, and, by placing the constellations there, might make the irrational course of life on earth appear rational. Thus the high-spirited and he who is crushed with toil, the temperate and the intemperate, the indigent and the wealthy, are what they are simply because of the controllers of their nativity. For the delineation of the zodiacal circle is the work of gods. And, when the light of one of them predominates. as they express it, it deprives all the rest of their honor; and he who now is conquered at another time gains the predominance. And the seven planets are well pleased with them, as if they were amusing themselves with dice. But we are superior to fate, and instead of wandering demons, we have learned to know one Lord who wanders not [ibid., 9].
greek: Τοιοῦτοί τινές εἰσιν οἱ δαίμονες· οὗτοι οἳ τὴν εἱμαρμένην ὥρισαν. στοιχείωσις δὲ αὐτοῖς ἡ ζώωσις ἦν. τὰ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἑρπετὰ καὶ τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι νηκτὰ καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τοῖς ὄρεσι τετράποδα, μεθ' ὧν ἐποιοῦντο τὴν δίαιταν ἔκβλητοι τῆς ἐν οὐρανῷ διαίτης γεγενημένοι, ταῦτα τῆς ἐπουρανίου τιμῆς ἠξίωσαν, ἵνα τε νομισθῶσιν αὐτοὶ διατρίβν ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ τὴν ἄλογον ἐπὶ γῆς πολιτείαν εὔλογον διὰ τῆς ἀστροθεσίας ἀποδείξωσιν. ὥστε ὁ θυμικὸς καὶ ὁ ἐπίμοχθος καὶ ὁ ἐγκρατευόμενος καὶ ὁ ἀκρατὴς καὶ ὁ πτωχεύων καὶ ὁ πλουτῶν ἐστι τῶν νομοθετησάντων τὴν γένεσιν. ἡ γὰρ τοῦ ζωδιακοῦ κύκλου γραφὴ θεῶν ἐστι ποίημα. καὶ τὸ ἐπικρατῆσαν, ὥς φασιν, ἑνὸς αὐτῶν φῶς τοὺς πλείονας παραβραβεύει, καὶ ὁ νικώμενος νῦν εἰσαῦθις ἐπικρατεῖν εἴωθεν· εὐαρεστοῦσι δὲ αὐτοῖς οἱ ἑπτὰ πλανῆται ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν τοῖς πεσσοῖς ἀθύροντες. ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ εἱμαρμένης ἐσμὲν ἀνώτεροι καὶ ἀντὶ πλανητῶν δαιμόνων ἕνα τὸν ἀπλανῆ δεσπότην μεμαθήκαμεν.

Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Context: Tatian (c. 120–180 AD) was an Assyrian Christian apologist and a student of St. Justin Martyr in Rome. His Address to the Greeks is a scathing, satirical, and often angry critique of Greek culture, philosophy, and religion, written to demonstrate the superiority of Christianity, which he calls "our philosophy."

    The Attack on Fate (Heimarmenē): Belief in fate and determination by the stars was pervasive in the Greco-Roman world, especially in popular Stoicism and various mystery religions. Tatian’s claim that "we are superior to fate" was a radical and liberating declaration. It positioned Christianity as a path to true freedom from a deterministic, impersonal cosmos, offering instead a relationship with a personal, sovereign Lord.

    Demonology and Astrology: Tatian presents a clear theory: demons are fallen spiritual beings who, after being cast out of heaven, sought to deceive humanity. They invented astrology by placing the images of the earthly animals they once associated with into the sky as constellations (the Zodiac). This was a trick to make humans believe their lives were governed by these celestial powers (i.e., the demons themselves) rather than by their own free will and the providence of the one true God.

    The Brilliant Wordplay on "Planets": The final sentence contains a masterful pun that is central to the passage's power.

        The Greek word for "planets" is πλανῆται (planētai), which literally means "wanderers," because they appear to wander across the sky relative to the fixed stars.

        Tatian contrasts these "wandering demons" (πλανητῶν δαιμόνων) with the "one Lord who wanders not" (ἕνα τὸν ἀπλανῆ δεσπότην). The word ἀπλανῆ (aplanē) means "not wandering," fixed, steady, and unerring.

        He is therefore contrasting the deceptive, erratic, wandering demons with the one true, stable, and unerring Lord of the universe. This is a powerful rhetorical conclusion.

    Satire in the Rest of the Chapter: The rest of the Greek text you provided (9.2-9.4) continues this mocking tone by listing the ridiculous mythological origins of other constellations (e.g., Erigone's dog, the scorpion that helped Artemis, the Centaur Chiron, etc.), essentially asking, "Was the sky empty before these silly events happened?" This satirical deconstruction of Greek myths is a hallmark of Tatian's style.

en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN We do not act as fools, O Greeks, nor utter idle tales. when we say that God was born in the form of a man [Address to the Greeks 21 (C. A.D. 170)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Author and Work

    Tatian the Syrian (c. 120–180 AD): Tatian was a second-century Christian writer and theologian. He was a pupil of the great apologist St. Justin Martyr in Rome. While his early works, like this one, are considered orthodox, he later broke from the mainstream Church and founded an ascetic sect known as the Encratites, who were condemned for their extreme views (such as rejecting marriage and wine).

    Address to the Greeks (Oratio ad Graecos): This work is a classic of early Christian apology. Unlike the more conciliatory tone of his teacher, Justin, Tatian’s address is aggressive, confrontational, and often contemptuous of Greek philosophy, religion, and culture. His goal is to demonstrate the bankruptcy of paganism and the supreme truth and antiquity of Christianity.

2. Immediate Context of the Quote (Chapter 21)

The quote you selected is the opening sentence of a masterful polemical argument. Tatian anticipates the primary objection a sophisticated Greek listener would have: "The idea of God being born in human form is a foolish and absurd fairy tale."

Tatian's strategy is a pre-emptive counter-attack known as the tu quoque ("you too") argument. He essentially says, "You think our story is absurd? Let's look at your own revered myths."

Immediately after your quote, he launches into a list of embarrassing and immoral stories about the Greek gods from their own literature:

    Athena disguising herself as the warrior Deiphobus to trick Hector.

    Apollo, the great god, having to work as a shepherd for a mortal king, Admetus.

    Hera, queen of the gods, visiting Semele disguised as an old woman.

    Asclepius, the god of healing, being killed.

    Heracles, the great hero, burning himself to death.

    Prometheus being punished by a jealous Zeus for helping humanity.

His point is devastatingly clear: The Christian proclamation of the Incarnation, while a profound mystery, is infinitely more noble and credible than the petty, deceptive, and all-too-human stories of the pagan gods.
3. Theological Significance

    A Bold Proclamation: This is one of the earliest, most direct, and unapologetic statements of the Incarnation found in apologetic literature. Tatian isn't trying to soften the message or explain it away philosophically. He uses the strong verb καταγγέλλοντες (katangellontes), which means "we proclaim" or "we announce." It is a term of public, authoritative declaration.

    The Form of a Man: The phrase ἐν ἀνθρώπου μορφῇ (en anthrōpou morphē - "in the form of a man") is a powerful echo of the language used by St. Paul in Philippians 2:7, where Christ Jesus "took the form of a servant" (μορφήν δούλου λαβών).

    A Foundational Claim: Tatian places the Incarnation at the center of the Christian message, presenting it not as a "tale" (λῆρος - lēros, idle talk, nonsense) but as the foundational truth upon which Christianity stands or falls.

en: TATIAN THE SYRIAN Simon Cephas answered and said. "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God." Jesus answered and said unto him, "Blessed are you, Simon, son of Jonah: flesh and blood has not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven. And say unto thee also, that you are Cephas, and on this rock will I build my Church; and the gates 01 hades shall not prevail against it" [Diatesseron 23 (c. A.D. 170)].

context:
Additional Relevant Details

    "Cephas" and "Petra": A Syriac/Aramaic Echo:
    The most striking feature of the Latin version you found is its directness. In Aramaic (and Syriac), the word for "rock" is Kēphā. Jesus names Simon Kēphā and says on this kēphā he will build his church. The pun is perfect.

        Greek creates a slight distinction: Petros (a masculinized name) and petra (the rock).

        The standard Latin Vulgate does the same: Petrus and petram.

        Your Diatessaron text, however, says tu es Petra ("You are Rock"). This is a very literal, un-gendered translation that preserves the force of the original Aramaic/Syriac pun much more directly than the standard Vulgate. This shows the Syriac influence on this version of the text.

    Harmonization of the Gospels:
    The Diatessaron is a "harmony," meaning it weaves the four gospels into one. While this specific passage is almost entirely from Matthew 16, Tatian places it within a sequence of events drawn from Mark and John as well. Your provided text shows this perfectly: it starts with events from Matthew 15 and John 4, transitions to the confession from Matthew 16, and then continues with events from Mark 8.

    Tatian's Importance:
    The Diatessaron was the standard Gospel text used in the Syriac-speaking Church for nearly two centuries. Its existence from such an early date (c. A.D. 170) is powerful evidence for the authority and widespread acceptance of all four canonical Gospels by the mid-second century.   Additional Relevant Details

    This IS the Syriac Quote You Were Looking For: Entry #1268 is the best scholarly reconstruction of the passage from Tatian's Diatessaron that you requested. The Syriac text is the direct source for the English translation you provided.

    The "Kepha" Pun is Clear:
    The Syriac makes the Aramaic wordplay even more explicit than the Latin or Greek:

        ܕܐܢܬ ܗܘ **ܟܐܦܐ** (d-ant hú Kēphā) - "that you are the Rock"

        ܘܥܠ ܗܕܐ **ܟܐܦܐ** (w-‘al hādē Kēphā) - "and upon this rock"
        It uses the exact same word, Kēphā, for both Peter's name and the foundation of the Church. This is the original, powerful force of Jesus's words.

    Understanding the Other Entries (#1269-1276):
    These are called textual variants. They show how other ancient Syriac gospels or writers quoted this passage. For example:

        #1269 & #1270: These are slightly different and abbreviated versions of the same story.

        #1271-1276: These are just tiny fragments of the confession ("You are the Son of the living God," "You are the Messiah," etc.). These might come from other Church Fathers who only quoted a small part of the verse.
        The footnotes at the bottom of the page tell scholars which ancient manuscript or author each of these variants comes from.

Conclusion: You have successfully found the original Syriac text of the passage from Tatian's Diatessaron. The main entry, #1268, is the most complete and authoritative reconstruction based on our best ancient witness, St. Ephrem the Syrian.

context:
Additional Relevant Details

    The Nature of the Diatessaron:
    The Diatessaron (meaning "Through the Four") is the most important Gospel harmony from the early Church. Written by Tatian the Syrian around A.D. 170, it masterfully weaves the four canonical Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John) into a single, continuous narrative. The passage you selected is a perfect example of this technique.

    How Tatian Harmonized This Passage:
    You can see Tatian's editorial hand at work. He creates a single, powerful command from Jesus by blending phrases from three different Gospels:

        He begins with Matthew 28:18 ("All authority in heaven and earth has been given to me").

        He inserts John 20:21b ("as my Father has sent me, so I also send you").

        He then uses Mark 16:15b ("Go into all the world, and preach my gospel in all the creation").

        He returns to Matthew 28:19-20 for the command to teach, the Trinitarian baptismal formula, and the promise of Christ's perpetual presence.

    The Source of Your Texts (This is fascinating):
    You have provided texts from two different and very important manuscript traditions of the Diatessaron.

        The Latin Text: The long Latin text you provided is from a later Latin translation of an Arabic version of the Diatessaron. The very end of your text tells its incredible story: it was translated from Syriac into Arabic by the famous scholar Abû-l-Pharaģ, from a manuscript written by a disciple of the legendary translator Honain ben Ishac. This shows the complex journey of the text: a likely Greek or Syriac original -> Syriac -> Arabic -> Latin.

        The Syriac Text: The image you provided is from a modern scholarly edition that presents the Syriac text of the Diatessaron, likely reconstructed from St. Ephrem the Syrian's commentary on it, as the original Syriac manuscript is lost. The Spanish translation in the image is a helpful modern guide but, as you can see, is not always a literal word-for-word rendering.

You have pinpointed a crucial passage from one of early Christianity's most influential, though now partially lost, documents.

context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: The author is Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), a brilliant and fiery Carthaginian writer often called the "Father of Latin Christianity." The work, Against Hermogenes, is a polemical treatise written around A.D. 203.

    Primary Theological Context: The entire book is an argument against the teaching of Hermogenes, a Christian painter who held a philosophical view common in Greek thought: that God did not create the world from nothing, but rather fashioned it from a pre-existing, co-eternal matter (materia).

    The Core Argument of the Quote: This passage is the heart of Tertullian's refutation. He uses a powerful and concise chain of logic to defend the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo (creation from nothing):

        God is One/Unique (unicus).

        To be truly unique and sole (solus), nothing can be co-eternal with Him.

        If matter were co-eternal, God would not be truly sole.

        Therefore, matter cannot be co-eternal.

        Therefore, all things must be from God (ab illo).

        And if they are from God alone, they must be created from nothing (ex nihilo).

    The Role of Scripture: Tertullian brilliantly uses Romans 11:34-35 as his ultimate proof. He argues that if God had to work with pre-existing matter, He would have been constrained by its properties. He would have effectively needed to "take counsel" with the matter to see what was possible. But St. Paul declares that God is absolutely sovereign and needed no counselor. This proves, for Tertullian, that God was not dependent on any pre-existing substance and created freely, from nothing.

    Significance: This text is a cornerstone of Western Christian theology on the doctrine of creation. It powerfully defends God's absolute sovereignty, omnipotence, and freedom. By refuting the idea of a co-eternal matter, Tertullian also refutes the Gnostic tendency to blame evil on a flawed material principle, insisting instead on the sole causality and goodness of the one God.

en: Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul: to what rule of faith the Galatians were brought for correction; what the Philippians, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians read by it; what utterance also the Romans give, so very near (to the apostles), to whom Peter and Paul conjointly bequeathed the gospel even sealed with their own blood [Against Marcion 4:5 (C. A.D. 209)].

Proxima est tibi Achaia? Habes Corinthum. Si non longe es a Macedonia, habes Philippos, habes Thessalonicenses. Si potes in Asiam tendere, habes Ephesum. Si autem Italiae adiaces, habes Romam, unde nobis quoque auctoritas praesto est. ... Videamus quod lac a Paulo Corinthii hauserint; ad quam regulam Galatae sint recorrecti; quid legant Philippenses, Thessalonicenses, Ephesii; quid etiam Romani de proximo sonent, quibus evangelium et Petrus et Paulus sanguine quoque suo signatum reliquerunt.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

This passage is one of the most famous and important articulations of the early Church's principle of Apostolic Tradition.

    The Context and Argument: Tertullian's opponent, Marcion, had created his own, heavily edited version of the New Testament. He threw out the entire Old Testament and most of the New, keeping only a mutilated Gospel of Luke and ten of Paul's epistles. Tertullian's brilliant counter-argument is to appeal to the public, historical, and verifiable teaching of the churches founded directly by the apostles. He is essentially saying, "You can't just invent your own Christianity. If you want to know the true gospel, go to the source—the apostolic churches. See what they have believed and taught from the very beginning. Their teaching is the authentic one."

    The "Rule of Faith" (Regula Fidei): When Tertullian mentions the "rule" to which the Galatians were corrected, he is referring to the regula fidei, or "rule of faith." This was a summary of core Christian doctrines (like a proto-creed) that was universally taught in the apostolic churches and used as a benchmark to identify and refute heresy.

    The Special Authority of Rome: Notice how Tertullian singles out the Church of Rome for special mention. He calls it the church "from which there comes even into our own hands the very authority." He highlights two unique qualifications for Rome's authority:

        Proximity: They are "so very near" (de proximo), not just in geography for him, but in their direct connection to the chief apostles.

        The Witness of Peter and Paul: Rome is the church where both Peter and Paul preached and, crucially, were martyred. They "bequeathed the gospel even sealed with their own blood." This foundation by the two most prominent apostles and their ultimate witness of martyrdom gave the Church of Rome a preeminent place of honor and authority in the early Christian world.

    Source Citation: You can find the original Latin text in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL), Volume 2, columns 366-367.

en: Touching the resurrection of the dead 1 Cor 15:12], let us first inquire how some persons then denied it. No doubt in the same way in which it is even now denied, since the resurrection of the flesh always has men to deny it. But many wise men claim a divine nature for the soul, and are confident of its undying destiny, and even the multitude worship the dead in the presumption they boldly entertain that their souls survive. As for our bodies, however, it is clear that they perish either at once by fire or the wild beasts, or even when most carefully kept by the passage of time. When, therefore, the apostle refutes those who deny the resurrection of the flesh, he defends, in opposition to them, the precise matter of their denial. that is, the resurrection of the body. You have the whole answer wrapped up in this. All the rest is superfluous. Now on this very point, the resurrection of the dead, it is necessary that the proper force of the words should be accurately maintained. The word dead expresses simply that which has lost the vital principle, by means of which it used to live. Now the body is what loses life, and as the result of losing it becomes dead. To the body, therefore, the term dead is only suitable. Moreover, as resurrection accrues to what iS dead, and dead is a term applicable only to a body, only the body alone has a resurrection incidental to it. So the word resurrection, or rising again, embraces only what has fallen down. "To rise," indeed, can be said of what has never fallen down, but had been lying down. But to rise again" can be said only of what has fallen down; because it is by rising again, in consequence of its having fallen down, that it is said to have re-risen. For the syllable "re" always implies repetition. We say, therefore, that the body falls to the ground by death, as facts show, in accordance with the law of God. For to the body it was said, "Dust you are, and unto dust shall you return" [Against Marcion 5:9 (c. A.D. 209)].
latin:
De resurrectione mortuorum prius est, quomodo negetur, retractare. Sine dubio eodem modo, quo et nunc, quia semper resusurrectio carnis negatores habet. Animas enim et divinas multi sapientes vocant, et superstites affirmant, et vulgus etiam mortuos ita honorat, praesumptione scilicet qua supersint. Corpora vero manifestum est interire, vel statim igni aut bestiis, vel diligentissime quoque reservata postremo tempore. Igitur cum apostolus refutat negantes resurrectionem mortuorum, id ipsum defendit adversus eos, quod negabatur, carnis scilicet resurrectionem. Totum in hoc habes. Superest cetera vacare.

    Tunc igitur, de resurrectione mortuorum, proprietatem vocabulorum necesse est custodiri. Mortuum non dicitur nisi quod animam amisit, de qua vivebat. Corpus est quod amittit animam, et amittendo fit mortuum. Ita mortui vocabulum non competit nisi corpori. Porro si resurrectio mortui est, mortuum autem non est nisi corpus, corporis erit resurrectio. Sic et resurrectionis vocabulum non complectitur nisi quod cecidit. Resurgere enim potest dici et quod omnino non cecidit, sed iacuit. Rursus autem resurgere non dicitur nisi quod cecidit; quia in eo rursus surgit, quod cecidit, ideo resurgit. 'Re-' enim syllaba iterationi praeponitur. Nos igitur dicimus corpus cadere in terram per mortem, sicut et accidit, ex Dei lege. Illi enim dictum est: Terra es, et in terram ibis.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
Context of the Argument

Tertullian is writing against Marcion, a second-century heretic who taught that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser, wrathful "Creator" god, distinct from the supreme, merciful God revealed by Jesus. A key part of Marcion's theology was a hatred of the material world and the flesh, which he saw as the flawed creation of this lesser god. Consequently, he denied the physical incarnation of Christ (promoting a docetic, or phantom-like, view of Jesus) and vehemently rejected the resurrection of the flesh. For Marcion, salvation was the soul's escape from the body, not the redemption of the body.

In Book 5 of Against Marcion, Tertullian is using the Epistles of St. Paul (the only part of the New Testament that Marcion accepted, albeit in a heavily edited form) to dismantle Marcion's own theology. This passage from chapter 9 is a direct assault on Marcion's denial of the bodily resurrection.
Tertullian's Method: A Lawyer's Precision

This passage is a perfect example of Tertullian's legalistic and philological approach to theology. He builds his case like a lawyer in court, based on the precise definition of terms:

    Define "Dead" (Mortuum): He argues that only the physical body truly "loses life" and can therefore properly be called "dead." The soul, he notes, is widely believed to survive.

    Define "Resurrection" (Resurrectio): He makes a brilliant etymological point.

        Surgere (to rise) can apply to anything that gets up.

        Re-surgere (to rise again) can only apply to something that has first fallen. The prefix "re-" implies repetition or restoration.

    The Conclusion: Since only the body dies (falls), only the body can rise again. The term "resurrection of the dead" can logically only mean "resurrection of the body." Any other interpretation does violence to the plain meaning of the words.

The Final Jab: Using Marcion's Hated Scripture

The final sentence is a masterstroke of polemics. By quoting Genesis 3:19 ("Dust you are, and unto dust shall you return"), Tertullian is using the scripture of the Creator God whom Marcion despises to prove the very nature of the body that will be resurrected. He is forcing Marcion to confront the fact that the Christian doctrine of resurrection is inextricably linked to the doctrine of creation found in the Old Testament.

en: TERTULLIAN OF CARTHAGE [T]he man of sin, the son of perdition, who must first be revealed before the Lord comes, "who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; who is to sit in the temple of God, and boast himself as being God?" [2 Thes 2:3-4]. According to our view, he is Antichrist; as it is taught us in both the ancient and the new prophecies, and especially by the apostle John, who says that "already many false prophets are gone out into the world,* the forerunners of Antichrist, who deny that Christ is come in the flesh 1 Jn 4:1-3], and do not acknowledge Jesus [to be the Christ], meaning in God the Creator [ Against Marcion 5:16 (c. This passage is a brilliant example of Tertullian's polemical genius. He isn't just defining the Antichrist; he is using the doctrine of the Antichrist as a weapon to destroy Marcion's theology.

    The Context: Refuting Marcion's Eschatology: In Book 5, Tertullian is systematically dismantling Marcion's interpretation of St. Paul's letters. Marcion accepted a heavily edited version of Paul's epistles but rejected the Old Testament entirely. He believed the God of the Old Testament (the "Creator") was a harsh, lesser deity, while the Father of Jesus was a different, "Good God" who was previously unknown.

    The Argument's Genius: Tertullian's argument goes like this:

        St. Paul, whom you (Marcion) claim to follow, speaks of a "man of sin."

        This figure will sit "in the temple of God". Tertullian asks Marcion: Whose temple? The "Good God" has no temple on earth; only the Creator God of the Jews does. Therefore, the Antichrist is defined by his opposition to the Creator God.

        Tertullian then masterfully connects Paul's "man of sin" with John's "Antichrist." He points out that the forerunners of Antichrist are those who "deny that Christ has come in the flesh."

        The Knockout Punch: He concludes with the phrase solventes Jesum, scilicet in Deo creatore ("dissolving Jesus, that is to say, in God the Creator"). For Tertullian, to deny the fleshly reality of Jesus (as Marcion and other Gnostics did) was to "dissolve" him from his identity as the Messiah of the Creator God, sent into the Creator's world to fulfill the Creator's prophecies.

    Unity of the Testaments: By showing that the Antichrist's primary rebellion is against the Creator God and His temple, Tertullian proves the unity of the divine plan across the Old and New Testaments. The enemy of Christ is the enemy of the God of Abraham. This directly refutes Marcion's core belief in two separate, opposing gods.

en: We do indeed believe that there is only one God, but we believe that under this dispensation, or, as we say, "divine economy," there is also a Son of this one and only God, his Word, who proceeded from him and through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made [Against Praxeas 2 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: ...unicum quidem Deum credimus: sub hac tamen dispensatione, quam oeconomiam dicimus, ut unici Dei sit et filius sermo ipsius, qui ex ipso processerit, per quem omnia facta sunt, et sine quo factum est nihil.
