Additional Relevant Details & Context

The passage you've highlighted is one of the most important and influential in the history of Western theology for several key reasons:

1. The Heresy Being Fought: Modalism (or Patripassianism)
Tertullian was writing against a teacher named Praxeas. To safeguard the strict monotheism of Christianity, Praxeas taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct Persons, but simply different "modes" or "masks" of the one God. This led to the conclusion that it was the Father himself who suffered and died on the cross, a heresy known as Patripassianism (from Latin Pater for "Father" and passus for "suffered").

2. Tertullian's Groundbreaking Solution: The Oeconomia
To refute this, Tertullian needed a way to explain how God could be both one and three. He brilliantly borrowed a term from Greek thought and Roman administration:

    Oeconomia (Greek, οἰκονομία): This word literally means "household management" or "stewardship." In a theological context, Tertullian uses it to mean the internal arrangement or divine plan of the Godhead. He argues that the unity of God is not compromised by an internal economy that includes the Son and the Spirit.

    Dispensatio (Latin): This is the Latin equivalent Tertullian uses, meaning "arrangement" or "disposition."

This concept allowed the Church to speak of distinctions within the one God without falling into polytheism.

3. The First Use of "Trinity" in Latin Theology
Just a few lines later in the same chapter you provided, Tertullian gives us one of the earliest clear uses of the Latin word Trinitas (Trinity) in a theological context:

    "...custodiatur oeconomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum."

    "...the mystery of the economy is safeguarded, which arranges the Unity into a Trinity, setting forth three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit."

4. The Language of "One Substance, Three Persons"
This chapter lays the foundation for all subsequent Western Trinitarian theology. Tertullian goes on to introduce the formula that would become standard: one substance (substantia) and three persons. He writes:

    "Tres autem non statu, sed gradu; nec substantia, sed forma... unius autem substantiae..."

    "Three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form... but of one substance."

In this work, Tertullian essentially created the Latin vocabulary that the Western Church would use for centuries to articulate the doctrine of the Trinity. Your quote is the opening statement of this revolutionary theological argument.

en: We, as we always have done (and more especially since we have been better instructed by the Paraclete, who indeed leads men into all truth), believe that there iS only one God, but under the following dispensation, or oikonomia, as it is called, that this one and only God has a Son, his Word, who proceeded from himself, by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. We believe he was sent by the Father into the Virgin, and was born of her -being both man and God, the Son of Man and the Son of God, and was called by the name of Jesus Christ; we believe he suffered, died, and was buried, according to the Scriptures, and, after he was raised again by the Father and taken back to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come to judge the living and the dead; and that this one God also sent from heaven, according to his own promise, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, the sanctifier of the faith of those who believe in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit. This rule of faith has come down to us from the beginning of the gospel, even before any of the older heretics [Against Praxeas (Cc. A.D. 218)].
latin: Nos vero et semper, et nunc magis, ut instructiores per Paracletum deductorem scilicet omnis veritatis, unicum quidem Deum credimus: sub hac tamen dispensatione, quam oeconomiam dicimus, ut unici Dei sit et filius sermo ipsius, qui ex ipso processerit, per quem omnia facta sunt, et sine quo factum est nihil: hunc missum a Patre in virginem, et ex ea natum hominem et Deum, filium hominis et filium Dei, et cognominatum Jesum Christum: hunc passum, hunc mortuum et sepultum secundum Scripturas, et resuscitatum a Patre, et in coelos resumptum, sedere ad dexteram Patris, venturum judicare vivos et mortuos, qui exinde miserit, secundum promissionem suam, a Patre Spiritum Sanctum Paracletum, sanctificatorem fidei eorum qui credunt in Patrem et Filium et Spiritum Sanctum. Hanc regulam ab initio Evangelii decucurrisse, etiam ante priores quosque haereticos, nedum ante Praxeam hesternum...

This passage is one of the most important in the history of Trinitarian theology. Here's why:

    The Context: Refuting Monarchianism: Tertullian wrote this book to refute a heretic named Praxeas. Praxeas taught a doctrine known as Modalistic Monarchianism (or Patripassianism), which held that God is a single person who simply reveals himself in different "modes"—sometimes as Father, sometimes as Son. This implied that it was God the Father Himself who suffered and died on the cross. Tertullian's goal is to defend the real distinction of the Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) while fiercely upholding that there is only one God.

    Key Term: Oikonomia / Dispensatio: This is the central concept Tertullian uses to solve the problem. The Greek term oikonomia (which he translates into Latin as dispensatio) literally means "household management" or "plan." Theologically, he uses it to describe God's internal plan or arrangement. There is one God, one divine substance, but within that unity, there is an "economy" or "dispensation" that arranges the unity into a Trinity of distinct persons. This was a revolutionary way of articulating the faith in Latin.

    The Regula Fidei (Rule of Faith): By laying out this creed-like summary, Tertullian is appealing to the Rule of Faith—the core, unwritten apostolic teaching that circulated in the churches before the formal creeds. His argument is that his Trinitarian view is not a new invention but is the ancient, original faith that has been held "from the beginning of the gospel." He contrasts this antiquity with the "novelty" of Praxeas, whom he dismissively calls "of yesterday" (hesternum).

    Influence of Montanism: The phrase "better instructed by the Paraclete" is a clear reference to Tertullian's adherence to Montanism. The Montanists believed in a "New Prophecy" of the Holy Spirit (the Paraclete) that was revealing deeper truths to the Church. Tertullian saw his advanced understanding of the Trinity as a fruit of this new revelation.

    Pioneering Trinitarian Language: Although not in the specific quote you asked for, the text you provided immediately following it contains the first clear articulation in Latin of the language that would define Western Trinitarianism for all time:

        "...custodiatur oeconomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum. Tres autem non statu, sed gradu; nec substantia, sed forma... unius autem substantiae..."
        "...the mystery of the economy is safeguarded, which arranges the unity into a Trinity, setting forth three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Three, however, not in status but in grade; not in substance but in form... but of one substance..."

    Tertullian is the first known Latin writer to use the word Trinitas (Trinity) and to apply the terms substantia (substance) and persona (person) to God, laying the groundwork for all future Latin theology on the subject.

en: [S]ome opportunity must be given for reviewing the statements of heretics], with a view to the instruction and protection of various persons; even if only so that it does not seem that each perversion of the truth is condemned without examination, and simply prejudged; especially in the case of this heresy, which supposes that possesses the pure truth, in thinking that one cannot believe in only one God in any other way than by saying that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the very same Person. As if in this way one were not all, in that all are of one, by unity of substance; while the mystery of the dispensation that distributes the unity into a Trinity is still guarded, placing in their order the three Personsthe Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance [Against Praxeas 2 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: Sed salva ista praescriptione, utique tamen propter instructionem et munitionem quorumdam, dandus est etiam retractatibus locus: vel ne videatur unaquaeque perversitas, non examinata, sed praejudicata damnari, maxime haec, quae se existimat meram veritatem possidere, dum unicum Deum non alias putat credendum, quam si ipsum eumdemque et Patrem et Filium et Spiritum Sanctum dicat: quasi non sic quoque unus sit omnia, dum ex uno omnia, per substantiae scilicet unitatem; et nihilominus custodiatur oeconomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum. Tres autem non statu, sed gradu; nec substantia, sed forma; nec potestate, sed specie: unius autem substantiae.

This passage is extraordinarily important for several reasons, as it introduces key concepts and vocabulary that would define Western Trinitarian theology for centuries.

1. The Heresy of Praxeas (Modalism):
Tertullian is writing against a heretic named Praxeas who taught Modalistic Monarchianism. This heresy "protected" the oneness of God (the monarchia) by claiming that "Father," "Son," and "Holy Spirit" were simply different modes or roles played by the one divine person. This led to the conclusion known as Patripassianism—the idea that God the Father himself was born, suffered, and died on the cross (since He is the Son). Tertullian begins the chapter by summarizing this view: "And so after a time the Father was born, and the Father suffered."

2. The Introduction of Key Latin Vocabulary:
This work is famous for being one of the first, if not the very first, to use specific Latin terms to articulate the doctrine of the Trinity:

    Trinitas (Trinity): Tertullian is one of the earliest Latin writers to use this term to describe the Godhead.

    Substantia (Substance): He uses this term to refer to the single, shared "divine stuff" or "being" of God. There is una substantia (one substance).

    Persona (Person): While not in this specific quote, he uses it throughout the work to refer to the distinct Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For Tertullian, a Roman lawyer, persona did not mean a self-conscious individual (our modern meaning) but rather a "face," "mask," or a party in a legal case—a distinct entity with a specific role.

3. The Oeconomia (Dispensation or Divine Plan):
Tertullian borrows the Greek word oikonomia (economy) to explain how the one God can exist as three. The oikonomia is God's divine plan or internal arrangement for His own being, by which the "unity is distributed into a Trinity." This concept allows for distinction within God without dividing His substance.

4. The Famous List of Distinctions:
The final sentence of your quote is a masterful piece of theological precision, defining how the Three are distinct:

    "Not in condition, but in degree" (non statu, sed gradu): They are not different in their fundamental state or status of being God, but there is an order or rank (degree) of procession: the Father is the source, from whom the Son proceeds, etc.

    "Not in substance, but in form" (nec substantia, sed forma): This is the core of his argument. They do not have different substances; they are distinct in their presentation or "form."

    "Not in power, but in aspect" (nec potestate, sed specie): There is only one divine power, but it is manifested in three distinct "aspects" or appearances.

You have identified one of the most foundational texts in the history of Western theology, where the language to speak of "one God in three Persons" was first forged.

en: And at the same time the mystery of the divine economy IS safeguarded, for the unity is distributed in a Trinity. Placed in order. the three are the Father, Son, and Spirit. They are three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in being, but in form; not in power, but in kind: of one being, however, and one condition and one power, because he is one God of whom degrees and forms and kinds are taken into account in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [ibid.].
latin: ...et nihilominus custodiatur oeconomiae sacramentum, quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum. Tres autem non statu, sed gradu; nec substantia, sed forma; nec potestate, sed specie: unius autem substantiae, et unius status, et unius potestatis; quia unus Deus, ex quo et gradus isti et formae et species, in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti deputantur.

Additional Relevant Details & Context

This passage is monumentally important for several reasons. It is one of the earliest instances of a Latin theologian systematically articulating what would become the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, and in doing so, Tertullian coins or popularizes the essential vocabulary for it.

1. The Author and Work:

    Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 A.D.) is known as the "father of Latin Christianity." He was a brilliant and fiery writer who was the first to produce a large body of Christian literature in Latin.

    Adversus Praxean was written to refute the teachings of a man named Praxeas.

2. The Heresy Being Refuted (Modalistic Monarchianism):

    Praxeas taught a heresy that tried to fiercely protect God's oneness (monarchianism). He argued that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but simply different modes or "masks" that the one God wears when acting in different ways.

    This led to a conclusion known as Patripassianism (from the Latin Pater for "Father" and passus for "suffered"). If the Son who suffered on the cross is just a "mode" of the Father, then it was God the Father who suffered and died. Tertullian found this absurd and blasphemous.

3. Tertullian's Theological Breakthroughs in This Quote:
Tertullian's genius was to develop a vocabulary that could affirm both God's unity and the real distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

    Oeconomia (Economy): Tertullian borrows this Greek term (which he translates as dispensatio) to refer to the internal "arrangement" or "ordering" of the Godhead. He argues that God is one in His being, but within that unity, there is an internal divine economy of three.

    Trinitas (Trinity): This is one of the first, if not the very first, appearances of the Latin word Trinitas in Christian writing. Tertullian effectively coins the term that would define the doctrine for all subsequent history.

    Una Substantia (One Substance): This is the philosophical bedrock of his argument. He states that the Father, Son, and Spirit are "of one substance" (unius substantiae). This means they share the single, undivided divine being. This is the Latin precursor to the crucial Greek term homoousios ("of the same being") used in the Nicene Creed over a century later.

    Three Persons (Expressed with Early Terminology): To describe the "threeness," Tertullian is still experimenting with language. In this passage, he uses:

        gradus (degree, rank, step)

        forma (form, shape)

        species (kind, appearance)
        He says the three are distinct in these aspects, but they are united in status (condition, state) and potestas (power). Later in the work, he would famously settle on the formula of one substance, three persons (personae), but this quote shows the theological workshop in action.

In summary, this single passage is a landmark moment. Tertullian provides the foundational language and conceptual framework for Western Trinitarian theology, brilliantly defending the mystery of the one God in three distinct persons against a heresy that tried to dissolve those distinctions.

en: I believe the Spirit to proceed from no other source than from the Father through the Son [ Against Praxeas 4 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: ...quia Spiritum non aliunde puto, quam a Patre per Filium.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Source and Context

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD)

    Work: Adversus Praxean (Against Praxeas)

    Chapter: 4

    Approximate Date: c. 213 AD

    Immediate Context: The entire work is a defense of the doctrine of the Trinity against the heresy of Monarchianism (also known as Modalism or Patripassianism). Praxeas taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or manifestations of the one God, not distinct Persons. This led to the conclusion that the Father himself must have suffered on the cross (hence "Patripassianism").

In the passage you provided, Tertullian is arguing that the orthodox belief in the Trinity does not destroy the "Monarchy" (the one rule of the one God), as Praxeas claimed.

    He first explains that the Son is not a rival to the Father, because He is "from the substance of the Father" and does nothing without the Father's will.

    He then applies this same principle to the Holy Spirit, whom he calls the "third grade." The Spirit's origin maintains the Monarchy because He comes from a single ultimate source—the Father—but in an ordered way—through the Son.

    Tertullian then brilliantly turns the accusation back on Praxeas, saying that it is Praxeas who destroys the divine order by collapsing the distinct Persons into one.

2. Theological Significance

This quote is one of the most significant early Latin statements on the procession of the Holy Spirit and has been foundational for Western Trinitarian theology.

    Pioneering Language: This work, Against Praxeas, is famous for being one of the first, if not the first, to use the Latin words Trinitas (Trinity), persona (Person), and substantia (substance) in the specific theological sense that would become standard in the West.

    Foundation of the Filioque: The formula a Patre per Filium ("from the Father through the Son") is a direct and crucial precursor to the later Western doctrine of the Filioque ("and the Son"). While not identical to the later formulation, Tertullian's text clearly establishes an active role for the Son in the Spirit's coming-forth from the Father. This concept would be developed by later Latin Fathers like Hilary of Poitiers, Ambrose, and Augustine, eventually leading to the inclusion of the Filioque clause in the Nicene Creed in the West. This clause remains a major point of theological difference between the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches.

You have identified a landmark passage that stands at the very beginning of Latin Trinitarian theology.

en: Thus does he make him equal to him: for by proceeding from himself he became his first-begotten Son. begotten before all things [Col 1:15 ; and his only-begotten also, because he alone is begotten of God, in a way peculiar to himself, from the womb of his own heart- even as the Father himself testifies: "My heart," says he, "has issued my most excellent Word" [Against Praxeas 7 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: Exinde eum parem sibi faciens, de quo procedendo Filius factus est, primogenitus, ut ante omnia genitus; et unigenitus, ut solus ex Deo genitus, proprie de vulva cordis ipsius, secundum quod et Pater ipse testatur: Eructavit cor meum sermonem optimum.

Additional Relevant Details

This passage is incredibly rich with theological significance. Here’s a breakdown of the context and importance:

1. The Overall Context: Arguing Against Modalism

    Tertullian is writing against a heretic named Praxeas.

    Praxeas taught a doctrine known as Modalism or Patripassianism. This heresy claimed that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct Persons, but simply different "modes" or "masks" of the one God.

    The logical conclusion of this view was that the Father himself (the Pater) must have suffered (passus) on the cross—hence, "Patripassianism."

    Tertullian's goal in this entire book is to prove that the Son is a distinct Person from the Father, yet without dividing the single divine substance.

2. The Argument in This Specific Passage

Tertullian is explaining how the Word (the Son) can be distinct from the Father without being separate or created out of nothing.

    Exinde eum parem sibi faciens ("Thus does he make him equal to him"): The generation of the Son establishes his equality with the Father. He is not a lesser, secondary being.

    de quo procedendo Filius factus est ("by proceeding from himself he became his Son"): This is the core of the argument. The Son is not "made" in the sense of a creature. He is "made Son" by an eternal procession from the Father's own being. This establishes both their relationship and their distinction.

    primogenitus... unigenitus ("first-begotten... only-begotten"): Tertullian grounds his argument in scriptural titles for Christ (Colossians 1:15, John 1:18, etc.) to show this is not his own invention but the teaching of the apostles.

    proprie de vulva cordis ipsius ("properly from the womb of his own heart"): This is a powerful, anthropomorphic metaphor. It emphasizes that the Son's generation is not a cold, intellectual act but an intimate, substantial procession from the very core of the Father's being. It is a true Sonship, not an adopted or figurative one.

    Eructavit cor meum sermonem optimum ("My heart has issued my most excellent Word"): This is Tertullian's key scriptural proof-text, a quotation from Psalm 45:1 (Psalm 44:1 in the Vulgate). The Latin verb eructavit is very strong, meaning "to belch forth" or "gush out." For Tertullian, this verse is the Father Himself testifying that the Word (Sermo, the Son) comes forth from His own substance, like a word from the heart.

3. Tertullian's Lasting Contribution

This chapter is a prime example of Tertullian's pioneering work in Latin theology. He was one of the first to use the terms that would become standard in the West:

    Substantia (Substance) to describe the one divine "stuff" of the Godhead.

    Persona (Person) to describe the distinct realities of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

This passage is a brilliant articulation of his famous formula: "una substantia, tres personae" (one substance, three persons).

en: Bear always in mind that this is the rule of faith I profess; by it I testify that the Father, and the Son, and the Spirit are inseparable from each other, SO you will know in what sense this IS said. My assertion is that the Father IS one, and the Son one, and the Spirit one, and that they are distinct from each other. This statement is taken in a wrong sense by every uneducated and perversely disposed person, as if it meant a diversity, or implied a separation among the Father, and the Son, and the Spirit [ibid., 9].
latin:
Hanc me regulam professum, qua inseparatos ab alterutro Patrem et Filium et Spiritum testor, tene ubique; et ita, quid quomodo dicatur, agnosces.

    Ecce enim dico alium esse Patrem, et alium Filium, et alium Spiritum. Male accipit idiotes quisque aut perversus hoc dictum, quasi diversitatem sonet, et ex diversitate separationem protendat, Patris et Filii et Spiritus.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Author and Work

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 A.D.), one of the most brilliant and influential early Latin Christian writers. He is often called the "father of Latin theology."

    Work: Adversus Praxean (Against Praxeas). This is one of the most important early works on the doctrine of the Trinity.

2. The Heresy Being Refuted: Modalism

    The opponent, Praxeas, was a proponent of a heresy known as Modalism or Patripassianism.

    Modalists taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but simply different "modes" or manifestations of the one God.

    This led to the conclusion that the Father himself was born of the Virgin and suffered on the cross (hence the name Patripassianism—from Latin Pater for "Father" and passus for "suffered"). They insisted on God's "Monarchy" (sole rule) to the point of erasing the distinct persons of the Trinity.

3. Tertullian's Groundbreaking Theological Language

The rest of the chapter you provided is where Tertullian explains his precise meaning, coining terms that would become foundational for all of Western theology:

    Distinction, not Division: Tertullian clarifies that when he says "another" (alius), he means a distinction (distinctio) of persons, not a division (divisio) or separation (separatio) of substance. The Godhead is one, but the persons within it are distinct.

    Economy (Oikonomia): Tertullian champions the concept of the Divine "Economy," which refers to the internal order and arrangement within the single Godhead. He argues that the Modalists, by denying this internal order, are the true "destroyers of the Monarchy."

    One Substance, Three Persons: While he doesn't use the exact phrase in this specific chapter, this work is where Tertullian develops the formula that would define the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity for centuries: "one substance, three persons" (una substantia, tres personae). He is also the first known writer to use the Latin word Trinitas (Trinity).

Your quote is the perfect setup for Tertullian's masterful argument. He states his position, acknowledges how it can be misunderstood, and then spends the rest of the chapter defining his terms with a precision that was unprecedented in Latin theology.

en: That there are two Gods and two Lords is something we will never say; it is not as if the Father and the Son were not God, nor the Spirit God, and each of them God; but formerly two were spoken of as Gods and two as Lords, so that when Christ would come, he might be acknowledged as God and be called Lord, because he is the Son of him who is both God and Lord [Against Praxeas 13 (c. A.D. 218)].
latin: Duos tamen Deos et duos Dominos nunquam ex ore nostro proferimus: non quasi non et Pater Deus, et Filius Deus, et Spiritus sanctus Deus, et Deus unusquisque; sed quoniam retro et duo dii et duo domini praedicabantur; ut, ubi venisset Christus, et Deus agnosceretur, et Dominus vocaretur, quia Filius Dei et Domini.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Opponent: Praxeas and Modalism (or Patripassianism)

To understand this quote, you must understand who Tertullian is fighting. Praxeas was a proponent of a heresy known as Modalism.

    Modalism taught that God is only one Person who reveals himself in three different "modes" or roles: as Father in creation, as Son in redemption, and as Holy Spirit in sanctification.

    The logical consequence of this, which Tertullian relentlessly pointed out, was Patripassianism—the belief that God the Father himself was born of Mary, suffered on the cross, and died. Tertullian famously quipped that Praxeas had "put the Paraclete to flight and crucified the Father."

    Praxeas and his followers claimed to be the true defenders of the "Monarchy" (the sole rule of God), accusing Tertullian and the orthodox of being polytheists for believing in a distinction between Father and Son.

2. Tertullian's Solution: The "Economy" (Oeconomia)

Tertullian's groundbreaking solution was to introduce the concept of the "Economy" (oeconomia), a Latin term derived from the Greek for "household management" or "dispensation." He uses it to describe God's plan for how the internal, eternal relationships of the Trinity are ordered and revealed in salvation history.

In the text you provided, he states this explicitly just before your quote:

    ...duos quidem definimus, Patrem et Filium, et jam tres cum Spiritu sancto, secundum rationem oeconomiae, quae facit numerum...
    "...we define two, the Father and the Son, and now three with the Holy Spirit, according to the principle of the economy, which makes a number..."

This is a revolutionary idea: the "number" of Persons (three) does not destroy the unity of the divine substance. It is simply the revealed order of God's own being and action.
3. The Apologetic and Pastoral Reason

Your quote reveals the pastoral reason why Christians must not go around saying "two Gods."

    The Problem: The Roman world was polytheistic. For Christians to proclaim "two Gods" would be confusing and scandalous. It would make them seem like they were just adding to the pagan pantheon.

    The Old Testament's Role: Tertullian's brilliant insight is that the Old Testament intentionally hinted at a plurality ("The LORD rained fire... from the LORD") in order to prepare the way for the revelation of the Son. It created a theological space for a second divine person to be revealed without shattering monotheism.

    The New Covenant's Clarity: Now that Christ has come, the relationship is clear. The "name of God and Lord" is brought back into "union." We worship one God and one Lord, but we understand this one Godhead subsists as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

In essence, Tertullian is arguing that while we confess that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Spirit is God, we must never speak in a way that implies we believe in three separate deities. Our language must safeguard both the distinction of the Persons (against Praxeas) and the unity of the one God (against polytheism).

en: Thus the connection of the Father in the Son, and of the Son in the Paraclete, produces three coherent persons, who are yet distinct one from another. These three are one essence, not one person, as it is said, "I and my Father are one" [Jn 10:30], in respect of unity of being, not singularity of number [ibid., 25].
latin: Ita connexus Patris in Filio, et Filii in Paracleto, tres efficit cohaerentes, alterum ex altero. Qui tres unum sint, non unus; quomodo dictum est, 'Ego et Pater unum sumus,' ad substantiae unitatem, non ad numeri singularitatem.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Work and Author

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), a prolific and brilliant early Christian author from North Africa who wrote in Latin.

    Work: Adversus Praxean (Against Praxeas), written around A.D. 213.

    Citation: The passage is from Chapter 25 of this work. The reference numbers 0187D and 0188A in your text correspond to the columns in Volume 2 of Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 2).

2. Historical Context: The Heresy of Praxeas

This work is a direct refutation of a heretical teacher named Praxeas. His teaching is known by several names:

    Monarchianism: It over-emphasized the "monarchy" (sole rule) of the one God to the point of denying the real distinction between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

    Modalism: It taught that the Father, Son, and Spirit were merely different "modes" or "masks" that the one God wears when interacting with creation.

    Patripassianism: The logical conclusion of this heresy was that the Father (Pater) must have suffered (passus est) on the cross, since he was the same person as the Son. Tertullian famously quipped that Praxeas "put the Paraclete to flight and crucified the Father."

3. Theological Significance of this Quote

This specific passage is one of the most important in the history of Western theology because it is where Tertullian introduces the linguistic tools that would define the Trinity for centuries.

    The Formula of the Trinity: This is the birthplace of the classic Latin Trinitarian formula: "one substance, three persons" (una substantia, tres personae). While he doesn't state it in exactly those four words here, the entire passage is built on this concept.

    The Genius of Unum vs. Unus: Tertullian’s legalistic mind makes a brilliant theological point through grammar. When he says the three are unum, he uses the neuter form, meaning "one thing" or "one essence." When he says they are non unus, he uses the masculine form, meaning "not one person." This grammatical precision allowed him to affirm both the unity of the divine substance and the distinction of the persons.

    Substantia and Persona: Tertullian was the first to use the Latin words substantia (substance, being) and persona (person, an individual with a distinct identity) in this technical, theological way. He adapted these terms from Roman law and philosophy to explain the Christian faith.

    Coherent and Connected (cohaerentes): His choice of "coherent" is perfect. It conveys that the three persons are not separate or isolated but are eternally connected and exist in inseparable communion with one another ("one from the other").

In short, you have located the very passage where the foundational language of Latin Trinitarian theology was forged. It is a direct response to a heresy that was confusing the identity of the Father and the Son.

en: After his Resurrection he promises in a pledge to his disciples that he will send them the promise of his Father [Lk 24:49]; and lastly, he commands them to baptize into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, not into a uni-personal God. And indeed it is not once but three times that we are immersed into the three Persons, at each mention of their names [Against Praxeas 26 (C. A.D. 218)].
latin: ...et post resurrectionem spondens missurum se discipulis promissionem Patris; et novissime mandans ut tinguerent in Patrem et Filium et Spiritum Sanctum, non in unum. Nam nec semel, sed ter, ad singula nomina in personas singulas tinguimur.
context:
Additional Details and Context
1. Author, Work, and Opponent

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), one of the most brilliant and foundational theologians of the Latin-speaking Western Church.

    Work: Adversus Praxean (Against Praxeas), written around 213 AD. This is arguably the most important early Latin work on the doctrine of the Trinity.

    Opponent: Praxeas was a heretic who promoted a doctrine known as Modalism or Patripassianism. He taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct Persons but simply different "modes" or manifestations of the one God. This led to the conclusion that it was God the Father who was born of the virgin and who suffered and died on the cross (hence, Patri-passianism, "the Father suffers").

2. Historical and Theological Significance

    Coining the Language of the Trinity: This work is famous because in it, Tertullian forged the Latin vocabulary that the Western Church would use to define the Trinity for centuries. He was the first known writer to use the Latin word Trinitas (Trinity) and to describe God as being of una substantia (one substance) in tres personae (three persons). This formula became the bedrock of Western Trinitarian orthodoxy.

    The Power of Liturgical Proof: In this specific quote, Tertullian’s argument is brilliant because he moves from scriptural exegesis to the lived, sacramental practice of the Church. He is saying, "Look at what we actually do." The very act of baptism, commanded by Christ Himself, refutes Praxeas.

3. Immediate Context in Chapter 26

The quote is the grand finale of the entire chapter. Before this concluding sentence, Tertullian has been building an overwhelming case from the Gospels to prove the distinction of the Persons. He lists:

    The Annunciation (Luke 1:35)

    Jesus as a boy saying he must be "in my Father's house" (Luke 2:49)

    The temptations ("If you are the Son of God...")

    Demons confessing Him as the "Son of God"

    Peter's confession of Christ as the Son of God

    Jesus praying and giving thanks to the Father

    Jesus stating that only the Father knows the final day and hour

After this long list, the command to baptize is the final, unanswerable proof.
4. Analysis of the Quote's Key Phrases

    ...non in unum ("...not into a uni-personal God" / "not into one"): This is a direct, surgical strike against Praxeas's core teaching. The command is not to baptize into a single entity, but into three distinct names.

    ...nec semel, sed ter... tinguimur ("...not once, but three times... we are immersed"): Tertullian points to the common liturgical practice of triple immersion. This physical act was a powerful catechetical tool. The convert was plunged into the water three separate times, once at the mention of each name, physically reinforcing the reality of the three distinct divine Persons. The very structure of the sacrament proclaimed the Trinity.

en: [L]et him who contends that the Sabbath is still to be observed as balm of salvation, and circumcision on the eighth day teach us that, for the time past, righteous men kept the Sabbath or practiced circumcision, and were thus rendered "friends of God." For if circumcision purges a man. since God made Adam uncircumcised, why did he not circumcise him, even after his sinning, if circumcision purges? Therefore, since God originated Adam uncircumcised and unobservant of the Sabbath, consequently his offspring, Abel, offering him sacrifices, uncircumcised and unobservant of the Sabbath, was by him [God] commended [Gn 4:1-7; Heb 11:4]. Noah also, uncircumcisedyes, and unobservant of the Sabbath- God freed from the deluge. For Enoch too, most righteous man, uncircumcised and unobservant of the Sabbath, he translated from this world, who did not first taste death in order that, being a candidate for eternal life, he might show us that we also may, without the burden of the Law of Moses, please God [ Answer to the Jews (c. A.D. 203)].
latin:
Denique, qui contendit et sabbatum adhuc observandum quasi salutis medelam, et circumcisionem octavi diei propter mortis comminationem, doceat in praeteritum justos sabbatizasse aut circumcidisse, et sic amicos Dei effectos.

    Nam, si circumcisio purgat hominem, Deus Adam incircumcisum cum faceret, cur eum non circumcidit, vel posteaquam deliquit, si purgat circumcisio? ... Igitur, cum neque circumcisum neque sabbatizantem Deus Adam instituerit, consequenter quoque sobolem ejus Abel offerentem sibi sacrificia, incircumcisum nec sabbatizantem laudavit...

    Noe quoque incircumcisum Deus, sed et non sabbatizantem, de diluvio liberavit. Nam et Enoch justissimum non circumcisum, nec sabbatizantem, de hoc mundo transtulit; qui necdum mortem gustavit, ut aeternitatis candidatus, jam nobis ostenderet nos quoque sine legis onere Moysi, Deo posse placere.

Additional Relevant Details

    Author and Work: Tertullian (c. 160 – c. 220 AD) was a brilliant and prolific early Christian author from Carthage. Adversus Judaeos (An Answer to the Jews) is a classic work of early Christian apologetics. Its primary goal is to demonstrate that Jesus is the promised Messiah and that the New Covenant in Christ has superseded the Old Covenant of the Mosaic Law.

    The Core Argument (Supersessionism): The passage you selected is a perfect example of Tertullian's central argument. He contends that the Mosaic Law, with its specific requirements like the Sabbath and circumcision, was a temporary and preparatory law given to one people for a specific time. It was not the original, universal, or eternal law of God.

    Tertullian's Method (The Appeal to Precedent): His legalistic and rhetorical genius is on full display here. To prove that the Mosaic Law is not essential for salvation, he cites revered figures from Genesis who were declared righteous by God before the Law was given to Moses.

        Adam: The original man, created in God's favor without circumcision or Sabbath.

        Abel: His sacrifice was accepted by God without these rituals.

        Noah: Found righteous and saved from the flood without the Law.

        Enoch: Deemed so righteous that he was taken to God without dying, all while being "uncircumcised and unobservant of the Sabbath."

        Enoch becomes the ultimate proof-text: his example shows that it is possible to "please God without the burden of the Law of Moses."

    Historical Context: This argument was vital for the early Church as it sought to define its own identity apart from Judaism while still claiming the Hebrew Scriptures as its own holy book. Tertullian's work powerfully articulated the Christian position that the Church was the true inheritor of the promises made to the patriarchs, and that faith in God, not adherence to the specifics of the Mosaic Law, had always been the path to righteousness.

en: We have faith for a defense, if we are not smitten with distrust, in immediately making the sign [of the cross] and commanding and smearing the heel with the beast. Finally, we often aid even the heathen in this way, who see that we have been endowed by God with that power that the apostle [Paul] first used when he despised the viper's bite [Acts 28:3] [Antidote for the Scorpion's Sting (C. A.D 211)].
latin: Nobis fides praesidium, si non et ipsa percutitur diffidentia signandi statim et adjurandi, et urgendi bestiae calcem: hoc denique modo etiam ethnicis saepe subvenimus; donati a Deo ea potestate, quam Apostolus dedicavit (Act., XXVIII), cum morsum viperae sprevit.

Additional Details & Context

This passage is even more profound when understood within the full context of the chapter you provided.

1. The Title and Central Metaphor:

    The work's title is Scorpiace, which is a Latinized Greek word for an "antidote for a scorpion's sting" (theriacam).

    Tertullian is not primarily writing about literal scorpions. The entire work is an allegory. As he explicitly states later in the chapter: "This, among Christians, is persecution" (Hoc apud Christianos persecutio est).

    The "scorpions" are the Gnostic heretics (he names the Gnostics and Valentinians) who appear during times of fiery persecution (Cum igitur fides aestuat, et Ecclesia exuritur). Their "sting" is the poisonous teaching that Christians should find clever ways to avoid martyrdom, rather than confessing Christ and dying for the faith.

2. The Structure of the Argument:

    Tertullian begins with a literal example to make a spiritual point. He says that Christians have real, tangible power over physical evil, like the sting of a scorpion.

    He lists the "remedies": Faith (fides praesidium), the Sign of the Cross (signandi statim), a verbal command or exorcism (adjurandi), and a physical act against the beast (urgendi bestiae calcem - "pressing/smearing the heel of the beast").

    This power is so real that Christians even use it to heal pagans (etiam ethnicis saepe subvenimus), proving it's a divine gift, first demonstrated by St. Paul with the viper on Malta.

3. The Pivot to the Real Topic:

    After establishing this point, he immediately pivots to the book's true purpose: "What then does this treatise promise, if faith is secure on its own? That it may also be secure on its own, when it suffers from its own scorpions (cum suos scorpios patitur)."

    The rest of the chapter describes how these heretics "sting" the simple and weak-minded with arguments like, "Why should innocent people suffer?" and "Why die for no reason?" Their venomous teaching leads the Christian's faith to "expire either into heresy or into the world" (vel in haeresim, vel in saeculum exspirat).

4. The Citation:

    The marginal notes in your text (0121B, 0122A) are column markers from Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL).

    The full citation for this passage is: Tertullian, Scorpiace, 1 (PL 2:121B-122A).

In summary, you have located a passage where Tertullian uses the very real and acknowledged spiritual power of Christians over physical evil as a launching point to address the more dangerous, internal threat of heretical teachings that sought to undermine the glory of martyrdom.

en: For though you think that heaven is still shut up, remember that the Lord left the keys of it to Peter here, and through him to the Church, which keys everyone will carry with him if he has been questioned and made a confession [of faith] [ Antidote for the Scorpion's Sting 10 (c. A.D. 211)].
latin: Nam et si adhuc clausum putas coelum, memento claves ejus hic Dominum Petro, et per eum, Ecclesiae reliquisse, quas hic unusquisque interrogatus atque confessus feret secum.
context:
Additional Details and Context

This quote is the knockout punch in a brilliant and often sarcastic argument Tertullian is making against a specific Gnostic heresy. To understand its full force, you need to know what he was refuting.

    The Opponent's Argument (The "Scorpion's Sting"):
    Certain Gnostics (specifically the Valentinians, whom he names) were teaching that Christians could deny Christ on Earth to avoid martyrdom. Their rationale was that the true and important confession of faith happens after death, in the heavenly realms. They imagined the soul ascending through different celestial levels, being interrogated by spiritual powers (aeons), and only then making its ultimate confession. Earthly persecution, they argued, was an inferior test that the spiritually elite could bypass.

    Tertullian's Refutation (The "Antidote"):
    The entire chapter you provided is Tertullian's systematic demolition of this idea.

        He starts by mocking the idea of a heavenly courtroom with Gnostic aeons as judges.

        He uses a reductio ad absurdum: If confession happens in heaven, then persecution must also happen in heaven. He sarcastically imagines heavenly prisons, heavenly executioners (the constellation Orion), and heavenly wild beasts (the constellations of the Bear, the Bull, and the Lion).

        He then points out the fatal flaw: All of these things—persecution, torture, death—require a body (ubi caro? ... ubi corpus?). Since the body is on Earth, the entire drama of persecution and confession must also take place on Earth.

    The Power of Your Quote:
    Your quote is Tertullian's grand finale to this argument. He says, in essence:
    "Stop talking about a heavenly ordeal. The entire mechanism for entering heaven was established 'hic' (here) on Earth. The Lord did not leave the keys up there for you to find after you die. He left them here with Peter, and through Peter, with the Church. The 'key' itself is the good confession made on Earth during interrogation. That earthly confession is the very thing you carry with you to unlock the gates of heaven. It is not a test you take after you arrive; it is the passport that grants you entry."

The emphasis on "hic" (here) is the central point of the entire chapter, grounding the means of salvation firmly in the earthly life of the visible Church, against the Gnostics' ethereal and esoteric fantasies.

en: In our case, murder being forbidden, we may not destroy even the fetus in the womb, while the human being derives blood from other parts of the body for its sustenance. To hinder a birth is merely a speedier mankilling; nor does it matter whether you take away life that is born, or destroy one that is coming to the birth. That is a man that is going to be one; you have the fruit already in its seed [Apology 9 (A.D. 197)].
latin: Nobis vero, homicidio semel interdicto, etiam conceptum utero, dum adhuc sanguis in hominem delibatur, dissolvere non licet. Homicidii festinatio est prohibere nasci; nec refert natam quis eripiat animam, an nascentem disturbet: homo est, et qui est futurus; etiam fructus omnis jam in semine est.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. The Immediate Context: A Powerful "Tu Quoque" Argument

The entire chapter you provided is a brilliant piece of rhetoric. Tertullian is defending Christians against the horrific pagan accusations of ritual murder, infanticide, and cannibalism. His strategy is to turn the tables on his accusers in a classic "you do it too!" (tu quoque) argument.

    Pagan Guilt: Before getting to the quote, he lists the ways Romans are guilty of the very things they accuse Christians of:

        Child Sacrifice: He reminds them of the (formerly public, now secret) sacrifices of infants to the god Saturn in their own province of Africa.

        Human Sacrifice: He points to sacrifices to Mercury among the Gauls and bloody rituals to Jupiter in Rome itself.

        Gladiatorial Games: He condemns the gladiatorial games where men are killed for entertainment and notes the gruesome practice of epileptics drinking the blood of the slain as a "cure."

        Infant Exposure: He directly confronts the common Roman practice of abandoning unwanted newborn children to die from cold, starvation, or animal attacks (frigori et fami et canibus exponitis).

2. The Quote's Function: The Ultimate Contrast

It is only after establishing this widespread pagan disregard for human life that Tertullian introduces the Christian position as a stark and absolute contrast. His point is devastatingly effective: "How can you, who are the real child-killers, accuse us? We are so far from killing children for rituals that our principles forbid us from harming them even at the earliest stage in the womb."

The quote functions as the moral climax of his defense against infanticide.
3. Key Theological and Philosophical Principles

This short passage is packed with foundational ideas:

    Continuity of Life: The core of Tertullian's argument is that there is no essential moral difference between a life already born (natam animam) and a life that is coming to birth (nascentem). The act of killing is the same, only the timing is different ("a speedier man-killing").

    Personhood in Potentiality: The phrase homo est, et qui est futurus ("That is a man who is also going to be one") is a profound philosophical statement. Tertullian defines the unborn not just by what it is at that moment, but by what it is destined to become. Its identity as a human being is present from the beginning.

    The "Fruit in the Seed" Analogy: The final line, etiam fructus omnis jam in semine est ("you have the fruit already in its seed"), is a powerful and universally understood metaphor. Just as an entire oak tree is contained in potential within an acorn, the entire human person is present in potential within the embryo. To destroy the seed is to destroy the fruit.

This passage is therefore not just a piece of apologetics but a cornerstone of the Christian tradition's teaching on the sanctity of human life from conception.

en: The object of our worship is the one God, who, by the word of his command, by the reason of his plan, and by the strength of his power has brought forth from nothing this whole construction of elements, bodies, and spirits for the glory of his majesty; which is why the Greeks have bestowed upon the world the name "cosmos" [Apology 17 (A.D. 197)].
latin: Quod colimus, Deus unus est; qui totam molem istam cum omni instrumento elementorum, corporum, spirituum, verbo, quo jussit, ratione, qua disposuit, virtute, qua potuit, de nihilo expressit, in ornamentum majestatis suae: unde et Graeci nomen mundo κόσμον accommodaverunt.
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Linguistic and Theological Analysis

Tertullian was a master rhetorician, and every word in this sentence is carefully chosen for maximum impact on his educated pagan readers.

    Verbo, Ratione, Virtute (Word, Reason, Power): This triad is a brilliant piece of apologetics. It uses language familiar to Stoic and Platonic philosophy while giving it a thoroughly Christian meaning.

        Verbo quo jussit (by the Word by which He commanded): This directly echoes the Genesis creation account ("And God said...") and also points towards the Christian doctrine of the Logos (the Word, as in John 1:1-3), the Son through whom all things were made.

        Ratione qua disposuit (by the Reason by which He planned): This appeals to the philosophical idea of a rational, ordered universe. The world is not chaotic but is the product of a divine mind and plan (Ratio / Λόγος).

        Virtute qua potuit (by the Power by which He was able): This emphasizes God's omnipotence. His plan wasn't just a concept; He had the sovereign power (Virtus) to bring it into being.

    De nihilo expressit (He brought forth from nothing): This is one of the clearest early Latin formulations of the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo (creation out of nothing). This was a radical idea that directly contradicted the prevailing Greek philosophical view, in which a "demiurge" or craftsman god fashioned the world out of pre-existing, eternal matter. Tertullian asserts that the Christian God's power is absolute; He needed no pre-existing material to create.

    κόσμον (kosmon): Tertullian makes a clever etymological argument. The Greek word κόσμος (cosmos) means both "world/universe" and "order/adornment." He points out that the very name the Greeks gave to the world implicitly acknowledges that it is an orderly and beautiful thing (ornamentum). His argument is that this inherent order points to the rational and powerful Creator God he has just described.

2. Context of the Full Chapter

The rest of the chapter you provided contains another of Tertullian's most famous arguments: the testimonium animae naturaliter Christianae ("the testimony of a soul that is naturally Christian").

After establishing God as the Creator of the visible world (cosmos), Tertullian pivots to an even more profound witness: the innate knowledge of God within the human soul. He argues that even pagans, in spontaneous, unguarded moments (of fear, joy, or distress), cry out phrases that acknowledge the one, true God:

    "DEUS MAGNUS" (God is great!)

    "DEUS VIDET" (God sees!)

    "DEO COMMENDO" (I commend it to God!)

He concludes that the human soul, when it is being its most natural and true self ("when it recovers its senses, as from a hangover, or a sleep"), instinctively knows and calls upon the one God of the Christians. It is a powerful argument for a natural, universal knowledge of God imprinted on every human being.

en: [T]hese have further set before us the proof he has given of his majesty in his judgments by floods and fires, the rules appointed by him for securing his favor, as well as the retribution in store for ignoring, forsaking, and keeping them, as being there at the end of all to judge his worshippers to everlasting life, and the wicked to the doom of fire without end and without break [ Apology 18 (A.D. 197)].
latin: ...exinde qui signa majestatis suae judicantis ediderit per imbres, per ignes; qui demerendo sibi disciplinas determinaverit, quas ignoratis aut deseritis; sed et observantibus praemia destinarit, ut qui prodacto aevo isto judicaturus sit suos cultores in vitae aeternae retributionem, profanos in ignem aeque perpetem et jugem...
context:
Additional Relevant Details
1. Immediate Context: The Authority of Scripture

The quote is part of a larger argument where Tertullian establishes the credibility of Christian belief. He has just stated that God, to make His will fully known, provided an "instrument of literature" (instrumentum litteraturae)—the Holy Scriptures. He argues that God sent divinely inspired prophets from the beginning of the world to reveal His nature and plan. The passage you quoted is a powerful summary of what these prophets preached:

    There is one God, the Creator.

    He has demonstrated His sovereign judgment throughout history (per imbres, per ignes - a clear reference to Noah's Flood and the destruction of Sodom).

    He has established a moral code (disciplinas).

    There will be a final judgment with eternal consequences for both the righteous and the wicked.

2. Key Vocabulary and Phrases

Tertullian's Latin is famously dense, legalistic, and powerful.

    Instrumentum litteraturae: This is a legal term. An instrumentum is a legal document, a deed, or a formal record. Tertullian is presenting the Bible not as a collection of myths, but as God's official, documented revelation.

    Per imbres, per ignes: "By floods, by fires." This phrase is intentionally evocative, immediately bringing to the mind of any reader familiar with the Hebrew Scriptures the great acts of divine judgment.

    Ignem aeque perpetem et jugem: "Fire equally perpetual and continuous." This is classic Tertullian—using two powerful, nearly synonymous adjectives to intensify the meaning.

        Perpetem means perpetual, lasting forever.

        Jugem (from jugum, a yoke) means yoked, joined, and therefore constant, uninterrupted, or without a break.
        He is stressing not just the duration but the unceasing nature of the punishment for the wicked.

3. A Famous Quote Hidden in Plain Sight!

The larger Latin text you provided contains one of the most famous sentences ever written by Tertullian, right after your specific quote. It is a profound statement on the nature of Christian identity:

    Fiunt, non nascuntur Christiani.

Translation: "Christians are made, not born."

This is a revolutionary concept in the ancient world, where religion was almost always tied to ethnicity or family heritage (you were born Roman, or Jewish, or Egyptian). Tertullian argues that becoming a Christian is a conscious act of conversion and transformation, not a matter of birthright. This single sentence encapsulates the universal, voluntary, and personal nature of the Christian faith.

en: As being there at the end of all to judge his worshippers to everlasting life, and the wicked to the doom of fire without end and without break, raising up again all the dead from the beginning, reforming and renewing them with the object of awarding either recompense [ Apology 18 (A.D. 197)].
latin: ...ut qui prodacto aevo isto judicaturus sit suos cultores in vitae aeternae retributionem, profanos in ignem aeque perpetem et jugem, suscitatis omnibus ab initio defunctis, et reformatis et recensitis, ad utriusque meriti dispunctionem.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

1. Author, Work, and Date:

    Author: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 A.D.), a brilliant and fiery Christian writer from North Africa, often called the "father of Latin Christianity" for his role in shaping theological vocabulary in the West.

    Work: Apologeticum (The Apology). This is his most famous work, a passionate and legally-styled defense of Christianity addressed to the Roman governors.

    Date: Written around A.D. 197. This makes it one of the earliest and most comprehensive Latin apologies for the faith.

2. Immediate Context of the Passage:
In this chapter, Tertullian is explaining to his pagan Roman audience the source and content of Christian belief. He has just stated that God, to make Himself known, provided humanity with "an instrument of literature"—the Holy Scriptures. The passage you have quoted is Tertullian's extremely concise summary of what these Scriptures teach about God's ultimate plan, specifically concerning the end of the age and the final judgment. It functions as a mini-creed, laying out the core tenets of Christian eschatology (the doctrine of the "last things").

3. Theological Significance:
This short passage is remarkably dense with foundational Christian doctrine:

    Universal Judgment: The phrase judicaturus sit ("is to judge") establishes the certainty of a final, divine judgment at the end of the age (prodacto aevo isto).

    Two Eternal Destinies: It presents a clear and stark contrast between the fates of the faithful and the unfaithful.

        The "worshippers" (cultores) receive the "recompense of eternal life" (vitae aeternae retributionem).

        The "profane" or "wicked" (profanos) are destined for "a fire equally perpetual and unceasing" (ignem aeque perpetem et jugem). The word jugem (from which we get "subjugate") implies a constant, unbroken state.

    Universal Resurrection of the Body: This is a crucial point. suscitatis omnibus ab initio defunctis ("all the dead from the beginning having been raised up"). He stresses that this resurrection is for everyone, not just believers.

    Transformation of the Resurrected Body: The participles reformatis et recensitis ("having been reformed and renewed/re-examined") are very significant. This is not a mere reanimation of a corpse, but a transformation of the body, preparing it for its final state.

    Justice According to Works: The final phrase, ad utriusque meriti dispunctionem, is pure legalistic Tertullian. It means "for the settling of the account of each one's merit." Dispunctionem is a technical term for auditing or balancing accounts. It affirms that the judgment will be based on the life a person has lived.

4. Tertullian's Style:
As a trained Roman lawyer, Tertullian's Latin is famous for being forceful, concise, and often legally phrased. This passage is a perfect example. It is structured like a legal pronouncement, laying out the terms of God's final judgment with precision and authority.

en: In former times the Jews enjoyed much of God's favor, when the fathers of their race were noted for their righteousness and faith. So it was that as a people they flourished greatly, and their kingdom attained a lofty eminence; and so highly blessed were they, that for their instruction God spoke to them in special revelations, pointing out to them beforehand how they should merit his favor and avoid his displeasure [Apology 21 (A.D. 197)].

Context within the Apology

    The Author and Work: Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a brilliant and fiery Christian writer from Carthage (in modern-day Tunisia). The Apology is his most famous work, a legal and philosophical defense of Christianity addressed to Roman magistrates. Its goal is to refute the wild accusations against Christians and argue that their persecution is unjust and irrational.

    The Argument of Chapter 21: This chapter addresses a key intellectual problem for early Christianity. How could Christians claim their faith was the ultimate truth, rooted in ancient prophecy, when their religion was known to be new (originating under the Emperor Tiberius)? To a Roman mind, which deeply valued antiquity (mos maiorum), newness was a sign of illegitimacy.

    The Role of Your Quote: Your quote is the crucial first step in Tertullian's brilliant two-part argument to solve this problem:

        Establish the Legitimacy of the Source (Your Quote): Tertullian begins not by attacking Judaism, but by affirming its past glory and divine origin. He acknowledges that the Jews were once God's chosen people, blessed with divine revelations and a lofty kingdom because of the faith of their patriarchs. This establishes the Jewish scriptures—the source of Christian prophecy—as ancient, venerable, and divinely inspired.

        Explain the Transfer of Divine Favor: Immediately after your quote, Tertullian explains that the Jews, through their own failings, lost this favor. He points to their current state—dispersed, exiled, and without a king (Dispersi, palabundi... extorres)—as proof of divine judgment. He argues that their own prophets had foretold this fall and had also predicted that God would then choose a new, more faithful people from all the nations of the world.

Conclusion: This quote is not just a historical observation. It is a masterful rhetorical move. By first praising the former glory of the Jews, Tertullian establishes the ancient authority of the very scriptures that he will then use to prove that Christianity is the prophesied fulfillment of God's plan, thus solving the problem of Christianity's "newness."

en: [T]hen the whole human race shall be raised again, to have its dues meted out according to what it merited in the period of good or evil, and then to have these paid out through the immeasurable ages of eternity. After this there is neither death nor repeated resurrections, but we shall be the same that we are now, and still unchanged the servants of God, ever with God, clothed with the proper substance of eternity; but the profane, and all who are not true worshippers of God, shall be consigned to the punishment of everlasting fire-that fire that, from its very nature, directly ministers to their incorruptibility [ibid., 48].
latin: ...tunc restituetur omne humanum genus, ad expungendum quod in isto aevo boni seu mali meruit, et exin dependendum in immensam aeternitatis perpetuitatem. Ideoque nec mors jam, nec rursus ac rursus resurrectio, sed erimus iidem qui nunc, nec alii post: Dei quidem cultores apud Deum semper, superinduti substantia propria aeternitatis; profani vero et qui non integri ad Deum, in poena aeque jugis ignis, habentis ex ipsa natura ejus, divinam scilicet subministrationem incorruptibilitatis.

    Work: Apologeticum (often translated as The Apology). This is Tertullian's masterpiece and one of the most important works of early Christian apologetics.

    Author and Date: Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD). He wrote the Apologeticum around A.D. 197 in Carthage (modern-day Tunisia). This text is a very early, pre-Nicene witness to foundational Christian beliefs.

    Context: The Apologeticum is a brilliant legal and philosophical defense of Christianity addressed to the Roman governors of the empire. Chapter 48 is part of the work's climax, where Tertullian contrasts the pagan belief in reincarnation (which he mocks) with the Christian doctrine of a final, bodily resurrection for judgment.

    Theological Significance of the Passage: This quote is a concise and powerful summary of early Christian eschatology, outlining several key doctrines:

        General Resurrection: "tunc restituetur omne humanum genus" (then the whole human race shall be restored). It is a universal event for all people.

        Final Judgment: The resurrection is for the purpose of judgment based on one's earthly life ("quod... boni seu mali meruit" - what one has merited of good or evil).

        Bodily Resurrection & Personal Identity: "erimus iidem qui nunc" (we shall be the same ones that we are now). This is a direct refutation of reincarnation. Christians believe we will be resurrected as ourselves, not as some other being.

        Two Eternal Destinies: The passage clearly defines two final states: the righteous are "apud Deum semper" (ever with God), clothed in an eternal substance; the wicked are in "poena aeque jugis ignis" (the punishment of an equally perpetual fire).

        The Paradoxical Nature of Hellfire: This is a famously "Tertullian" point. The fire of hell does not consume or annihilate the wicked. Instead, by its divine nature, it miraculously preserves them ("subministrationem incorruptibilitatis" - a supplying of incorruptibility). It makes them indestructible so that their punishment can be eternal. This is a sharp, paradoxical argument that Tertullian, a trained lawyer, uses to great rhetorical effect.

en: Come now, if some philosopher affirms, as Laberius holds, following an opinion of Pythagoras, that a man may have his origin from a mule, a serpent from a woman, and with skill of speech twists every argument to prove his view, will he not gain acceptance for it [among the pagans], and work in some conviction that, on account of this, they should abstain from eating animal food? May anyone be persuaded that he should abstain, lest by chance in his beef he eats an ancestor of his? But if Christian promises the return of a man from a man. and the actual Gaius [resurrected] from Gaius they will not grant him a hearing. If there is any ground for the moving to and fro of human souls into different bodies, why may they not return to the very one they have left? [Apology 48 (A.D. 197)].

At enim christianus, si de homine hominem ipsumque de Caio Caium reducem repromittat, statim illic vesica queritur, lapidibus magis, nec saltem caestibus a populo exigetur. Additional Relevant Details

This passage is a brilliant example of Tertullian's legal training, rhetorical skill, and fiery sarcasm. Here are some key details about it:

1. Author and Work:

    Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160 – c. 220 AD): Often called the "Father of Latin Christianity," he was a prolific and fiercely intelligent writer from North Africa. Trained as a lawyer in Rome, his writing is polemical, logical, and packed with legal and rhetorical devices.

    The Apology (c. 197 AD): This is Tertullian's masterpiece. It is structured as a legal defense of Christianity addressed to Roman magistrates. He refutes the common slanders against Christians (atheism, cannibalism, incest) and argues that Christianity is not only harmless but philosophically superior and morally beneficial to the Roman Empire.

2. Context of the Argument (Rhetorical Strategy):

    Tertullian is using a classic a fortiori argument (literally, "from the stronger"). His point is: "If you pagans can believe the more ridiculous thing, why is it so impossible for you to believe the less ridiculous and more logical thing?"

    He contrasts the pagan philosophical doctrine of Metempsychosis (the transmigration of souls into different bodies, including animals) with the Christian doctrine of the Resurrection of the Flesh (resurrectio carnis).

    His sarcastic example of a philosopher persuading people not to eat beef "lest by chance he eats an ancestor of his" is designed to show how absurd, yet socially acceptable, pagan philosophy could be.

3. Key Concepts and Terms:

    Pythagoras and Laberius: Tertullian names his sources to show he is well-read in pagan philosophy. Pythagoras (6th century BC) was famously associated with the doctrine of reincarnation. Laberius was a Roman writer of mimes.

    "Gaius from Gaius" (de Caio Caium): This is Tertullian's brilliant, concise summary of the Christian doctrine. "Gaius" was a very common Roman praenomen (like "John Doe"). The phrase powerfully emphasizes personal, individual resurrection. It is not just a human body that is restored, but the very same body that belonged to the very same person. This specificity was central to Christian teaching and stood in stark contrast to the vague soul-wandering of metempsychosis.

    "They will not grant him a hearing": The Latin is more violent. Tertullian says a Christian making this promise will be attacked with stones (lapidibus... exigetur), showing the visceral, prejudiced rejection Christians faced, while philosophers were listened to respectfully.

4. Theological Significance:

    This passage is a cornerstone of early Latin theology on the resurrection. It defends the idea that the very same flesh which died will be raised for judgment.

    The rest of Chapter 48 (which you provided) goes on to argue that God, who created man from nothing, can certainly re-create man from his dissolved remains. He uses analogies from nature—the daily "resurrection" of the sun, the seasons, and seeds—to make his case.

    The core reason for the resurrection of the same body is divine judgment. As Tertullian states later in the chapter: "the same person who had existed will of necessity be presented, in order to receive from God the judgment for his good or contrary deserts." The soul and body sinned or did good works together, so they must be judged together.

en: Happy is our sacrament of water, in that, by washing away the sins of our early blindness, we are set free and admitted into eternal life. [But] a viper of the Cainite heresy, lately conversant in this quarter, has carried away a great number with her most venomous doctrine, making it her first aim to destroy baptism. This iS in accordance with nature: for vipers and asps themselves generally live in arid and waterless places. But we, little fishes after the example of our [great] fish, Jesus Christ, are born in water, have safety in no other way than by permanently abiding in water; so that most monstrous creature, who had no right to teach even sound doctrine, knew full well how to kill the little fishes, by taking them away from the water! [Baptism (c. A.D. 203)].

This opening chapter is packed with theological imagery and historical context.

    The Work and Author: This is the opening of De Baptismo, the earliest known treatise dedicated entirely to the sacrament of baptism. It was written by Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. A.D. 155 – c. 220), a brilliant and fiery apologist from Carthage, often called the "father of Latin Christianity."

    The "Viper" and the Cainite Heresy: Tertullian wrote this work to combat a specific threat. The "viper" (vipera) he mentions was a female teacher of the Cainite heresy. The Cainites were a Gnostic sect who, like many Gnostics, held a dualistic worldview: they believed the material world was evil and created by an inferior deity (the Demiurge, often identified with the God of the Old Testament). Consequently, they rejected material sacraments like baptism that used "evil" matter (water). Tertullian’s metaphor is sharp: just as real vipers thrive in dry, waterless places, this spiritual viper preaches a doctrine that despises the life-giving water of baptism.

    The Fish (ΙΧΘΥΣ) Symbolism: This is one of the most famous and beautiful uses of early Christian symbolism. Tertullian makes a profound theological pun.

        He refers to Jesus Christ as our ἰχθὺν (ichthun), the Greek word for "fish."

        This was a direct reference to the famous acrostic ΙΧΘΥΣ (Ichthys), a secret symbol for early Christians:

            Ι (Iota): Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous) — Jesus

            Χ (Chi): Χριστός (Christos) — Christ

            Θ (Theta): Θεοῦ (Theou) — of God

            Υ (Upsilon): Υἱός (Huios) — Son

            Σ (Sigma): Σωτήρ (Sōtēr) — Savior

        His point is theological: If Christ is the great Fish (ΙΧΘΥΣ), then we Christians are the "little fishes" (pisciculi).

    Theology of Baptismal Regeneration: The imagery is deeply tied to the doctrine of being "born again." Tertullian declares that we "are born in water" (in aqua nascimur). For him, the baptismal font is the womb of the Church where Christians are brought to new, spiritual life. To survive, these "little fishes" must remain in the water of the Church's faith. The heretic, by denying baptism, is committing spiritual murder: she "knew full well how to kill the little fishes, by taking them away from the water."

[Baptism 1 (c. A.D. 203)].

This is one of the most famous and beautiful passages in all of early Christian literature. The details surrounding it are rich with historical and theological significance.

    The Author and the Work: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160 – c. 225 AD) was a brilliant and fiery North African writer, often called the "Father of Latin Christianity." His work De Baptismo is the earliest surviving complete treatise on the sacrament of baptism, making it a document of immense historical importance.

    The Heretic ("The Viper"): Tertullian identifies the heretical teacher as a "viper of the Cainite heresy" (de caina haeresi vipera). The Cainites were a Gnostic sect who held a radical theology. They believed the God of the Old Testament was an evil, lesser creator (the Demiurge) and that figures he condemned—like Cain, Esau, and the people of Sodom—were actually spiritual heroes who possessed secret knowledge (gnosis). As a Gnostic group, they typically rejected the material world and, therefore, material sacraments like baptism with physical water. This is why Tertullian says her primary aim was to "destroy baptism"—it was central to her anti-material theology.

    The Christological Symbol of the Fish (ΙΧΘΥΣ): This is the most brilliant part of the passage.

        Tertullian calls Jesus our "ἰχθὺν" (ichthyn), using the actual Greek word for "fish." This is a direct reference to one of the earliest and most profound Christian symbols.

        ΙΧΘΥΣ (Ichthys) is a Greek acrostic, a "word puzzle" where each letter stands for another word:

            Ι (Iota) = Iesous (Jesus)

            Χ (Chi) = Christos (Christ)

            Θ (Theta) = Theou (of God)

            Υ (Upsilon) = Huios (Son)

            Σ (Sigma) = Soter (Savior)

        Together, the acrostic spells out the core Christian creed: "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior." This symbol was used as a secret sign among persecuted Christians.

    The Power of the Imagery: Tertullian creates a masterful and powerful allegory:

        Jesus is the great Fish (Ichthys).

        We Christians are the "little fishes" (pisciculi).

        We are "born in water" (in aqua nascimur), a direct reference to the waters of baptism and the concept of being "born again."

        Our spiritual safety and life depend on "permanently abiding in water" (in aqua permanendo salvi sumus), meaning remaining in the grace of our baptism.

        The heretic, by contrast, is a viper, a creature of the dry, waterless desert—the antithesis of the life-giving water. Her "venomous doctrine" kills the little fishes precisely by "taking them away from the water"—that is, by convincing them to abandon the sacrament of baptism.

This single paragraph is a perfect fusion of polemic, theology, and poetic imagery, powerfully defending the necessity of baptism against its Gnostic detractors.
