greek: Τότε θεάσῃ τυγχάνων ἐπὶ γῆς, ὅτι Θεὸς ἐν οὐρανοῖς πολιτεύεται· τότε μυστήρια Θεοῦ λαλεῖν ἄρξῃ· τότε τοὺς κολαζομένους ἐπὶ τῷ μὴ θέλειν ἀρνήσασθαι Θεὸν, καὶ ἀγαπήσεις καὶ θαυμάσεις· τότε τῆς ἀπάτης τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τῆς πλάνης καταγνώσῃ, ὅταν τὸ ἀληθῶς ἐν οὐρανῷ ζῆν ἐπιγνῷς· ὅταν τοῦ δοκοῦντος ἐνθάδε θανάτου καταφρονήσῃς, ὅταν τὸν ὄντως θάνατον φοβηθῇς, ὃς φυλάσσεται τοῖς κατακριθησομένοις εἰς πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον, ὃ τοὺς παραδοθέντας αὐτῷ μέχρι τέλους κολάσει. Τότε τοὺς ὑπομένοντας ὑπὲρ δικαιοσύνης θαυμάσεις τὸ πῦρ τὸ πρόσκαιρον, καὶ μακαρίσεις, ὅταν ἐκεῖνο τὸ πῦρ ἐπιγνῷς.
context:
Additional Details and Context

    Work: Epistle to Diognetus (Greek: Πρὸς Διόγνητον Ἐπιστολή).

    Author: Anonymous. The author is unknown, though various figures from the early Church have been suggested. He was clearly a highly educated and eloquent writer.

    Date: The date is uncertain, but it is generally placed in the 2nd century (c. A.D. 130–200), making it a precious example of early Christian apologetics. Your date of c. A.D. 160 is a very reasonable estimate.

    Original Language: The epistle was written in elegant, classical Greek. The Latin version you provided is a standard early translation.

    Context of the Quote: Chapter 10 is the climax of the epistle's argument. After explaining who Christians are (Chapter 5-6) and the divine origin of their faith (Chapter 7-8), the author describes the profound benefits of accepting this faith. The chapter begins by explaining that faith leads to an imitation of God's own goodness (imitatio Dei). The passage you selected is the powerful conclusion, describing the radical shift in perception that this new life brings: the believer begins to see earthly life from a heavenly perspective.

    Theological Significance: This passage is rich with early Christian themes:

        Realized Eschatology: The believer begins to experience the realities of heaven ("you will see, while still on earth...").

        Veneration of Martyrs: It shows a deep love and admiration for those who suffer for their faith, seeing their temporary suffering in light of eternal realities.

        The Two Deaths: It makes a sharp distinction between physical death, which is now despised, and true, spiritual death (eternal fire), which is to be feared.

    Unique Manuscript History: This is one of the most fascinating aspects of this text. The Epistle to Diognetus survived into the modern era in a single 13th-century manuscript. Tragically, this sole manuscript was destroyed during the Franco-Prussian War when the municipal library of Strasbourg, where it was housed, was shelled and burned in 1870. All modern editions of the text are based on copies made by scholars before the original was lost.

en: TO DIOGNETUS [The Father] sent the Word, that he might be manifested to the world. . This is he who was from the beginning, who appeared as if new, and was found old. This is he who, being from everlasting, is today called the Son [ To Diognetus 11 C. A.D. 160) emphasis added].
latin: Cujus rei gratia sermonem misit, ut a mundo conspiceretur... Hic ab initio erat, qui novus apparuit, et vetus inventus... Hic qui semper, hodie Filius habitus.
greek: Οὗ χάριν ἀπέστειλε λόγον, ἵνα κόσμῳ φανῇ... Οὗτος ὁ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, ὁ καινὸς φανείς, καὶ παλαιὸς εὑρεθείς... Οὗτος ὁ ἀεὶ, σήμερον Υἱὸς λογισθείς.
context:
Additional Details and Context

    The Work: The Epistle to Diognetus is an anonymous masterpiece of early Christian apologetics, likely written in the mid-to-late 2nd century (c. A.D. 150-180). It is highly regarded for its elegant Greek prose and profound theological insights.

    The Manuscript and the Missing Word "Old": This is a crucial detail. The single surviving Greek manuscript for this text was destroyed in a fire in 1870. In that manuscript, there was a gap, or lacuna, in the text. The Greek text literally read: ...ὁ καινὸς φανείς, καὶ . . . εὑρεθείς... (...who appeared new, and ... was found...). The word for "old" (παλαιός) is a famous and universally accepted scholarly emendation (a proposed correction) first suggested by the 16th-century scholar Henri Estienne (Stephanus). It is accepted because it creates a beautiful and theologically rich paradox ("new yet old") that is perfectly in keeping with the author's style. The Latin translation (vetus) reflects this emendation.

    Key Theological Concepts:

        Pre-existence of the Word: The phrases "from the beginning" (ἀπ' ἀρχῆς) and "He who is everlasting" (ὁ ἀεὶ) are powerful affirmations of the Son's eternal existence before his incarnation, echoing the prologue of John's Gospel.

        Paradoxical Revelation: The author loves paradox. The eternal Word "appeared new" in the Incarnation, yet he is "found old" because he is the ancient, pre-existent Creator. This theme of newness and timelessness is central to the chapter.

        "Today Called the Son": The phrase σήμερον Υἱὸς λογισθείς ("today reckoned/regarded as Son") does not imply that he only became the Son at a certain point in time. Rather, it signifies that his eternal Sonship is manifested and proclaimed in time within the history of salvation. It is a clear allusion to Psalm 2:7 ("You are my Son; today I have begotten you"), a foundational text for early Christian understanding of Jesus's divine identity.

en: TO DIOGNETUS Then the fear of the Law is chanted, and the grace of the prophets is known, and the faith of the Gospels is established, and the Tradition of the apostles IS preserved, and the grace of the Church exults [To Diognetus 11 (C. A.D. 160)].
latin: Deinde metus legis decantatur, et prophetarum gratia cognoscitur, et Evangeliorum fides stabilitur, et apostolorum traditio custoditur, et Ecclesia gratia exsultat.
greek: Εἶτα φόβος νόμου ᾄδεται, καὶ προφητῶν χάρις γινώσκεται, καὶ Εὐαγγελίων πίστις ἵδρυται, καὶ ἀποστόλων παράδοσις φυλάσσεται, καὶ Ἐκκλησίας χάρις σκιρτᾷ.
context:
Additional Relevant Details

    Work and Author: The Epistle to Diognetus is a celebrated work of early Christian apologetics. The author is anonymous, though he describes himself as a "disciple of the Apostles." The date you provided (c. A.D. 160) is a common scholarly estimate, placing it firmly in the 2nd century among the works of the Apostolic Fathers.

    Original Language: The original language of the epistle is Greek. The Latin text you have is a standard, ancient translation.

    Context of the Quote: This beautiful sentence comes at the climax of Chapter 11. The author has just described how the eternal Word (Logos), who appeared new in the world, enriches the Church and expands grace in the saints. The quote is a magnificent, five-part summary of the harmonious elements that constitute the life and understanding of the Church.

    Theological Significance: The quote provides a powerful snapshot of 2nd-century Christian self-understanding:

        φόβος νόμου ᾄδεται (fear of the Law is chanted): This shows the Old Testament Law is not discarded but is understood with reverence ("fear") and integrated into the Church's life, likely through liturgical reading ("chanted").

        προφητῶν χάρις γινώσκεται (grace of the prophets is known): The prophecies of the Old Testament are now understood in their true light, as a gift ("grace") pointing to Christ.

        Εὐαγγελίων πίστις ἵδρυται (faith of the Gospels is established): The apostolic accounts of Jesus are the firm foundation of Christian belief.

        ἀποστόλων παράδοσις φυλάσσεται (Tradition of the apostles is preserved): This is a key phrase. Παράδοσις (Gr.) / Traditio (Lat.) refers to the authoritative body of teaching "handed down" from the Apostles. Its preservation is seen as essential to the Church's identity.

        Ἐκκλησίας χάρις σκιρτᾷ (grace of the Church exults): The result of this harmony is a dynamic, living community. The Greek verb σκιρτᾷ (skirta) is particularly vibrant; it means "to leap" or "bound," famously used to describe John the Baptist leaping in his mother's womb (Luke 1:41). It conveys a sense of exultant, active joy.

en: TREATISE ON RE-BAPTISM [Ut has been asked among the brethren what course ought specially to be adopted towards the persons of those who baptized in heresy and subsequently departing from their heresy, and fleeing as supplicants to the Church of God, should repent with their whole hearts, and only now perceiving the condemnation of their error, implore from the Church the help of salvation. .. . [A]ccording to the most ancient custom and ecclesiastical tradition, it would suffice, after that baptism that they have received outside the Church . . that only hands should be laid upon them by the bishop for their reception of the Holy Spirit, and this imposition of hands would afford them the renewed and perfected seal of faith [Treatise on Re-Baptism (C. A.D. 257)].
latin: Animadverto quaesitum apud fratres quid potius observari oportet in personam eorum qui in haeresi quidem... sint tincti; postmodum inde digressi, et suppliciter ad Ecclesiam Dei advolantes, totis praecordiis poenitentiam agerent; et erroris sui damnationem nunc demum intelligentes auxilium salutis ab ea implorarent;     ...utrum vetustissima consuetudine ac traditione ecclesiastica, post illum quod foris quidem... accceperuut Baptisma, tantummodo imponi eis manum ab episcopo ad accipiendum Spiritum sanctum sufficeret, et haec manus impositio signum fidei iteratum atque consummatum... eis praestaret:
context:
Context: What the Rest of Your Latin Text Says

The portion of your Latin text that follows the quote you were looking for is the author setting up the entire debate. He explains:

    The Alternative Position: He contrasts the ancient tradition with the other view being debated: an vero etiam iteratum Baptisma his necessarium esset — "or whether, on the other hand, a repeated Baptism would be necessary for them."

    The Author's Frustration: He immediately shows his own position. He states that this "new question" (nova quaestione) would never have arisen if everyone had just contented themselves with the "venerable authority of all the Churches" (venerabili Ecclesiarum omnium auctoritate) and practiced humility.

    Condemnation of Innovation: He strongly condemns those who are challenging the ancient custom, accusing them of disrupting the peace of the Church and acting out of pride and a desire for "empty glory." He even says they are bringing shame upon Mother Church.

    The Plan for the Treatise: He concludes by stating his purpose: to gather all the relevant passages from Holy Scripture (quaecumque sanctarum Scripturarum... capitula... congeremus) to demonstrate the "most healthy and peaceful custom" (consuetudinem saluberrimam atque pacificam) to all the brethren.

en: [Bly imposition of the bishop's hands the Holy Spirit is given to everyone who believes, as in the case of the Samaritans, after Philip's baptism, the apostles did to them by laying on of hands [Acts 8:14-177: in this same way they conferred on them the Holy Spirit [ibid., 3].
latin: Nam cum per manus impositionem episcopi datur unicuique credenti Spiritus sanctus, sicut Apostoli circa Samaritanos post Philippi Baptisma manum eis imponendo fecerunt, et hac ratione Spiritum sanctum in eos contulerunt...
context:
Additional Context from Your Provided Text

The full passage you posted is a brilliant piece of theological reasoning. Here is the flow of the argument:

    The Opponent's Position: The author begins by imagining an opponent (representing the Cyprianic view) quoting Jesus in John 3:5: "Nisi quis denuo natus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum coelorum" ("Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven"). The opponent uses this to argue that water baptism and the reception of the Holy Spirit are an inseparable package.

    The Author's Agreement (with a twist): The author then says, "No one among us is so insane or stubborn as to dare contradict this." He agrees that, ideally and in the normal practice of the Church (rebus integris), this is true.

    The Crucial Distinction: Then he makes his key point: "But if in the New Testament we find that these things... are sometimes found in a way divided and separated (divisa ac separata)... let us see if they can sometimes stand alone."

    The Prime Example (Your Quote): He then presents his "Exhibit A" for this separation: the case of the Samaritans in Acts 8. They received water baptism from Philip but did not receive the Holy Spirit until Peter and John came and laid hands on them. This, for the author, is the scriptural proof that the gift of the Spirit (conferred by a bishop's hands) can be separated from, and can complete, an earlier water baptism.

en: TREATISE ON RE-BAPTISM [O]utside the Church there is no Holy Spirit. Sound faith moreover cannot exist, not only among heretics, but even among those who are established in schism [Treatise on Re-Baptism 10 (c. A.D. 257)].
latin: ...si vero ab alienis traditum fuerit, ut potest hoc negotium et ut admittit, corrigatur: quia Spiritus sanctus extra Ecclesiam non sit, fides quoque non solum apud haereticos, verum etiam apud eos qui in schismate constituti sunt sana esse non possit. Idcircoque poenitentiam agentibus...
context:
Context of the Passage

This is a fascinating and historically important text. The anonymous author of the Treatise on Re-Baptism is arguing for a position that differs from that of St. Cyprian of Carthage.

    The Problem: Someone has been baptized with water in the name of Jesus, but by a heretic or a schismatic. What should the Catholic Church do when that person wants to become a member?

    St. Cyprian's Position: All sacraments outside the true Church are invalid. Therefore, the person must be completely re-baptized.

    The Author's Position (in your text): The author argues for a middle way. He says the invocation of Jesus' name is a powerful act that should not be repeated. However, he agrees that the Holy Spirit is missing from the heretical baptism.

    The Solution: Therefore, the person should not be re-baptized with water. Instead, the Church should "supply" what was missing by having a bishop lay hands on the person to confer the Holy Spirit.

The sentence you found is the author's theological justification for this practice: The reason we need to lay on hands is precisely because "outside the Church there is no Holy Spirit," and therefore a "sound faith" could not have been present in the original schismatic ceremony.

en: ST. VICTORINUS OF PETTAU God produced that entire mass for the adornment of his majesty in six days; on the seventh he consecrated it with a blessing [ Creation of the World (c. A.D. 270)].
latin: COGITANTI mihi, una cum animo meo conferenti, de fabrica mundi istius, in quo clausi tenemur, etiam velocitas fabricae istius haec est; sicut in libro Moysis continetur, quem de conditione ipsius scripsit, qui Genesis appellatur. **Totam molem istam, Deus sex diebus in ornamento majestatis suae expressit, septimo quibus benedictione . . . consecravit.** Idcirco igitur, quoniam septenario numero dierum...
context:
Context and Significance

This sentence serves as the thesis statement for the entire short treatise, De Fabrica Mundi (On the Creation of the World).

    Location: As the opening declaration, it sets the theme. Victorinus immediately establishes the framework of the seven days of creation as his starting point.

    Numerology: The rest of the treatise is a fascinating and highly symbolic exploration of numbers, especially the numbers seven, four, and twelve. He uses this opening statement about the seven days to launch into a discussion of how these key numbers structure not only creation but all of salvation history (e.g., the four Gospels, the four rivers of Paradise, the seven spirits of God, the twelve apostles, the twenty-four elders).

en: ST. VICTORINUS OF PETTAU This sixth day [Friday] is called parasceve, that IS to say, the preparation of the kingdom. For he perfected Adam, whom he made after his image and likeness. But for this reason he completed his works before he created angels and fashioned man, lest they should falsely assert that they had been his helpers. On this day also, on account of the Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, we make either a station to God, or a fast. On the seventh day he rested from all his works, and blessed it, and sanctified it. On the former day we are accustomed to fast rigorously, that on the Lord's Day we may go forth to our bread with thanksgiving. And let the parasceve become a rigorous fast, lest we should appear to observe any Sabbath with the Jews, which Christ himself, the Lord of the Sabbath, says by his prophets that "his soul hates" [Is 1:13-14]; which Sabbath he in his body abolished [Creation of the World (A.D. 270)].
latin: Hic dies sextus parasceve appellatur, praeparatio scilicet regni; Adam enim quem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam consummavit. Idcirco autem prius opera sua consummavit, quam angelos creavit, et hominem fabricavit, ne forte adjutores se fuisse falsa dictione asseverant. Hoc quoque die ob passionem Domini Jesu Christi aut stationem Deo, aut jejunium, facimus. Die septimo requievit ab omnibus operibus suis, et benedixit eum et sanctificavit. Hoc die solemus superponere; idcirco, ut die Dominico cum gratiarum actione ad panem exeamus. Et parasceve superpositio fiat, ne quid cum Judaeis sabbatum observare videamur, quod ipse Dominus sabbati Christus per prophetas suos odisse animam suam dicit; quod sabbato corpore suo resolvit...
context:
Context and Analysis

You've found a very important passage from one of the earliest Latin exegetes.

    Typology: Victorinus masterfully links the sixth day of Creation (the making of Adam) with the sixth day of Redemption (Christ's Passion on Good Friday). For him, Friday (Parasceve, "Preparation") is a day of perfecting and preparing.

    Early Christian Practice: The text is a priceless witness to Christian worship in the 3rd century. It clearly describes the practice of fasting on Friday in memory of the Passion.

    The "Superpositio": This was a technical term for a "rigorous fast." It meant extending the Friday fast through all of Saturday, breaking it only at the Sunday liturgy. This practice was specifically designed to distinguish the Christian observance from the Jewish Sabbath, which was a day of feasting and rest. Victorinus's explicit statement—ne quid cum Judaeis sabbatum observare videamur ("lest we should appear to observe any Sabbath with the Jews")—is a powerful statement of developing Christian identity.

    Lord of the Sabbath: He reinforces this distinction by quoting the Old Testament prophets (Isaiah 1:13-14) to show that God Himself was displeased with mere formal observance, and then stating that Christ, as "Lord of the Sabbath," fulfilled and "abolished" its old requirements in his own body.

en: ST. VINCENT OF LERINS I have often then inquired earnestly and attentively of very many men eminent for sanctity and learning, how and by what sure and universal rule may be able to distinguish the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity; and I have always, and in almost every instance, received an answer to this effect: That whether I or anyone else should wish to detect the frauds and avoid the snares of heretics as they rise, and to continue sound and complete in the Catholic faith, we must, the Lord helping, fortify our own belief in two ways: first, by the authority of the divine law, and then, by the Tradition of the Catholic Church. But here someone perhaps will ask, "Since the canon of Scripture is complete, and sufficient of itself for everything, and more than sufficient, what need is there to join with it the authority of the Church's interpretation?" For this reason-because, owing to the depth of Holy Scripture, all do not accept it in one and the same sense, but one understands its words in one way, another in another; so that seems to be capable of as many interpretations as there are interpreters. For Novatian expounds it one way, Sabellius another, Donatus another, Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, another, Photinus, Apollinarius, Priscillian, another, lovinian, Pelagius, Celestius, another, and lastly, Nestorius, another. Therefore, it is very necessary, on account of so great intricacies of such various error, that the rule for the right understanding of the prophets and apostles should be framed in accordance with the standard of ecclesiastical and Catholic interpretation. Moreover, in the Catholic Church itself, all possible care must be taken, that we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. For that is truly and in the strictest sense Catholic, which, as the name itself and the reason of the thing declare, comprehends all universally [Notebooks 2:4-6 (c. A.D. 434)].
latin:
Saepe igitur magno studio et summa attentione perquirens a quamplurimis sanctitate et doctrina praestantibus viris quonam modo possim certa quadam et quasi generali ac regulari via catholicae fidei veritatem ab haereticae pravitatis falsitate discernere, hujusmodi semper responsum ab omnibus fere retuli, quod sive ego, sive quis alius vellet exsurgentium haereticorum fraudes deprehendere laqueosque vitare, et in fide sana sanus atque integer permanere, duplici modo munire fidem suam, Domino adjuvante, deberet: primùm scilicet divinae legis auctoritate, tum deinde Ecclesiae catholicae traditione.

    Hic forsitan requirat aliquis: Cum sit perfectus Scripturarum Canon, sibique ad omnia satis superque sufficiat, quid opus est ut ei Ecclesiasticae intelligentiae jungatur auctoritas? Quia videlicet Scripturam sacram pro ipsa sua altitudine non uno eodemque sensu universi accipiunt, sed ejusdem eloquia aliter atque aliter alius atque alius interpretatur; ut pene quot homines sunt, tot illinc sententiae erui posse videantur. Aliter namque illam Novatianus, aliter Sabellius, aliter Donatus exponit, aliter Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius; aliter Photinus, Apollinaris, Priscillianus, aliter Jovinianus, Pelagius, Caelestius; aliter postremo Nestorius. Atque idcirco multùm necesse est, propter tantos tam varii erroris anfractus, ut propheticae et apostolicae interpretationis linea secundum Ecclesiastici et Catholici sensus normam dirigatur.

    In ipsa item Catholica Ecclesia magnopere curandum est ut id teneamus quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est. Hoc est etenim vere proprieque catholicum, quod ipsa vis nominis ratioque declarat, quae omnia fere universaliter comprehendit.
context:
Additional Detail and Context
Author and Work

St. Vincent was a fifth-century monk and priest who lived in the renowned monastery on the island of Lérins (off the southern coast of modern-day France). He wrote the Commonitorium (meaning "Memorandum" or "Notebooks") around the year 434, under the pseudonym "Peregrinus" (pilgrim). Its purpose was to create a practical, reliable guide for distinguishing authentic Christian doctrine from heresy.
Historical Context

St. Vincent was writing in a period of intense theological turmoil.

    The Council of Ephesus (431) had just condemned Nestorius for his teachings on the nature of Christ.

    Debates were raging over the complex teachings of St. Augustine on grace and predestination, which had arisen in response to the Pelagian heresy.

    Older heresies like Arianism were still a recent and painful memory.

Vincent saw "novelties" cropping up everywhere. His goal was not to innovate but to establish a clear, conservative principle for preserving the faith that had been handed down from the apostles.
Breakdown of the Argument

This famous passage contains a three-step argument that is both brilliant and foundational for Catholic and Orthodox theology.

    The Twofold Rule: Vincent establishes that a Catholic must fortify their faith with two sources of authority: Scripture (divinae legis auctoritate) and Tradition (Ecclesiae catholicae traditione). This immediately sets him against any notion that Scripture can be interpreted in a vacuum.

    The Problem of Interpretation: He masterfully anticipates the objection: "Isn't Scripture sufficient on its own?" His answer is a resounding "no," not because Scripture is flawed, but because its depth allows for it to be twisted. He proves his point by listing a "rogue's gallery" of heretics—from Arius to his contemporary, Nestorius—who all used Scripture to justify their errors. Therefore, Scripture requires an authoritative interpretive key.

    The Vincentian Canon: This leads to his most celebrated formulation—the threefold test for identifying authentic Catholic Tradition. The true faith is that which has been believed:

        Everywhere (quod ubique) - This is the test of Universality or Ecumenicity.

        Always (quod semper) - This is the test of Antiquity or Apostolicity.

        By All (quod ab omnibus) - This is the test of Consent or Consensus.

This principle, often called the "Vincentian Canon," became the gold standard for theological orthodoxy. A doctrine is not an innovation if it can be shown to have been held by the whole Church, from the earliest times, with the universal consent of the Church Fathers.
Legacy and Enduring Influence

This passage is one of the most quoted texts from the patristic era because of its clarity and utility.

    It was highly influential during the Counter-Reformation, as the Council of Trent reaffirmed the dual authority of Scripture and Tradition against the Protestant principle of sola Scriptura.

    It perfectly encapsulates the Orthodox Church's understanding of Holy Tradition as the proper context for interpreting Scripture.

    It was famously adopted by Anglican theologians (most notably John Henry Newman before his conversion to Catholicism) as a pillar of the via media (the "middle way"), which sought a path between Roman Catholicism and Protestantism based on the faith of the ancient, undivided Church.

en: ST. VINCENT OF LERINS Nestorius, whose disease iS of an opposite kind, while pretending that he holds two distinct substances in Christ, brings in of a sudden two Persons, and with unheard of wickedness would have two sons of God, two Christs one God, the other man, one begotten of his Father, the other, born of his Mother. For which reason he maintains that St. Mary ought to be called not Theotokos the Mother of God], but Christotokos [the Mother of Christ], seeing that she gave birth not to the Christ who is God, but to the Christ who is man [Notebooks 12:35 C. A.D 434)].
latin: Nestorius autem contrario Apollinari morbo, dum sese duas in Christo substantias distinguere simulat, duas introducit repente personas, et inaudito scelere duos esse vult filios Dei, duos Christos, unum Deum, alterum hominem, unum qui ex Patre, alterum qui sit generatus ex matre. Atque ideo asserit sanctam Mariam non Theotocon, sed Christotocon esse dicendam: quia scilicet ex ea non ille Christus qui Deus, sed ille qui erat homo, natus sit.
context:
Additional Detail and Context
The "Rogues' Gallery" of Heretics

In this section of the Commonitorium, St. Vincent is providing concrete examples to illustrate his main thesis. He has just explained that even great teachers can fall into error, and that God allows this to "test" the faith of the Church. To demonstrate this, he briefly outlines the errors of three major heretics: Photinus, Apollinaris, and Nestorius. His summary of their teachings is a masterclass in precision and clarity.
The Heresy of Apollinaris (The "Opposite Disease")

To explain the error of Nestorius, Vincent first brilliantly describes its opposite, the heresy of Apollinaris.

    Apollinaris's Error: Apollinaris taught that in the Incarnation, the divine Word (Logos) took the place of the human rational soul in Jesus. In his view, Christ had a human body and a human "animal soul," but his mind and will were purely divine.

    The Consequence: This heresy "mutilates" Christ's humanity. It results in a being who is not fully human and not fully divine, but a strange fusion or mixture of the two. Apollinaris's error was one of confusion and fusion of the natures.

The Heresy of Nestorius (A Heresy of Separation)

Vincent describes Nestorianism as the contrario morbo—the "contrary disease." If Apollinaris confused the natures, Nestorius separated them too radically.

    Nestorius's Error: Nestorius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, insisted on a sharp distinction between Christ's human nature and his divine nature. While this was orthodox in principle, he took it so far as to imply that there were not only two natures but two distinct persons in Christ: the divine Person (the Son of God) and a separate human person (the man Jesus).

    The Consequence: According to Nestorius, these two persons were united only by a moral bond or a "conjunction of wills," not in a true, single personal identity (the "hypostatic union"). Vincent powerfully summarizes this outcome as the belief in "two sons of God, two Christs." There was the eternal Son begotten of the Father, and the human son born of Mary. These were not one and the same Person.

The Crucial Distinction: Theotokos vs. Christotokos

This deep theological error had a very practical and public consequence, which became the flashpoint of the controversy: the title of the Virgin Mary.

    Theotokos (θεοτόκος): The traditional and orthodox title, meaning "God-bearer" or "Mother of God." This title affirms that the Person Mary carried in her womb and gave birth to is, in fact, God the Son. It is a direct statement about the identity of Jesus Christ: He is one divine Person with two natures.

    Christotokos (χριστοτόκος): The title Nestorius insisted upon, meaning "Christ-bearer" or "Mother of Christ." For Nestorius, this was the more accurate term because Mary gave birth only to the human person Jesus, who was the "temple" or "vehicle" for the divine Son. This title reflects his belief in two separate persons.

St. Vincent correctly identifies that this debate over Mary's title was not primarily about Marian devotion; it was the clearest possible test of one's Christology. What you call Mary reveals who you believe Jesus to be. By rejecting Theotokos, Nestorius revealed his heretical belief in two separate Christs. This heresy was formally condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431, just a few years before Vincent wrote his Commonitorium.
